articles.title: The Marker Drift Problem: Measuring LLM-Assisted Writing with Unstable Lexical Indicators
articles.authors: Serhii Nazarovets
articles.abstract: Lexical markers are increasingly used to estimate the prevalence of large language model (LLM)-assisted writing across large publication corpora. However, longitudinal applications of this approach rely on an important assumption: that the relationship between these markers and LLM use remains sufficiently stable over time. Recent research suggests that once publicly identified, individual markers may lose their diagnostic value due to adaptation by users and the evolution of language models. Furthermore, lexical markers may reflect not only LLM use, but also linguistic competence, AI-assisted editing, and broader forms of stylistic convergence. This paper introduces the Marker Drift Problem to describe a methodological challenge in which indicators change alongside the phenomenon they are intended to measure. Marker drift raises questions about temporal comparability, as observed changes in marker prevalence may reflect changes in LLM use, changes in the indicators themselves, or both. Without attention to the temporal stability and construct validity of lexical indicators, increasingly precise estimates of LLM-assisted writing may be based on unstable measurement instruments.

articles.title: Automatic Prompt Optimization for Policy Documents Classification
articles.authors: Hanif Sajid
articles.abstract: In this paper, I leverage three automatic prompt optimization (APO) algorithms to search for optimal prompts that enable large language models to classify policy documents accurately, without requiring task-specific training data. I evaluate the performance of these optimized prompts using OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini model, comparing them against prompts created by domain experts as a baseline. Experimental results show that all three algorithms significantly outperform the baseline. Among the algorithms, APE, which induces simple prompts from input-output example pairs, significantly outperforms GRIPS and performs comparably to ProTeGi. Additionally, ProTeGi demonstrates similar performance to GRIPS. However, neither the optimized prompts nor the human-designed ones achieve a research-grade performance (defined as an F1-score of 70%) with the GPT-4o-mini model. To reach research-grade performance in policy document classification using APO methods, future work could explore the use of more powerful models, hybrid APO systems, cross-model evaluations, and inference-time enhancements.

articles.title: Open Here, There and Everywhere? A Comparative Review of Open Access Definitions and Typologies in Monitoring Instruments
articles.authors: Louis Bachaud; Didier Torny
articles.abstract: Open Access (OA) monitoring has become a policy instrument for governments, institutions, and research funders globally, yet the typologies and definitions underlying OA monitors have never been systematically compared. Drawing on a global dataset of 30 OA monitors, we conduct the first systematic comparative review of their operational OA definitions and typologies. Our findings reveal dynamics of standardization, as well as enduring differences. Unpaywall/OpenAlex occupies a near-hegemonic position as metadata provider (77% of monitors), shaping classification choices across the landscape. Nevertheless, significant heterogeneity persists: monitors diverge on whether Bronze publications constitute true OA, on how to count Green OA publications, on the relevance of open licenses, and on whether economic dimensions (APCs, Diamond OA) belong in typologies at all. Only two monitors share both a common typology and identical operational criteria. These divergences pose challenges for cross-national comparability and call for greater methodological transparency in open science monitoring infrastructures.

articles.title: Crossref as a source of open bibliographic metadata
articles.authors: Nees Jan van Eck; Ludo Waltman
articles.abstract: There is a growing recognition of the importance of open availability of bibliographic metadata of scholarly publications. We present an up-to-date overview of the open availability of bibliographic metadata through the infrastructure of Crossref, focusing on six metadata elements: reference lists, abstracts, ORCIDs, author affiliations, funding information, and license information. Our analysis shows that the availability of these metadata elements has improved over time, at least for journal articles. However, the analysis also shows that many publishers need to make additional efforts to realize full openness of bibliographic metadata.

articles_hidden.title: Guidance for defining outcomes in clinical trials
articles_hidden.authors: Xiangji Ying; Tianjing Li; Joanne McKenzie; Matthew James Page; Kiran Ninan; Jean-Pierre Oberste; Colby J. Vorland; Andrew William Brown; Riaz Qureshi; Nicholas J DeVito
articles_hidden.abstract:
Defining outcomes completely before conducting clinical trials helps to mitigate reporting biases; however, there is limited guidance to help investigators define outcomes completely. We aimed to develop a structured approach for defining trial outcomes completely and consistently.
We reviewed literature, developed preliminary rules for defining outcomes, and refined them iteratively. We randomly selected randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on ClinicalTrials.gov that registered before their start dates and posted results by January 4, 2024. The 225 included RCTs evaluated 3,424 outcomes. Two raters independently applied preliminary rules to define each outcome. When raters encountered outcomes they could not define, we refined the rules. We continued this process until no further changes were needed. We discussed and finalized our approach in a consensus meeting.
We define an “outcome” as a value for each participant that will be used in analysis to generate study results. A complete outcome definition includes six elements: outcome domain, specific measurement, specific metric, cutoff, variable type, and timepoint. We developed rules for naming specific measurements for both subjective and objective outcomes. We expanded on prior work by developing more comprehensive categories for specific metrics. We introduced "cutoff" as a distinct element with three subelements. To clarify the boundary between outcome definitions and statistical methods, we replaced a previously described element, "method of aggregation," with "variable type," which refers to whether the value for each individual is continuous or categorical.
Trialists and sponsors could use this approach alongside other guidelines to define outcomes in trial registrations, protocols, and result reports.

articles_hidden.title: Credit, recognition, and reward for non-traditional research artefacts in the Life Sciences
articles_hidden.authors: Gavin Farrell; Eva Alloza; Adel Bouhraoua; Salvador Capella-Gutierrez; Carole Goble; Henning Hermjakob; Maria Makaronidou; Andrew Smith; Shoaib Sufi; Thanasis Vergoulis
articles_hidden.abstract: Publication metrics remain the primary academic performance assessment in modern academia. This focus has fostered the publish or perish culture, negatively impacting research output quantity and quality. Consequently, a gap exists in the recognition and reward of impactful non-traditional research artefacts, such as curated datasets, research software, and training materials. To address this, we share perspectives to expand the assessment consideration for researchers producing these outputs. We also highlight the dedicated roles and need for wider consideration of career paths of digital research technical professionals, including academic data curators, research software engineers and domain expert trainers. Through a mapping of valuable non-traditional artefacts illustrated by Life Science examples of ELIXIR Europe, we aim to foster a productive and sustainable Open Science ecosystem where these outputs are made visible and considered. We examine the technical solutions for credit and sociological barriers to recognition and reward, while also considering the impacts of generative AI. Furthermore, we discuss policy and funder mandate reforms to ensure those responsible for non-traditional research artefacts are properly recognised and rewarded, to accelerate global scientific discovery.

articles.title: Chatbot and Problematic Integration: Two Tests among U.S. Users
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are token-based, probabilistic engines that produce most likely answers based on trained models and user input. In this work, I draw upon the problematic integration (PI) theory to conceptualize human-AI interaction (HAII) as communication processes that are aimed to address users’ problematic probabilistic orientations (PP). I propose that (1) PP prompt people to seek answers from AI chatbots and (2) that the extent to which chatbot responses address PP shapes interaction outcomes. Two studies tested these propositions using national age-matching samples of AI chatbot users in the United States (age range=18-85 years; mean age=41 years). Study 1 was a cross-sectional survey and Study 2 was an interactive experiment where participants talked to chatbots about one of twenty validated and pretested life concerns and rated chatbot-generated responses addressing their concern. Findings lend partial support to my propositions and offer insights into how AI chatbots may shape communication and human cognition.

articles.title: LEWIS: Lund Everyday Waste Image Set of Naturally Sourced, Normalised, and Evaluated Waste Images
articles.authors: Anton Prip Wrisberg; Annika Wallin; Philip Pärnamets
articles.abstract: Waste sorting is a cognitively demanding task with high environmental stakes. To support research on the categorisation and decision processes underlying waste sorting behaviour, this paper introduces an evaluated stimulus set of 790 images of naturally occurring waste items. The images were sampled from Danish and Swedish household waste, visually standardised, and evaluated by 526 Swedish participants on real-world frequency, how good an example they are of their waste category, and ease of categorisation. The resulting database offers a valuable resource for experiments in categorisation, judgment and decision-making, and sustainability interventions, enabling researchers to study real-world categorisation with both experimental control and ecological validity.

articles.title: Factors structuring lexical development intoddlers: The effects of parental education,language exposure, and age
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Camila Scaff; Laia Fibla; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract:
A growing body of research suggests that individual variation in young children's word comprehension (indexed by response times and accuracy) is structured and meaningful. In this paper, we assess how children’s word comprehension correlates with three factors: socio-economic status (indexed by maternal education), lingual status (based on language exposure), and age. We present results from 91 2- to 3-year-old children using a paired forced-choice task built on a child-friendly touch screen. Effects associated with maternal education and exposure to the tested language (French) were small, and they were greater for accuracy than response times. This pattern of results is compatible with an interpretation whereby the greatest effects of these two variables are on cumulative knowledge (vocabulary size) rather
than on processing. Effects for age were larger and affected both accuracy and response times. Finally, response time variation did not mediate the effects of socio-economic status on accuracy or vice versa

articles.title: Why the body comes first: Effects of experimenter touch on infants’ word finding
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Amanda Seidl; Ruth Tincoff; Christopher Baker; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract:
The lexicon of 6-month-olds is comprised of names and body part words. Unlike names, body part words do not often occur in isolation in the input. This presents a puzzle: How have infants been able to pull out these words from the continuous stream of speech at such a young age? We hypothesize that caregivers’ interactions directed at and on the infant’s body may be at the root of their early acquisition of body part words. An
artificial language segmentation study shows that experimenter-provided synchronous tactile cues help 4-month-olds to find words in continuous speech. A follow-up study suggests that this facilitation cannot be reduced to the highly social situation in which the directed interaction occurs. Taken together, these studies suggests that direct caregiver-infant interaction, exemplified in this study by touch cues, may play a key role
in infants’ ability to find word boundaries and suggests that words linked with caregiver touches may comprise early vocabulary items.

articles.title: AI-Podcast Misinformation: Testing Active versus Passive Inoculations
articles.authors: Paul McIlhiney; Emily Rebecca Spearing; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: Realistic, misleading AI-generated audio content is a new threat to digital-media consumers. This study examined the effects of misleading AI-generated podcasts that presented false claims about nanoparticles in sunscreen (Experiment 1; N = 463), or microwaves damaging foods (Experiment 2; N = 500). U.S. participants either received a misleading podcast, misleading article, or a neutral podcast (control). To test interventions, misleading podcasts were preceded by either a passive inoculation explaining how AI-generated information can deceive, an active inoculation that added an educational activity, or no intervention. The podcast and article produced comparable increases in misinformed beliefs. Both inoculations significantly reduced general trust in AI-generated information and attenuated the podcast’s impact on beliefs. Results demonstrate that AI-generated audio can influence health-related beliefs as strongly as text-based misinformation, and that brief AI-source-focused inoculations can mitigate, but not eliminate, its persuasive impact. Findings inform interventions targeting emerging forms of AI-driven misinformation.

articles.title: Relationship Quality Moderates Depressive-Symptom Associations With Negative Self-Perceptions and Partner Metaperceptions
articles.authors: Nida Civici; Andrew Martin
articles.abstract: Depression is associated with persistent negative self-beliefs and altered social information processing. Although considerable research has examined self-perception in depression, less is known about how depressive symptoms relate to beliefs about how romantic partners perceive the self and whether relationship quality moderates these associations. The present study investigated associations between depressive symptoms, self-perceptions, metaperceptions of partner evaluations, and memory for self-referential information across multiple social perspectives. A sample of 171 adults in romantic relationships completed measures of depressive symptoms and relationship quality, an adapted Self-Referential Encoding Task assessing evaluations from the self, a romantic partner, and a neutral researcher, and a subsequent memory assessment. Higher depressive symptoms were associated with more negative self-perceptions and more negative beliefs about how romantic partners viewed the self, but not with perceptions attributed to the neutral researcher. Relationship quality moderated the association between depressive symptoms and negative self- and partner-related perceptions, with weaker associations observed among participants reporting higher-quality relationships. Memory analyses focused on self-reference effects across social perspectives. Memory sensitivity was higher for self- and partner-encoded items than for researcher-encoded items and for negative than positive items. However, there was no consistent evidence that depressive symptoms, relationship quality, or their interaction predicted these self-reference effects. These findings suggest that depressive symptoms extend beyond self-evaluation to include assumptions about how emotionally significant others perceive the self, with relationship quality shaping the strength of these associations. The findings underscore the importance of considering partner-related metaperceptions and relationship context when examining interpersonal processes associated with depression.

articles.title: Minds Meet Machines: Trust and Intellectual Humility as Necessary Conditions for AI Persuasion
articles.authors: Devora Newman; Almog Simchon; Ruth Mayo
articles.abstract: Recently, AI models demonstrated a remarkable ability to facilitate opinion change, a notoriously difficult task between human communicators. Here, we focus on the dispositions that characterize message recipients, specifically identifying trust in AI, intellectual humility (IH), and their interplay as key factors in acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Across two studies with an online British sample (N=294), we replicated findings showing significant attitude change regarding legal immigrants following brief interactions with GPT. Crucially, our findings reveal that opinion change is contingent on higher IH and greater trust in AI, independently and jointly, predicting greater acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Experimentally capturing the centrality of open-mindedness (IH) and source sensitivity (Trust) highlights how epistemic vigilance constrains AI’s persuasive impact and sheds new light on the persuasion literature by revisiting the role of source credibility. Future research should examine whether these dispositional effects extend to long-term behavioral patterns across broader real-world contexts.

articles.title: Selective reproduction of spatial–emotional mappings in large language models
articles.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Fumiya Yonemitsu; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: The vertical-valence metaphor refers to the association between emotional valence and vertical space, whereby positive and negative emotions are linked to upward and downward directions, respectively. While this mapping has been robustly observed in human cognition, it remains unclear whether such associations are also reproduced in artificial intelligence systems. The present study investigated the vertical-valence metaphor in ChatGPT. In Experiments 1–3, ChatGPT-4 showed a consistent pattern in which “up” was evaluated more positively than “down,” and emotional words were spatially organized such that “joy” was placed above “sadness,” with “surprise” positioned in between. This pattern persisted even when the coordinate system was reversed. In Experiments 4–6, we compared silicon and human samples and observed a more nuanced pattern. While the vertical-valence mapping was largely preserved across both groups, the intermediate positioning of “surprise” was not consistently reproduced in ChatGPT-5.2. An additional pilot experiment indicates that this reduction in differentiation may be influenced by prompt language, although the relative contributions of model characteristics and language could not be determined. Exploratory analyses revealed that the horizontal-valence metaphor showed less consistent patterns across all the experiments, indicating lower robustness. Taken together, these findings suggest that large language models do not uniformly reproduce human cognitive mappings but instead exhibit a graded pattern of representation. Robust mappings are preserved, whereas intermediate or weaker mappings may be compressed or destabilized.

articles.title: How Employees Experience (Im)balance with W-ICTs: an Ideal Type Analysis of Digital Well-being
articles.authors: Lore Geldof; Ann DeSmet; Alice Verlinden; Elfi Baillien
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The rapid digitalization of work has intensified employees' connectivity to work-related information and communication technologies (W-ICTs), creating both opportunities and risks for digital well-being. While prior research highlights these ambivalent effects, little is known about how employees emotionally experience digital (im)balance with W-ICTs. Hence, we aim to develop a typology detailing such emotional experiences.
Design/Methodology/Approach: Drawing on 40 qualitative interviews (60% female; Mage = 40.25; SD = 9.16), this study abductively develops an experiential typology of digital (im)balance with W-ICT using Ideal Type Analysis. The identified types capture variations in emotional experiences (i.e., affective and cognitive) and digital connectivity processes (DCPs; i.e., interference, boundary blurring, exposure, and time displacement).
Findings: Eight Ideal Types are identified, comprising four experiences of digital imbalance and four experiences of digital balance. The types differ in emotional valence with configurations of DCPs. A comparison of the types show distinct emotional experiences while similar DCPs may occur. This is contextualized in the organisational setting.
Originality: By integrating emotional experiences and DCPs, the typology advances a configurational understanding of employee digital well-being. By contextualizing the types in organizational conditions, the findings suggest that highly connected work environments are not inherently tied to experiences of imbalance.

articles.title: Social readiness and public legitimacy of vaccine mandates: comparative evidence from three countries
articles.authors: Uwana Evers; Joshua Lake; Katie Attwell
articles.abstract: Vaccine mandates are used to increase vaccine uptake during infectious disease emergencies; however, they expose enduring tensions between collective protection and individual autonomy. Existing research treats public opinion toward mandates as a binary – recording only whether people support or oppose them. This study conceptualizes mandate attitudes as comprising two distinct dimensions – perceived public-health protection and concern for rights/autonomy – and examines these in survey data from Australia (N=4,208), France (N=3,858), and Italy (N=3,973). In this framework, mandate legitimacy encompasses both perceived collective benefits and perceived infringements on individual autonomy. Analysis revealed divergent patterns: the protection dimension was more strongly associated with institutional trust and vaccination behavior across all three countries, while rights-based attitudes were more variable. Moreover, trust in health-relevant institutions was more robustly associated with the protection dimension than trust in political institutions or media, but this did not extend uniformly to rights-based attitudes. In France, rights-based attitudes were independent of health system trust; in Italy, rights attitudes were unrelated to national government trust, suggesting rights-based objections operate partly independently of institutional confidence. Feeling compelled to vaccinate against COVID-19 was negatively associated with both dimensions across all countries, indicating coercive vaccination experiences may deplete legitimacy capital available for future mandate deployment. Findings suggest that general mandate approval can conceal substantial rights-based resistance, and that institutional trust is insufficient to reduce rights-based mandate resistance Communication strategies that build health institution trust, minimize coercive framing, and are sensitive to political contexts might sustain the public legitimacy required for effective pandemic preparedness.

articles.title: Narrative Entropy
articles.authors: Devin R Wright; Fritz Breithaupt; Anthony F. Beavers; Jacob G. Foster; Jisun An
articles.abstract: Narrative Entropy Theory (NET) proposes that we inhabit narrative environments: ecosystems of cultures, communities, and personal histories constructed from overlapping stories. Narrative entropy is a dynamic, relational property of these ecosystems: the degree of constraint and uncertainty over the interpretive possibility space available within them. At relatively lower entropy, interpretive activity concentrates around recurrent structures, makes narrative and shared worlds easier to navigate and facilitates shared meaning and experience. At relatively higher entropy, more possibilities remain available, which makes interpretation less anticipable and preserves opportunities for interpretive plurality, perspective-taking, and the generation of new meaning. In this way, narrative environments shape how meaning is interpreted and shared and which experiences and perspectives become available for recognition. NET connects the structure of these environments to cognition, communication, and social coordination while treating narrative as both organized structure and embodied activity. We provide an initial empirical demonstration using 475,716 English-language news articles from sources in 65 countries. We operationalize narrative entropy through topic attention, microframe complexity, and narrative fluency (the compressibility of traversal through narrative networks) and compare these measures with national indices of expressive freedom. All measures covary with these indices in the predicted directions and together account for more than one-third of the cross-national variance in the World Press Freedom Index. Together, these results show that narrative environments leave measurable traces in the artifacts they produce, making their structure empirically tractable for scientific inquiry.

articles.title: Factor Structure and Convergent Validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) Among Filipino Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles.abstract: The Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP) distinguishes between striving for high yet attainable standards (i.e., excellencism) and the pursuit of rigid, inflexible ones (i.e., perfectionism). The current study examines the psychometric validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) among two samples of Filipino adults preparing for a licensure examination. Results from confirmatory factor analyses supported the two factor structure of the SCOPE. Convergent validity was supported through expected cross-sectional associations with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale as well as time-lagged associations with subjective well-being. Time 1 excellencism was positively associated with Time 2 life satisfaction and positive affect, whereas Time 1 perfectionism was positively linked with Time 2 negative affect. Overall, these findings provide support for the validity of the SCOPE and the assumptions of the MEP, suggesting that pursuing excellencism—rather than perfectionism—is associated with greater well-being during intense career preparation.

articles.title: Learning from others’ mistakes: differential effects of observing target errors versus adaptation errors
articles.authors: Beverley Larssen; Anthony Sze; Ryan Jin; Sarah N Kraeutner; Nicola Jane Hodges
articles.abstract: How we learn from observing others perform reaching tasks is debated in the adaptation literature. When observers see a hand intentionally miss a target to correctly counteract rotated visual feedback (adaptation error), after-effects are typically absent. In contrast, observing consistent target errors, has resulted in unintended compensatory after-effects. The type of observed “error” (adaptation versus target error) may therefore have different effects on observation-induced behaviour, although this has not been tested within the same experiment. We compared participants in a four-group orthogonal design, who saw a model hit or miss a target, with or without rotated cursor feedback. Small compensatory after-effects (pre- to post-test) were seen when reaching to perceived midline in groups that observed target errors (misses). However, there were also small imitative after-effects after observing adaptation errors without target errors, but only when reaching to visual targets. Observing adaptation errors with or without target misses aided later performance in the same rotated environment and was accompanied by explicit knowledge of the rotation. Knowing the task goal is relevant information for eliciting small compensatory aiming biases in observers, perhaps because target errors matter more than adaptation errors when observing, leading to an unintended resolution not needed for “correct” actions.

articles.title: Recent Clinical Encounters for Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviours: Disclosure, Assessment, Missed Opportunities, and Implications for Practice
articles.authors: Jennifer Q. P. Nguyen; Glenn A Melvin; David John Hallford
articles.abstract:
Objective: Many individuals who die by suicide have contact with healthcare services in the months preceding their death, making these interactions critical opportunities for identification, intervention, and support. However, little is known about how individuals experiencing suicidal thoughts and behaviours (STBs) perceive recent clinical encounters, including how these experiences are discussed and managed.
Method: Australian adults (N = 266; Mage = 32.9; range = 18-71 years) who had experienced STBs and consulted with a mental health professional within the past two weeks completed an online survey examining suicide-related enquiry, disclosure experiences, clinician responses, and satisfaction.
Results: Psychologists were the most commonly consulted clinicians (49.2%), and 90.8% reported having seen the same clinician previously. Although 95.7% of participants considered discussing their STBs at least somewhat important, only 67.9% reported discussing these experiences with clinicians. Among those who did not discuss STBs, 50.0% reported that they had not been asked. Participants also reported that clinicians more frequently enquired about general emotional wellbeing (80.6%) than directly about STBs (55.3%). Among participants who did discuss STBs, 52.1% reported withholding information, while 46.2% reported feeling hesitant to disclose. Safety planning (36.9%) and follow-up (37.4%) were reported infrequently despite being viewed as important and helpful. Nevertheless, 75.4% reported being satisfied with their recent interactions.
Conclusions: Despite generally positive experiences with these interactions, the findings highlight opportunities to strengthen suicide prevention by creating opportunities to discuss STBs beyond initial clinical encounters, supporting disclosure through compassionate care, and ensuring that suicide-specific care is provided where appropriate following identification.
Key words: suicide; suicidal ideation; suicidal behaviour; disclosure; non-disclosure; clinician-patient communication

articles.title: BoundBase-EN (BBEN): A database of English bound bases in texts for children and young people
articles.authors: Maria Korochkina; Nicola Dawson; Danielle Colenbrander
articles.abstract: Sensitivity to morphological structure is considered a hallmark of skilled reading; however, much of the extant literature has focused on affixation (e.g., -er in teacher) and complex words with free bases (e.g., teach in teacher). This focus has left bound bases (e.g., ceiv(e) in receive) relatively unexplored, despite their prevalence in English and potential importance as a source of morphological regularity in print experience. Using a combination of automated and manual procedures, we developed BoundBase-EN (BBEN), a publicly available database providing lexical statistics and etymological information for 328 English bound bases occurring in texts for readers from age 5 to young adulthood. The BBEN data provide key insights into the distributional properties of these units. First, most bound bases occur infrequently and in a limited number of distinct words, with only a small set accounting for the majority of readers’ exposure. Second, children encounter bound-base words from the earliest years of independent reading, with developmental increases in exposure reflecting greater token frequency (i.e., more encounters with the same words) rather than type frequency (i.e., greater diversity in words containing bound bases). Third, although relatively infrequent overall, many bound-base words occur more frequently than complex words containing free bases, suggesting that they occupy a middle ground in children’s experience of morphological regularities. These findings highlight the importance of investigating bound bases for understanding how morphological knowledge is acquired and processed, and for informing approaches to morphology instruction. The BBEN database provides a foundation for such research.

articles.title: Psychology in 2125: A Developmental Science of Living Sense-Making
articles.authors: Peter J. Marshall
articles.abstract: A century from now, the computational framework at the center of psychology will no longer organize the discipline. As used here, "computational" names a broad information-processing ontology: meaning is specified in advance, rather than generated through the activity, history, and situation of living beings. This assumption fits engineered systems, but it misdescribes living ones. This article argues that three converging shifts are destabilizing that framework. The first undermines the computational account of inheritance: organisms develop through activity within configurations of constraints reconstituted across generations, not through the readout of genetic programs. The second displaces its account of psychological structure: psychological phenomena unfold as trajectories of coordination rather than as stable traits, with reliability and variability arising from the same generative process. The third sharpens the first two: artificial intelligence systems produce fluent performance without embodiment, developmental history, or any stake in the world. This contrast reveals what living organization contributes. The psychology implied by these shifts treats development as foundational, not as a subfield. It understands psychological constructs as patterns of activity that persons sustain over time, and is better positioned to address a century of changing human ecologies. This future psychology will be a developmental science of living sense-making.

articles.title: Blending Sources of Evidence: Meta-Analysis Combining Aggregated Data and Individual Participant Data from Multilab Replications
articles.authors: Jingru Zhang; James E Pustejovsky
articles.abstract: Conventional meta-analyses synthesize average treatment effects from sample-level aggregated data (AD) and are limited to addressing questions of moderation only at the sample level. Although associations between study-mean covariates and effect sizes need not reflect individual-level relations, individual-level moderating effects can be investigated using individual participant data (IPD). Multilab replication projects have recently made large, preregistered IPD collections publicly available for effects also synthesized in conventional meta-analyses, so the two data sources could, in principle, be combined. Determining whether they should be combined, however, requires judgment about their compatibility. We propose four guiding questions for the preliminary evaluation of such syntheses, concerning outcome measurement, primary study sample sizes, the distribution of study features, and publication bias, and show how graphical and tabular summaries can inform each consideration. We then describe meta-analytic models for combining AD and IPD from studies with continuous outcomes. We review two-stage and one-stage approaches for estimating the overall effect distribution and study-level moderation, as well as for separating within-study from between-study moderation of individual characteristics, including a novel bivariate two-stage formulation that jointly synthesizes treatment and moderation effects. We illustrate the framework with two examples, each pairing an AD meta-analysis with a multilab replication of the same effect. In an example of moral licensing effects, the preliminary evaluation indicates that combining the sources is not warranted; in an example of social heuristics effects, synthesizing across data sources is warranted. Together, the examples show that whether two sources can be combined is an empirical question best settled before modeling begins, and that the specification that follows should be tailored to the features of the data that the preliminary evaluation brings to light.

articles.title: Preschoolers can coordinate with each other to communicate about novel referents
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Robert Zane Sparks; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: Learning language requires learning not only the content of language, but also how to use language to communicate. Iterated reference games provide a window into such skills, requiring sustained interactive communication as participants converge on mutually understandable names for initially novel referents. Some early experiments are interpreted as evidence that 4-5-year-old children cannot converge on the mutually understandable names needed to succeed in an iterated reference game. Here, we revisit young children's referential communicative abilities using a simpler, child-friendly version of the iterated reference game paradigm. Across 4 experiments and 82 pairs of children (N=158), we found that 4-5-year-olds could successfully establish reference with each other. Children were 81% accurate, and they often used descriptions similar to their partner's. These findings suggest that children’s capacity to construct effective referring expressions in novel contexts emerges earlier than previously thought, consistent with the view that children show early pragmatic competence in supportive contexts.

articles.title: Intuitions about trait responsibilities
articles.authors: Yang Xiang; Stephanie Hsu; Samuel J. Gershman
articles.abstract: Popular depictions of mental life often feature a bustling society of personality traits—distinctive characters whose actions collectively determine behavior, much like how the actions of individual people collectively determine the behavior of a group. Do these depictions capture something important about folk psychology? One implication is that people should reason about trait responsibility similarly to how they reason about personal responsibility in groups. To test this implication quantitatively, we first collected data on judgments about the predictive relationship between traits and actions (Experiment 1), and then elicited trait responsibility judgments for the same actions (Experiment 2). The data from Experiment 1 were used to construct models of responsibility attribution (adapted from prior work on personal responsibility in groups), which we then compared to data from Experiment 2. We found that participants treated personality traits as entities that can bear responsibility for behavior, and their responsibility judgments were best explained by an actual contribution model that assigns responsibility based on a trait’s predictive contribution to behavior. In contrast to findings from studies of personal responsibility, counterfactual-style models did not fare as well. These findings reveal both similarities and differences between responsibility attribution to traits within a person vs. people within a group.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Social Sharing of Emotion: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Sarah Taylor O'Brien; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Sooyeon Kim; Peter Koval; Elise Katherine Kalokerinos
articles.abstract: After experiencing an emotional event, people almost always talk to other people about their experience. People generally believe this process—labelled social sharing of emotion—is beneficial, but empirical findings on the outcomes are mixed. We argue that underlying these mixed findings is an issue with the conceptual clarity of social sharing. In pursuit of conceptual clarity and in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we conducted a scoping review to map how social sharing has been defined and operationalized in the literature. Our review included 99 articles, including 128 studies, empirically investigating social sharing of emotion (sourced from PsychInfo (Ovid), ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, PsyArXiv, and PubMed). From these articles, we identified common features of researchers’ definitions and operationalizations of social sharing, highlighting what researchers deem central to the process. We found large heterogeneity in how social sharing has been conceptualized, which may contribute to the mixed findings on sharing thus far. For instance, we identified 16 unique features of social sharing in researchers’ definitions, 11 unique features in self-report study operationalizations, and 10 unique features in manipulation study operationalizations. Based on our findings, we propose a new consensus definition of social sharing, outlining necessary and sufficient features of the process. In all, this review elucidates a common behavior that is gaining relevance in a world with more ways to connect with each other than ever before.

articles.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles.title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence Research in Aphasia: An AI-Assisted Scoping Review and Semantic Network Analysis
articles.authors: Mengyang Qiu; Siena Sun; Sara NassrElgrgawi; Zirui Feng
articles.abstract:
Purpose: A shared view of artificial intelligence (AI) research in aphasia is needed to locate related work across clinical and computing publications. This scoping review mapped research topics and connections, AI method families over time, and reported evaluation and participant characteristics relevant to clinical applicability.
Method: Seven sources were searched for publications from January 2010 through June 2026. Two large language models (LLMs) independently screened records and extracted information from publication abstracts. Disagreements within and across LLMs were manually reviewed and resolved. To check screening accuracy, three human reviewers independently screened a sample without seeing model responses. Semantic network analysis of the abstracts identified research communities and connecting studies.
Results: LLM-assisted screening identified 412 primary studies. Its decisions agreed with the human majority on 91% of 145 sampled records. Network analysis identified 12 communities, with partial separation between clinical and computing publications and general separation between post-stroke aphasia and primary progressive aphasia studies. Deep learning and generative AI first appeared in clinical and computing publications in the same respective years and represented larger proportions of computing publications. Abstracts often lacked key evaluation and participant information: only 28 abstracts (7%) reported independent model testing, 21 (5%) clinical evaluation, and 34 (8%) aphasia severity.
Conclusions: The map provides entry points for exploring related research, and the workflow offers a foundation for future evidence syntheses in communication disorders. Clearer reporting of evaluation and participant characteristics could improve communication across disciplines and help readers identify relevant publications.

articles.title: Popular nonfiction can durably shift politically relevant attitudes—and so can a much shorter AI summary
articles.authors: Joshua Paul White; Adam J. Berinsky; James Patoriza; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Can reading a chapter of popular nonfiction shift politically relevant attitudes among resistant partisans, and, if so, can an AI-generated summary do so just as effectively? In a preregistered experiment, N = 555 Republicans were randomized to read “The Cyber Sleuth” by Geraldine Brooks—a profile of IRS cybercrime investigators from Michael Lewis’s Who Is Government?—or a control text, and further randomized to either the full text (∼5300 words) or a much shorter AI-generated summary (∼1400 words). Reading “The Cyber Sleuth” produced wide-ranging attitude change relative to control: IRS favorability increased substantially (d = 0.62), with spillover to civil-service favorability (d = 0.37) and opposition to DOGE-led workforce reductions (d = 0.40). These effects remained significant two months later (ds 0.14–0.19). Strikingly, the AI-generated summary produced effects statistically indistinguishable from the full text. Popular nonfiction, and an AI summary thereof, can be an effective tool for politically relevant attitude change, even on a polarized, partisan issue.

articles.title: LLM-Generated Social-Desirability Ratings for Forced-Choice Questionnaire Construction: A Preregistered Downstream Validation
articles.authors: Yui Furukawa; Kyosuke Bunji; Kensuke Okada
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly produce evaluative judgments, but rating-level human–model agreement does not establish whether they can replace human inputs in a downstream task. Using HEXACO personality items as a case study, we conduct a preregistered three-stage validation of whether LLM-generated social-desirability ratings can serve as inputs to forced-choice scale construction, a psychometric task that requires costly human ratings. In Stage I, three LLMs served as raters of item-level social desirability for sentence- and adjective-format items, with human ratings serving as references. In Stage II, human- and LLM-based ratings were entered into the same constrained optimization procedure. In Stage III, 400 participants completed the resulting forms, and latent trait estimates were compared using graded Thurstonian item response theory. LLM ratings showed strong item-level correspondence with human ratings (sentence: r = 0.942–0.963; adjective: r = 0.979–0.980), but optimized forms showed partial item overlap and sparse exact pair overlap. Despite these design differences, LLM-based forms produced latent trait estimates that closely matched those from human-based forms (mean r = 0.815 for sentence items and 0.768 for adjective items). These results support the conditional use of LLM-generated ratings as scalable construction inputs while showing why downstream validation is necessary.

articles.title: What Race Means for Health among Black Americans: How Microaggressions Shape Self-Efficacy and Readiness for Behavior Change
articles.authors: Amanda Almond
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives: Persistent racial disparities in cardiovascular health among Black Americans reflect not only structural inequities in the United States, but also the racialized meanings of cardiovascular disease reproduced through public and private health communication. Drawing on ecological systems theory, this research examines how beliefs linking race and cardiovascular disease are reinforced through routine clinical interactions and how these meanings shape health behavior change. Method: Across two experimental mixed-methods studies, a model integrating ecological, social–cognitive, and behavior-change frameworks was tested. In Study 1 (N = 374), health-message framing was experimentally manipulated to examine effects on self-efficacy and decisional balance while controlling for prior experiences of racial microaggression in medical contexts. Study 2 (N = 589) extended this work by testing whether conceptualizations of race as biological/genetic and social/political moderated these effects. A subset of participants (n = 57) voluntarily provided narratives of racially charged healthcare experiences, which were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to contextualize quantitative findings. Results: Racial microaggressions from health professionals disrupted self-efficacy and decisional balance for cardiovascular health behaviors. Endorsement of biological versus social race beliefs moderated these effects, shaping both their magnitude and direction. Qualitative findings revealed how everyday clinical interactions reproduce racialized meanings of disease risk and personal control. Conclusions: These findings identify clinical communication as a consequential site where racial meanings of disease are constructed and psychologically internalized, influencing motivation for health behavior change. Addressing biologically essentialist framing in healthcare may therefore be critical for strengthening self-regulation and reducing cardiovascular disparities among Black Americans.

Keywords: racial microaggressions; health communication; self-efficacy; decisional balance; Transtheoretical Model; ecological systems theory; racial essentialism; cardiovascular health disparities

Public significance statement: How health professionals and public campaigns talk about race matters for behavior change. This research shows that subtle racialized cues in medicine can weaken Black patients’ sense of control and readiness to take preventive action. Training clinicians to avoid biological essentialist framing may improve patient engagement and help reduce cardiovascular health disparities.

articles.title: Taking the speaker’s perspective? Investigating quantifier and implicature processing in an AI-language training paradigm using EEG-VR
articles.authors: Maria Spychalska; Ludmila Reimer; Marjolijn Dijkhuis; Peter Hagoort
articles.abstract:
Interpreting speaker meaning requires taking into account the speaker’s epistemic perspective, i.e., their access to relevant information. The extent to which listeners integrate this perspective during comprehension is known as the perspective-taking problem. We present the first EEG study to investigate the role of perspective-taking in the processing of quantifiers and scalar implicatures. Using immersive virtual reality, we asked participants to assist an AI, represented by a virtual agent, in learning to use quantifiers appropriately. Critically, the agent had limited access to the reference domain compared to the participant.

Our results show that when the speaker’s information access is restricted, listeners initially process the semantic content of quantified statements from an egocentric perspective. Effects of the speaker’s perspective emerge only later, reflected in a sustained anterior negativity. For pragmatically ambiguous sentences containing ``some", we observe neither an effect of speaker perspective nor evidence for scalar implicature processing. We argue that contexts requiring consideration of the speaker’s knowledge primarily support Gricean, weak implicatures, which are computed relatively late as post-propositional inferences.

articles.title: Selective reductions amid global increases in neural information dynamics jointly track self-dissolution in meditation
articles.authors: Daniel Andrew Atad; Pedro A. Mediano; Fynn-Mathis Trautwein; ‪Yair Dor-Ziderman‬‏; Henrik Röhr; Yoav Schweitzer; Ohad Nave; Stephen Fulder; Aviva Berkovich-Ohana
articles.abstract: The sense of self is fundamental to experience, yet its neural basis remains unresolved. Contemplative traditions and empirical evidence suggest it can be voluntarily dissolved while retaining awareness, offering a window onto this question. We combined magnetoencephalography with in-depth phenomenology in long-term meditators (N=45, mean 3,832 practice hours) who reliably modulated self-boundaries across rest, self-maintenance and self-dissolution. Meditation broadly increased entropy and information transfer, yet selective reductions characterized self-dissolution. Reduced posterior-medial high-beta entropy and within-cingulate information transfer differentiated dissolution from maintenance. Information transfer reductions from occipital, cingulate, limbic, and subcortical regions, alongside orbitofrontal entropy stabilization, correlated with dissolution phenomenology. Combined with posterior-medial high-beta power reductions, these correlates explained 52% of dissolution depth variance, yet only information transfer predicted held-out participants. We propose selfhood relies on distributed processes that can be reconfigured in meditation through relaxed priors, gated bottom-up evidence, and stabilized evaluative dynamics, distinct from global disruption during psychedelic ego-dissolution.

articles.title: A Continuous Model of Mother, Father, and Infant Relations
articles.authors: Rukmini Mukkamalla; Benito Chen-Charpentier
articles.abstract: Many couples' relationship satisfaction declines after the birth of a child, and this decline is usually strongest in mothers. Other mathematical models of couple dynamics treat the mother and father in isolation, but the infant is also an emotional agent, coupled bidirectionally with both parents. We extend the continuous marital-satisfaction model of Chen-Charpentier et al.\ to a three-agent family consisting of a mother, a father, and an infant, using measured data whenever we can. Using equilibrium and stability analysis, a global Sobol sensitivity analysis, and a time-dependent extension, we find that the family has a single stable equilibrium. The sensitivity analysis shows that all three baseline emotional states largely affect the location of this equilibrium, with the infant's and father's baselines contributing the largest share of the variance. The mother's baseline plays a different role, however. It acts as a tipping point as mild maternal depression gets absorbed by the family while severe maternal depression drives the entire family into a distressed state. A time-dependent simulation of the first year, in which the parent--infant coupling is strong early and eases smoothly, shows that the early periods govern the speed of adjustment but not the destination. For example, a healthy family reaches contentment sooner, whereas a family with severe maternal depression dips further before settling into distress. Maternal mental health is thus the key factor in whether the family's emotional outcome is content or distressed.

articles.title: Humanlike AI May Strengthen Women’s Agreement With Sexist Stereotypes
articles.authors: Sterling Williams-Ceci; Rachel Minkowitz; Lior Zalmanson; Michael MACY; Mor Naaman
articles.abstract: AI can influence societally-consequential attitudes by generating biased arguments – but can it influence our attitudes without changing its arguments at all? In four experiments (N = 2,762), we show that the mere presence of humanlike features in an AI chatbot influences women to more strongly accept ideologically-compatible sexist stereotypes, biases that often resist influence and have societal harm. This influence operates indirectly by increasing “mind perception” – the belief that AI is conscious and thinking – which increases perceptions of its trustworthiness. Our contribution is that anthropomorphism’s influence extends beyond increased trust toward AI itself, impacting women’s broader attitudes about their competence and status. This influence happens when women are attentive during conversations with AI. As developers add more anthropomorphic features to AI, the harms of stereotypes it repeats will increase for vulnerable groups – but making AI appear less humanlike can mitigate this risk.

articles.title: Culturally Prompted Large Language Models Remain Anchored to Western Values
articles.authors: Zhao Wang; Yilin Xu; Joshua Conrad Jackson
articles.abstract: One proposed solution for reducing cultural bias in large language models (LLMs) involves “cultural prompting,” in which LLMs are explicitly instructed to respond on behalf of a cultural group. However, past studies have yielded inconsistent claims about the efficacy of cultural prompting. Here we test whether these inconsistent findings can be explained through an anchoring and adjusting account, whereby cultural prompting moves LLM responses away from a default representation anchored in wealthy Western values, but this adjustment is insufficient. We test this account by prompting three commercial LLMs to answer 117 items from the World Values Survey on behalf of 66 countries. We then compare their responses with data from 97,220 humans. Consistent with our predictions, we find that cultural prompting moves LLMs closer to human responses, but the shift is insufficient, particularly for poorer and culturally distant countries. Culturally prompted LLM responses remained more secular and emancipative than human responses. We also find that the biases of culturally prompted models were clustered by cultural heritage. Countries in closer geographic proximity and with more similar religious profiles showed similar patterns of misrepresentation. In addition to these results, we find a surprising pattern for Western countries in which cultural prompting makes responses more secular and emancipative than the model’s default representations. Many of our findings are broadly consistent with an anchoring and adjustment account, but this account cannot fully explain why cultural prompting leads models to overshoot human means for Western countries.

articles.title: Maternal Childhood Experiences and Mother–Infant Bonding: A Longitudinal Path Analysis of Perinatal Mental Health and Psychosocial Resources
articles.authors: Ana Rabasa Serrano; Sandra Doval; Alejandro de Miguel Álvaro; Maria Laura Quintanilla Cobián; Marta Giménez-Dasí
articles.abstract: Maternal childhood experiences may shape perinatal mental health and mother–infant bonding (MIB). This longitudinal study examined pathways linking adverse (ACEs) and benevolent childhood experiences (BCEs) to MIB through pregnancy adaptation and postpartum mental health, considering resilience and social support. We followed 404 pregnant women to 3 months postpartum. Path analyses showed that higher ACEs were associated with poorer pregnancy adaptation (β = .108, p = .020), which predicted greater postpartum depressive symptoms and poorer MIB. Social support and resilience protected against prenatal maladjustment and postpartum depression, while social support buffered the association between pregnancy adaptation difficulties and depressive symptoms (β = −.104, p = .006). BCEs were associated with better pregnancy adaptation through psychosocial resources. The model showed excellent fit (CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 23.6% of MIB variance. Similar patterns emerged for anxiety. Findings highlight indirect pathways and the protective role of psychosocial resources.

articles.title: When truthful innocent suspects become less forthcoming: Effects of memory constraints in SUE-based mock interviews
articles.authors: Helen Wyler; Martina Buchli; Flavia Zaidi-Tinner
articles.abstract: Past Strategic Use of Evidence studies found innocent suspects to be forthcoming, but usually implicitly assume that they can remember the critical details needed to provide evidence-consistent accounts. Building on Sukumar et al. (2018), we examined how encoding intentionality, retention interval, and type of critical detail affect forthcomingness in a mock investigative interview (S1; N = 193) and observers’ veracity judgements (S2; N = 402). Encoding intentionality had no statistically significant effect. The three-week retention interval substantially reduced forthcomingness among innocent suspects relative to immediate retrieval, although guilty suspects remained less forthcoming. Delayed innocent suspects were descriptively more likely to be judged as deceptive, but this effect was not confirmed by the preregistered interaction. Exploratory analyses suggested that incidental details were both most vulnerable to delay and associated with deception judgements. The findings highlight the importance of conceptualising forthcomingness as a function of both strategic information management and memory constraints.

articles.title: Predictive coding unifies neural and behavioral signatures of contextual facilitation
articles.authors: Samer Nour Eddine; Anthony Yacovone; Gina R. Kuperberg
articles.abstract: During comprehension, words that are primed or predictable are processed more quickly and elicit smaller N400 responses than words that are less consistent with their preceding context. Although these behavioral and neural effects are both commonly interpreted as evidence of facilitated processing, they have typically been explained within different computational frameworks that impose seemingly conflicting constraints: behavioral facilitation requires more activity to accumulate over expected representations, allowing a decision threshold to be reached earlier, whereas N400 facilitation requires less neural activity to be generated overall. Here, we show that an implemented model of predictive coding provides a unified mechanistic account of both phenomena and, in doing so, resolves three longstanding puzzles. First, it explains how facilitated processing can simultaneously produce faster behavioral responses and reduced neural activity: expected representations accumulate activity more rapidly in state units while generating less activity in error units. Second, an asymmetry between top-down priors and bottom-up evidence allows context to pre-activate multiple lexical candidates without inducing premature competition or misprediction costs. Third, it reconciles apparently conflicting claims about the timing of contextual facilitation by showing that behavioral and neural measures can reflect different phases along a single continuous trajectory of lexico-semantic processing, rather than distinct processing stages.

articles.title: Self-reported emotional change in conversations with an emotional support assistant: an observational analysis in TerapIA
articles.authors: Alejandro Vaca Serrano; Alberto Vaca Escribano; José María González de Echevarri
articles.abstract: People who talk to an emotional support assistant usually want to feel a bit better by the time they stop talking. Measuring whether that happens, and under what conditions, is a different thing from proving clinical efficacy. We analyze the change in a continuous emotional score in [0, 1] that users record at the beginning and at the end of their conversation with Pía, the assistant of the TerapIA app. The analysis is restricted to conversations where both ratings are present, where the slider was moved away from the interface default at both ends, and where the dialogue reached at least ten user messages. Once we discount the automatic greeting that opens the chat, that threshold amounts in practice to a conversation with actual content. Over n = 1935 conversations from 909 people, the mean score went from 0.42 at the beginning to 0.56 at the end (Δ = +0.138; 95% CI by user-clustered bootstrap [+0.121, +0.155]; dz = 0.54; Wilcoxon p < 0.001), and 63.4% of conversations improved. The mean change is zero in very short dialogues and consistently positive from ten user messages onwards, with an association between length and improvement that is statistically significant and robust to clustering by person. The result holds, and is in fact slightly larger, if only the first eligible conversation of each person is used (Δ = +0.147; dz = 0.57). Among the people who contributed at least three such conversations, the end score of the last one minus the start score of the first was +0.195, and 70% of them went up; the emotional starting point also rises with the number of accumulated conversations within each person. The design is observational: there is no control group, filling in the rating is optional, the score is a self-report, and regression to the mean is present. We do not infer causality, and we do not claim equivalence with a clinical outcome. What we do document is a robust association between talking with Pía for enough turns and a better self-reported emotional state at the end, of a magnitude close to the one observed in other deployed conversational agents with a pre/post within-session measure.

articles.title: The Adaptation Dilemma: Cultural Fit Does Not Guarantee Safety in Mental-Health LLMs
articles.authors: Maya Low; Ian Gold; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: People increasingly take mental-health concerns to general-purpose AI chatbots. A first wave of safety research has begun to map LLM failure points in this context. When that work considers culture, it usually reads the problem as a lack of fit: if the model does not match the user, the fix is to make it match more closely. We argue that this perspective is incomplete, because cultural fit and safety are not the same thing. By safety we mean the absence of harm caused by the interaction itself. We sort these harms into two classes: imposition, where the model forces its default on a user it does not fit, and collusion, where it adapts to a framing that keeps the user unwell. Because a response that fits a user’s own framing is more credible to them, moving a model toward that framing lowers the risk of imposition while raising both the likelihood of collusion and the damage collusion does when it occurs, so improved cultural sensitivity trades one exposure for another rather than reducing exposure overall. We argue that the reinforcement learning layer increasingly pushes these models toward collusion, while the safeguards in current use are poorly suited to detecting that failure or to limiting the harm it does. We propose a taxonomy of six culture-related failure modes, three of imposition and three of collusion. We argue that evaluating safety requires an anchor outside the user’s in-the-moment approval: responses must be assessed against the harms and benefits the interaction produces for the user, judged both by an external standard and against the goals the user has stated for their care.

articles.title: Recovery from Work via Physical Activity: A Longitudinal Study Among Workers with Intellectual Disabilities
articles.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Clément Ginoux; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles.abstract: Beyond the established physical and mental health benefits for people with intellectual disabilities (PwID), physical activity may also enhance workplace well-being, as demonstrated in the general population. Given that PwID are susceptible to work-related exhaustion, the restorative role of physical activity could be particularly relevant. This study aimed to investigate recovery processes engaged through off-job physical activity and their contribution to the workplace well-being of PwID. To address this objective, forty-two workers were followed over a six-week cycle of physical activities. Participants reported recovery experiences (i.e., psychological detachment, relaxation, mastery, control, affiliation, and affect) after each session, while trainers recorded session characteristics (i.e., duration and intensity). Workplace well-being (i.e., burnout, need for recovery, and vigor) was assessed at the beginning and end of the cycle. Multilevel analyses revealed only one significant relationship: a positive association between session duration (between-person level) and mastery experience. Regression analyses indicated that relaxation positively predicted exhaustion, while detachment positively predicted cognitive impairment and need for recovery. Conversely, mastery and affiliation were positively associated with physical vigor. These exploratory findings provide initial empirical evidence regarding the recovery role of physical activity for PwID. Further research is needed to validate and expand upon these results.

articles.title: Predictive coding unifies neural and behavioral signatures of contextual facilitation
articles.authors: Samer Nour Eddine; Anthony Yacovone; Gina R. Kuperberg
articles.abstract: During comprehension, words that are primed or predictable are processed more quickly and elicit smaller N400 responses than words that are less consistent with their preceding context. Although these behavioral and neural effects are both commonly interpreted as evidence of facilitated processing, they have typically been explained within different computational frameworks that impose seemingly conflicting constraints: behavioral facilitation requires more activity to accumulate over expected representations, allowing a decision threshold to be reached earlier, whereas N400 facilitation requires less neural activity to be generated overall. Here, we show that an implemented model of predictive coding provides a unified mechanistic account of both phenomena and, in doing so, resolves three longstanding puzzles. First, it explains how facilitated processing can simultaneously produce faster behavioral responses and reduced neural activity: expected representations accumulate activity more rapidly in state units while generating less activity in error units. Second, an asymmetry between top-down priors and bottom-up evidence allows context to pre-activate multiple lexical candidates without inducing premature competition or misprediction costs. Third, it reconciles apparently conflicting claims about the timing of contextual facilitation by showing that behavioral and neural measures can reflect different phases along a single continuous trajectory of lexico-semantic processing, rather than distinct processing stages.

articles.title: Differential Associations of Excellencism and Perfectionism with Mental Health Outcomes Among Licensure Examinees
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles.abstract:
Objective: Licensure examinees are vulnerable to the mental health consequences of perfectionism. However, previous work did not distinguish the pursuit of high yet attainable standards from the pursuit of exacting, inflexible ones. Guided by the Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP), this study examined how excellencism and perfectionism are differentially associated with well-being outcomes among Filipino adults preparing for a high-stakes licensure examination.
Method: A total of 1,206 psychometrician licensure examinees (Mage = 23.94, SD = 3.58) from two 2025 cohorts participated in the study.
Results: Structural equation modelling revealed that excellencism was significantly and positively associated with life satisfaction and positive affect while negatively associated with depression. In contrast, perfectionism was positively associated with negative affect, anxiety and depression. Comparison of predicted values for excellence and perfection strivers show better mental health outcomes for excellence strivers. 
Conclusions: These findings provide support for the MEP in the licensure examination context, suggesting that some of the desirable outcomes previously associated with perfectionism may be better accounted for by excellencism. The study contributes to the growing literature on excellence- and perfection-oriented goal pursuit and points to their potentially distinct implications for mental health in high-stakes evaluative settings.

articles.title: Sensitivity to Prosody at 6 Months Predicts Vocabulary at 24 Months
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia; Amanda Seidl
articles.abstract: Children’s language acquisition appears effortless, and advances enormously between the first word period, at about 12 months, to the stage at which complete and often complex sentences are produced, at about 3 years. However, this apparently miraculous process may in fact rely on knowledge that the child has began to accumulate even before birth. Indeed, work on infant speech perception in the last 40 years suggests that infants begin to attune to their native language during the first year of life.

articles.title: Ethical Considerations Around Surveillance Technologies for Suicide Prevention in Public Places: Bringing Together Staff and Lived/Living Experience Perspectives
articles.authors: Bethany Cliffe; Ian Marsh; Alex Dark; Andy Willis; Penny Phillips; Laura Joyner; Lisa Marzano; Keith Hawton; Carlisle George; Peter Craig
articles.abstract: This research brings together lived/living experience and professional stakeholder perspectives to explore ethical considerations around the use of surveillance technologies for suicide prevention in public places. The study employed qualitative interviews with people who have lived/living experience, focus groups with professional stakeholders, online ethnography of suicide discussion forums, and ethnography at public sites which have high rates of suicides. Framework analysis was used to interpret the interview and focus group data, which was then triangulated with ethnography notes to develop three themes: 1) Expectations around surveillance in public; 2) Experiences of surveillance: balancing harms with saving lives, and 3) Human response matters: experiences of intervention. Our findings show that surveillance technologies are typically associated more so with criminality than suicide, which can lead to anxieties around possible consequences of their use for suicide prevention. We also identified tensions between the pressures on staff to prevent suicides, through using surveillance technologies for example, versus the risk of causing harm in the process. Additionally, surveillance may detect someone in distress, but the prevention comes from the human intervention, which needs to prioritise empathy, retaining autonomy and ongoing care to support the individual. A key conclusion from this work is that surveillance technologies do not operate in isolation and so the broader context and systems should be considered to ensure that suicide prevention is done so in ways that are ethical and that aim to reduce harm.

articles.title: The psychological burden of “mild” aphasia: Greater associations with psychosocial well-being than with language severity
articles.authors: Deborah Levy; Kent Meinert; Katelyn Urena; Julianne M Alexander; Davida Fromm; Brian MacWhinney; Brielle C Stark
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Depression is common following stroke and neural injury, and individuals who develop aphasia—a language disorder—face an increased risk. However, people with aphasia are rarely assessed, referred, or treated for post-injury depression, an issue that may be further exacerbated in mild cases that lead to direct discharge home. Here, we examined the prevalence and correlates of depression in a cohort characterized, on average, by very mild or “latent” aphasia.  

Methods: Using the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB), we investigated relationships between depression and aphasia in 79 individuals with and 73 individuals without aphasia. Subgroup analyses investigated (a) sentiment in response to the open-ended question “How do you think your speech is these days?” and (b) self-reported psychosocial quality of life (Stroke Aphasia Quality of Life; SAQOL-39). 

Results: Individuals with aphasia showed higher rates of depression than neurologically healthy peers. Depression severity did not relate to aphasia severity. However, depression severity did relate to (a) the emotional valence of participants’ descriptions of their speech, (b) younger age, and (c) poorer psychosocial quality of life.  

Conclusions: These findings indicate that depressive symptoms are elevated even among individuals with very mild aphasia, and are more closely associated with younger age, negative valence about speech, and poorer psychosocial quality of life than with objectively measured aphasia severity. This underscores the importance of assessing the lived impact of communication changes across the full spectrum of post-injury aphasia.

articles.title: Conceptual combination as a window on representational format:  scope relations between “all” and “not” in combination with representations of “same.”
articles.authors: Jean-Rémy Hochmann; Rebecca Zhu; Susan Carey
articles.abstract: In Array Match to Sample (AMTS), participants are trained to sort arrays (e.g., of 16 items) containing  identical icons (16s) with other 16s arrays and arrays containing uniquely different icons (16d) with other 16d arrays.   This training is consistent with several different bases of sorting; 1) low entropy (variability) goes with low entropy, high entropy goes with high entropy, 2) match all same with all same, not all same with not all same; 3) match all same with all same, all not same with all not same, and 4) match all different with all different, not all different with not all different.  Testing with intermediate samples (i.e., 12s-4d, 8s-8d, 4s-12-d), keeping the choice cards the same (16s, 16d) probes the basis of each individual’s sorting behavior.  By age 4, more than ½ of humans sort by categorical rules 2 or 3 above, combining a representation of same with representations of all and not under one of two scope relations between all and not.  Animals and almost all 3-year-olds sort by entropy, an analog magnitude ensemble statistics, and animals cannot be taught to sort according to a criterion that combines all, not, and same as in 2 or 3 above.  No population sorts according to rule 4, combining “all,” “not” and “different.”.  Here we told participants a rule to follow; rule 2 in Experiments 1 and 2 and rule 4 in Experiment 3.  We found that the proportion of child participants sorting categorically matched the proportion of children who know the words “same” and “different”, and that telling children the rule increased sorting categorically at age 3, and increased sorting according to the stated rule in 4-year-olds and adults.  Both 4-year-olds and adults, equally and catastrophically, failed to follow rule 4 when instructed, instead sorting on the basis of the categorical distinction between all same and not all same.  We discuss the implications of these results for characterizing the development of the capacity to combine all and not under consistent scope relations, and for characterizing the formats of prelinguistic and linguistic representations of sameness and difference.

articles.title: The Common Format Hypothesis: The Central Form Integrates Causal Information from Different Domains into a Common Format
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: This paper investigates the structure of human concepts within Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, and proposes and tests the Common Format Hypothesis.
