Form Theory proposes that each concept contains a central form—a unitary structure that encodes a compressed subset of the concept’s conceptual information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a linked set of strong form-generated beliefs. The Common Format Hypothesis proposes that although causal knowledge and causal schemas differ across domains, central forms instantiate a common representational format. Across three experiments, participants learned about novel categories and their properties, with properties introduced either as satisfying a causal schema (which varied by domain) or as central form properties. The studies then tested the immediate activation of strong property-focused beliefs—specifically, beliefs about certainty, stability, and normativity. Results showed that while participants sometimes used causal cues to guide form encoding, they only exhibited these strong beliefs when a property had been encoded as part of the central form. This pattern held across domains (animals and artifacts), despite different causal structures. These findings support the Common Format Hypothesis and offer new insight into conceptual combination,  linguistic creativity, and concept learning.

articles.title: Acoustic correlates of phonological status
articles.authors: Maarten Versteegh; Amanda Seidl; Alejandrina Cristia; Alicia Horton-Mastin
articles.abstract: Languages vary not only in terms of their sound inventory, but also in the phonological status certain sound distinctions are assigned. For example, while vowel nasality is lexically contrastive (phonemic) in Quebecois French, it is largely determined by the context (allophonic) in American English; the reverse is true for vowel tenseness. If phonetics and phonology interact, a minimal pair of sounds should span a larger acoustic divergence when it is pronounced by speakers for whom the underlying distinction is phonemic compared to allophonic. Near minimal pairs were segmented from a corpus of American English and Quebecois French using a crossed design (since nasality and tenseness have opposite phonological status in the two languages). Pairwise time-aligned divergences between contrasts were calculated on the basis of 7 mainstream spoken feature representations, and a set of linguistic phonetic measurements. Only carefully selected phonetic measurements revealed the expected cross-over, with larger divergences for English than French tokens of the tenseness contrast, and larger divergences for French than English tokens for the nasality contrast. We conclude that the phonetic effects of phonological status are subtle enough that only linguistically-informed (or supervised) measurements can pick up on them.

articles.title: Superior retention but not integration of information in memory in children versus adults
articles.authors: Emma James; Layla Unger
articles.abstract: Across childhood, we amass thousands of experiences from which we build knowledge about the world. Knowledge can come from both encoding memories for experiences (e.g., seeing items A and B on one occasion or A and C on another) and integrating information that spans multiple experiences (e.g., that B and C both occurred with A). Experiments that train overlapping AB-AC pairs show that when tested immediately afterwards, BC integration is relatively weak in children even when they successfully encode and remember pairs. In this study, we ask whether children can capitalise upon superior offline consolidation abilities to integrate this information at a delayed test one week later. Children aged 8-10 years (n = 137) and adults aged 18-31 years (n = 204) encoded overlapping pairs of cartoon creatures (A), objects (B), and scenes (C), as well as unique non-overlapping pairs (DE). Children showed similar memory for non-overlapping pairs to adults at the immediate test, and superior retention one week later. However, their weaker accuracy when integrating across overlapping pairs remained stable at both test points, even when both overlapping pairs had been successfully retrieved. We conclude limited evidence that children’s superior offline consolidation can compensate for weaknesses in memory integration.

articles.title: Experienced vs. actual gaze reciprocity in repeated social interactions: A gateway toward social connectedness
articles.authors: Julian Gutzeit; Luise Hölting; Antonia Sophie van Duijn; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: In many contexts, direct gaze is regarded as a socially rewarding signal that promotes positive interpersonal evaluations, yet most evidence stems from single, in-the-moment judgments of briefly presented faces. Across three eye-tracking experiments, we examined whether repeated gaze-contingent interactions shape more enduring social evaluations. Participants repeatedly exchanged gaze with a few on-screen virtual partners who reciprocated their gaze with systematically different probabilities. Afterwards, participants estimated gaze reciprocity rates for each partner and completed several ratings (e.g., feelings of social connectedness, social agency). Notably, participants reliably distinguished between gaze reciprocity rates of interaction partners even when differences in actual gaze reciprocity were small and close to chance (40% vs. 60%), though estimates were compressed toward the middle of the range. Critically, while objective gaze reciprocity rates showed little consistent relation to social evaluations, subjectively perceived reciprocity rates were robustly associated with social connectedness and social agency across experiments. Additionally, some experiments pointed to associations with likability and trust (entrusted money in an economic Trust Game). However, these associations did not extend to implicit behavioral measures (free-choice gaze selection, gaze cueing). A pooled multilevel mediation analysis confirmed that objective gaze reciprocity rates predicted connectedness indirectly, via subjective perception. Together, these findings suggest that social evaluation is shaped more by the experience of being looked at than by objective gaze reciprocity itself, at least when gaze reciprocity levels are somewhat difficult to differentiate.

articles.title: How observers decode pain from facial reactions. Distributed patterns of facial muscle contractions drive pain judgments in both naturalistic and synthetic expressions.
articles.authors: Nurefşan Üzmez; Ilaria Mirlisenna; Daniele Pugliese; Giada Dirupo; Laura Riontino; Corrado Corradi-Dell'Acqua
articles.abstract: Assessing others' pain relies heavily on facial expressions, yet how individuals translate observable facial features into pain judgements remains poorly understood. We combined a retrospective analysis of naturalistic spontaneous pain expressions across three different cohorts (Study 1, N = 398) with a reverse correlation experiment using synthetic facial stimuli (Study 2, N = 63), to investigate which facial muscle contractions (Action Units, AUs) drive pain judgments. Across both studies, we consistently found brow lowering (AU 4), nose wrinkling (AU 9) and brow raising (AU 1/2) as key contributors, alongside a more variable role of mouth movements. Multivariate pattern analysis indicated that pain judgments rely on a distributed set of facial AUs, rather than on single diagnostic cues. Finally, tailored co-engagement analysis from Study 2 identified AU pairs that, when combined, facilitate (AUs 1 + 12, AUs 4 + 24) or inhibit (AUs 4 + 9) pain assessments. Neither participants' own sex, the sex of the displayed face, nor participants' empathy traits substantially influenced pain judgments. These findings provide a first systematic mapping of the observable facial muscle contractions that drive human pain decoding. The identified facial features are best interpretable in terms of multiple, partly independent patterns of facial response, rather than a single prototypical template of pain expression.

articles.title: The Long Shadow of the Wall: Socialization Signatures in Public-Events Knowledge Across East and West Germany
articles.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Priscilla Achaa-Amankwaa; Oliver Wilhelm
articles.abstract: Germany’s division and subsequent reunification provide a rare historical possibility to examine how regionally segregated information environments are reflected in what people know and how long such differences persist. In a national sample of 1,012 German adults aged 30–80 years, participants completed a 120-item multiple-choice test of public-events knowledge spanning 1960–2019, including items specifically targeting East- and West-German events from the pre-1990 period. While overall knowledge levels were similar among East- and West-socialized respondents, the item-level differences were pronounced, especially for East-specific items in pop culture, arts and literature. Nested cross-validated elastic-net models yielded near-perfect discrimination between East and West socialization in older cohorts (ages 51–80; AUCs > .96), slightly lower discrimination among ages 41–50 (AUC = .93), and a sharp drop in the youngest cohort (ages 30–40; AUC = .67). East-specific items contributed most strongly to classification, which is consistent with the concept of cultural hegemony and an asymmetric information flow. Despite post-1990 convergence, persistent geographic patterns in knowledge profiles remain. Public-events knowledge thus carries a cohort-dependent socialization signature, leaving detectable traces of historical division even after societal convergence.

articles.title: ‘It is my life don’t take that choice from me’: Autistic young adults’ experiences, preferences and needs regarding autistic peer support
articles.authors: Tohid Zarei; Caelan Farr; Maxx Fischer; Summer Marchiori; KJ Hepworth; Caroline Ellison; Tobias Loetscher
articles.abstract: Autistic peer support, as a two-way system of help, is uniquely positioned to address high rates of loneliness and mental health challenges among autistic young adults. We aimed to inform the development of autistic peer support programs aligned with participants’ preferences and needs through a mixed methods online survey study. A total of 73 autistic young adults (aged 18-30; 34 women, 19 non-binary, 11 men, 7 transgender men, 1 transgender woman, 1 undisclosed) completed a survey covering peer interactions, peer support preferences and needs, as well as delivery preferences. While following participatory research processes, we used reflexive thematic analysis to identify an overarching theme: flying together through shared understanding and shared struggles. This maps onto participants’ desire for reciprocal connections that enable understanding and safe unmasking, and their preference for in-person programs adapted to a range of support needs with meaningful participation in decision-making. Autistic Burnout and social connection were most participants’ preferred areas to be addressed. Especially when co-produced or peer-led, autistic peer support programs can contribute to providing a sense of collective movement with preserved self-determination for participants.

articles.title: Infant-directed songs as a source of language input: Do infants segment words from playsongs?
articles.authors: Arina Shandala; Eniko Ladanyi; Mridula Sharma; Natalie Boll-Avetisyan
articles.abstract: Singing is an important communicative feature in caregiver-infant interaction that potentially provides infants with linguistic information. Nonetheless, little is known about how infants process words in songs. Therefore, the present study investigated infants’ ability to segment words from playsongs. German-learning 8-9- and 11-12-month-olds (n = 67, 43% female, 57% male) were familiarized with playsongs containing repetitions of a pseudoword. Subsequently, their word recognition was tested by measuring their looking behavior while listening to spoken familiar and novel pseudowords. Results revealed a significant listening preference for novel over familiar pseudowords in 11-12-month-olds, indicating their ability to segment pseudowords encountered in playsongs (β = -0.14, p = .014). In 8-9-month-olds, no group-level evidence for a preference was detected. Exploratory analyses of music-related questionnaires revealed no links with task performance. Our results provide the first findings that by their first birthday, infants are able to segment words from playsongs, a song genre whose value for learning is commonly assumed but has rarely been studied empirically.

articles.title: From Psychological States to Survey Responses: A Theory of Latent States and Response Style
articles.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles.abstract:
Understanding human behaviour, thoughts, and experiences often relies on self-report measures,
yet responses frequently conflate multiple sources of information. We propose a theory in which
self-reported responses reflect both the constructs being assessed (latent states) and how
respondents choose to communicate that information (response style). We apply this theory to
Likert scale data through the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, an
ordinal-probit approach that separates these sources of variance, yielding cleaner latent state
estimates and interpretable measures of response behaviour. LASARS represents response styles
as stable, three-dimensional signatures describing how individuals map internal experiences onto
response options. Our theory enables quantitative tests of previously difficult-to-evaluate
predictions. Across a series of empirical studies, we show that response styles can be selectively
adjusted to task demands without corresponding changes in latent state expression, and that they
are relatively stable across time and survey instruments, often matching or exceeding the stability
of latent psychological states. We also support a novel prediction: response style information
from one survey can be used to deconfound response style from substantive latent state signal in a
separate survey, even when that survey cannot identify the two. Together, these findings support a
unified theory of self-report responding in which response styles are meaningful, stable, and
informative individual differences rather than mere measurement error. LASARS, therefore,
provides a principled framework for improving the precision, interpretability, and validity of
survey-based measurement.

articles.title: Affective Framing of Environmental News Headlines Influences Engagement, Donations, and Memory
articles.authors: Alyssa Hannah Sinclair; Danielle Cosme; Jose Carreras Tartak; Emily B. Falk
articles.abstract: Negativity captures attention and motivates people to read and share news, but can also harm mental health and sometimes discourage action to address long-term problems like climate change. Negative affect also has complex effects on memory—for example, focal details may be enhanced, but peripheral details can be distorted or forgotten, leaving individuals vulnerable to future misinformation. Here, we investigated an alternate route to increasing engagement with news: evoking positive affect by emphasizing opportunity and progress toward future goals. In two experiments, we adapted environmental news headlines to feature different aspects of each story, emphasizing Crisis or Opportunity. Both Crisis and Opportunity framing (and negative and positive affect, respectively) motivated reading and sharing, relative to the unaltered headlines. Crucially, consistent with theoretical predictions, we identified a trade-off: Crisis framing had the strongest effects on immediate engagement (increasing sharing and real charitable donations), but impaired memory for peripheral details; in contrast, Opportunity framing enhanced memory for news content. In a third study, we investigated real-world engagement with news about climate change by computationally classifying content in >25,000 news headlines on social media; Opportunity and Crisis framing were both associated with increased likes, reposts, and replies. Overall, we demonstrate that the affective framing of news modulates reading, sharing, donations, and memory in laboratory and real-world settings.

articles.title: What Race Means for Health among Black Americans: How Microaggressions Shape Self-Efficacy and Readiness for Behavior Change
articles.authors: Amanda Almond
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives: Persistent racial disparities in cardiovascular health among Black Americans reflect not only structural inequities in the United States, but also the racialized meanings of cardiovascular disease reproduced through public and private health communication. Drawing on ecological systems theory, this research examines how beliefs linking race and cardiovascular disease are reinforced through routine clinical interactions and how these meanings shape health behavior change. Method: Across two experimental mixed-methods studies, a model integrating ecological, social–cognitive, and behavior-change frameworks was tested. In Study 1 (N = 374), health-message framing was experimentally manipulated to examine effects on self-efficacy and decisional balance while controlling for prior experiences of racial microaggression in medical contexts. Study 2 (N = 589) extended this work by testing whether conceptualizations of race as biological/genetic and social/political moderated these effects. A subset of participants (n = 57) voluntarily provided narratives of racially charged healthcare experiences, which were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to contextualize quantitative findings. Results: Racial microaggressions from health professionals disrupted self-efficacy and decisional balance for cardiovascular health behaviors. Endorsement of biological versus social race beliefs moderated these effects, shaping both their magnitude and direction. Qualitative findings revealed how everyday clinical interactions reproduce racialized meanings of disease risk and personal control. Conclusions: These findings identify clinical communication as a consequential site where racial meanings of disease are constructed and psychologically internalized, influencing motivation for health behavior change. Addressing biologically essentialist framing in healthcare may therefore be critical for strengthening self-regulation and reducing cardiovascular disparities among Black Americans.

Keywords: racial microaggressions; health communication; self-efficacy; decisional balance; Transtheoretical Model; ecological systems theory; racial essentialism; cardiovascular health disparities

Public significance statement: How health professionals and public campaigns talk about race matters for behavior change. This research shows that subtle racialized cues in medicine can weaken Black patients’ sense of control and readiness to take preventive action. Training clinicians to avoid biological essentialist framing may improve patient engagement and help reduce cardiovascular health disparities.

articles.title: The Brain Dynamical Repertoire and the Evolution of Clinical Symptoms
articles.authors: Damien Depannemaecker; Florencia Altschuler; Hélène Soydemir; Gabriele Casagrande; Cecilia Gonzalez Campo; Pierpaolo Sorrentino; Antoine Lefrère; Christophe Gauld; VIktor Jirsa
articles.abstract: The brain continuously reconfigures through a repertoire of transient states and transitions. However, most studies on neuropsychiatric disorders still relate symptoms to static or time-averaged measures of brain organization. Here, we review emerging evidence that clinically relevant information is also contained in the brain dynamical repertoire, including the states accessible to an individual, their occupancy, persistence, and transition structure. Across psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, neurological, and neurodegenerative disorders, alterations in these dynamical features have been associated with symptom severity, cognitive impairment, functional outcome, and treatment response. Importantly, emerging longitudinal studies further suggest that brain dynamics can change with clinical state and, in some cases, provide information about subsequent symptom trajectories. We argue that these findings motivate a shift from viewing brain dynamics primarily as cross-sectional correlates of diagnostic categories toward examining how changes in an individual's dynamical repertoire relate to the evolution of symptoms over time.

articles.title: Inconclusive mediated effect of adverse childhood experiences on suicide risk among depressed adolescents: A reanalysis of Ye et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix published by Ye et al., we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model linking adverse childhood experiences to suicide risk in adolescents with depression. We show that the observed associations can be reproduced almost exactly by a different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional assumptions advanced in the original study. Within this alternative framework, self-reported adverse childhood experiences, anhedonia, self-hate, and suicide risk are treated as observable manifestations of a broader construct reflecting core self-evaluation. The results illustrate the challenge of model underdetermination in observational research, whereby competing theoretical accounts may provide equally good representations of the same data. These findings suggest that alternative model specifications should be considered and that correlational evidence alone offers limited support for specific influencing mechanisms.

articles.title: A longitudinal investigation of Germany’s 2025 general election: Implications for system-legitimacy, governmental (dis)trust, and electoral trust
articles.authors: Evan A. Valdes; Rosalind Searle; James H Liu; Cornelia Sindermann
articles.abstract: This registered study examined whether Germany’s 2025 general election shaped system-legitimizing beliefs and governmental (dis)trust, and whether electoral trust moderated these responses over time. Using multiply imputed data from a three-wave online longitudinal panel (N = 518; 1,554 observations), we found that system-legitimizing beliefs increased immediately after the election results were announced but were no longer reliably elevated one month later. More right-leaning respondents reported stronger system-legitimizing beliefs overall, although ideology did not reliably predict change over time. Governmental (dis)trust showed a more politically asymmetric pattern: trust increased among respondents more aligned with the election’s rightward direction, but distrust increased among those less aligned. Electoral trust was associated with stronger system legitimacy and greater governmental trust overall, but did not consistently buffer post-election reactions. At the final wave, higher electoral trust amplified ideological divergence in governmental (dis)trust, including increased distrust among left-leaning respondents. Exploratory party-based analyses further indicated that alignment with the election outcome in a multiparty system depended not only on ideology, but also on party support, coalition participation, and control over governing authority. These findings show that elections can produce distinct system-level and government-specific responses in complex multiparty contexts.

articles.title: Estudio diacrónico de los snowclones del español: un análisis de corpus
articles.authors: Monika Lisowska; Bárbara Marqueta-Gracia; Antonio Benítez-Burraco
articles.abstract: En el presente artículo se aborda la productividad y evolución temporal de una selección de 60 estructuras semiidiomáticas conocidas como snowclones en español a partir de un corpus de textos correspondiente al periodo de 2011-2023. Se compara la frecuencia de uso de cada una de las innovaciones atestiguadas con la de las frases originales de las que proceden. Los resultados muestran que solo un número reducido de patrones genera snowclones altamente productivos, destacando algunos procedentes de los ámbitos del cine y la televisión. Por otro lado, son también escasos aquellos que presentan un comportamiento claramente expansivo en el tiempo, pues la mayoría mantiene una frecuencia estable o descendiente paralela a la de la expresión original. En conjunto, los resultados muestran que la productividad de los snowclones no es homogénea, sino que depende de propiedades estructurales y semánticas que condicionan tanto su difusión como su evolución temporal.

articles.title: Maintenance Orientation in Top-Down Political Communication Increases Pro-Environmental Policy Support
articles.authors: Yael Ecker; Joris Lammers
articles.abstract: Despite overwhelming evidence of the consequences of climate change, many voters—in particular conservatives—oppose pro-environmental policies. Research shows that this opposition can be overcome by reframing the issue in ways that appeal to conservatives’ motives. An important limitation to this literature is that it relies heavily on artificial stimuli in controlled settings, leaving open whether the framing of real political communication shapes conservatives' support for climate action. To address this gap, we examine natural variation in how climate change is framed in top-down political communication across the political spectrum. Drawing on the ternary goal model, we distinguish between progress, maintenance, and protection as three fundamental goals that guide climate action. We propose that maintenance-oriented messaging—reflecting a desire to maintain valued current states—is more effective in increasing conservative political support for climate action. To test this, we use a multilingual machine learning model to rate the goal orientations of pro-environmental policy statements from party platforms across four democracies and then testing voters’ support of these statements. We find that conservatives’ support for pro-environmental statements increases with the degree of maintenance orientation in the text (β = 0.27, p < .001). Moderately strong (+1SD vs -1SD) maintenance orientation reduced the liberal-conservative gap by 31%. In contrast, the degree of progress or protection orientation did not affect conservatives’ support. These findings confirm the importance of policy framing in the debate about climate change and support the practical relevance of maintenance frames to increase conservative support for climate action.

articles.title: “Suicide is cringe!”: Content analysis of 46,071 mental health videos from adolescents’ TikTok feeds
articles.authors: Rebecca Godard; Amber van der Wal; Ine Beyens
articles.abstract: Adolescents frequently watch videos related to mental health on TikTok. Despite significant risks (e.g., pro-suicide/self-harm messages) and opportunities (e.g., helpful resources, social support) posed, there has not yet been a large-scale, comprehensive investigation of this content. To address this gap in the literature, we used data donations to identify 46,071 TikTok videos about mental health viewed by 102 Dutch adolescents over a five-year period. Using a combination of supervised automated and manual content analysis approaches, we described the topics, content presentation styles, and creators of these videos. Videos were primarily related to mental health symptoms and experiences (e.g., anxiety and depressive symptoms) and mental health disorders (e.g., autism, depression, eating disorders), with a smaller number discussing positive aspects of mental health (e.g., recovery, coping) and mental health treatment. Videos predominantly shared personal experiences, often in a humorous and/or supportive manner; with relatively few videos presenting information or giving advice. The majority of videos discussed the creator’s own experiences with mental health, with few videos created by self-described mental health experts. Harmful elements, such as pro-suicide or eating disorder messages, were rare. We identified strong gendered patterns in both the creators and viewers of mental health videos, pointing to specific areas of concern for girls (eating disorders and body image) and boys (suicide). Overall, this content analysis paints a nuanced picture of the mental health content viewed by adolescents. Findings highlight the need for more expansive theories of the multifaceted impacts of mental health content, and for interventions that empower adolescents to capitalize on the opportunities provided by this content while minimizing potential harms.

articles.title: Revisiting Parental Strictness: Integrating When into How Parents Engage in Socialization
articles.authors: Huiguang Ren
articles.abstract: Parenting research has richly examined how parents socialize children, including whether responses are warm, controlling, autonomy-supportive, harsh, or culturally meaningful. This article argues that a complementary question remains undertheorized: when do parents respond and engage in socialization? I define parental strictness as the response thresholds through which parents decide whether children’s behavior is good or bad enough to warrant specific types of socialization. I next propose the Strictness Framework that distinguishes positive strictness from negative strictness, behavioral strictness from cognitive strictness, and their domain-specific patterns of stability and change. Crossing positive and negative strictness yields four strictness styles—disciplinarian, withholding, regulatory, and nurturing—that may shape children’s tendencies of engagement and disengagement as well as their openness to socialization. Integrating when into how parents engage in socialization clarifies familiar parenting patterns and generates new questions about development across cultures, contexts, and developmental domains.

articles.title: Why don't the victims of bullying seek help? The effect of underestimating bystanders’ defending intentions
articles.authors: Guanghui Chen; Zhang anyi; fan Wang; Li Chao; Pei Yongshun; Wei Cui; Wenxin Zhang
articles.abstract: Seeking help from others is an important strategy for coping with difficult situations; however, victims of bullying are often reluctant to seek help. Using a series of behavioral experiments with 968 primary and secondary school students, the present study examined individuals’ prediction bias regarding bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective, its association with willingness to seek help, and whether this bias could be modified through an information-based intervention. The results showed that participants reported significantly lower levels of bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective than from the bystander perspective, indicating a systematic underestimation of bystanders’ willingness to defend. This underestimation bias was robust across different types of bullying, genders, and educational stages. Greater underestimation of bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective significantly predicted lower willingness to seek help. Positive contextual information cues significantly reduced the underestimation bias and increased willingness to seek help, whereas negative contextual information cues significantly increased the underestimation bias and decreased willingness to seek help. These findings provide a plausible explanation for victims’ reluctance to seek help and offer practical implications for enhancing help-seeking willingness in school bullying prevention and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Engagement begins at recruitment: Comparing videoconference verification to passive online screening for participant retention and study engagement
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Howard; Johanna Peetz
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers who conduct studies online increasingly struggle with fraudulent respondents, programmable bots, inattention or carelessness, and ineligible impostors. This study tested whether participants in a longitudinal intervention study who were recruited using videoconference eligibility verification—meeting participants one by one on Zoom to verify their identities—were more engaged in the study tasks and showed better longitudinal retention. Using existing data from a sample of Canadian young adult women (N = 1,257), we compared participants who were screened via videoconference to participants who were passively screened (i.e., possessed valid email addresses) and participants who were pre-screened members of a commercial participant platform (Prolific.com) on seven measures of retention and six measures of engagement with study tasks. Results showed that videoconference verified participants had better rates of study initiation and retention, with over 90% completing all study waves. However, we found no meaningful differences between recruitment streams as a function of time to survey completion, engagement with the study’s intervention activities, or honest responding. Videoconference eligibility verification may be a practical tool for recruiting participants likely to remain enrolled in longitudinal research and limit attrition.

articles_hidden.title: Electrophysiological signatures of statistical segmentation: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Liesa Ravijts; Isabella Toselli Prequero Sbrocco; Brent Vernaillen; Rodrigo Dal Ben; Débora de Hollanda Souza; Louisa Bogaerts
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning (SL), the ability to extract regularities from continuous sensory input, is widely studied using segmentation in embedded pattern learning (EPL) paradigms. Different electrophysiological measures, including event-related potentials (ERPs), steady-state responses (SSRs), and event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs), have been proposed as neural signatures of statistical segmentation. However, the extent to which these measures provide consistent evidence remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of EEG and MEG studies to assess the evidence for these signatures in the current literature. After screening 635 records, 39 studies (46 experiments) contributed to the quantitative synthesis. We conducted separate meta-analyses of four signatures: N1 and N400 pattern-onset effects, emergence of pattern-rate SSRs, and suppression of item-rate SSRs. The results provided some evidence for an N400 effect and strong evidence for pattern-rate SSR enhancement, whereas neither N1 nor item-rate SSR effects reached statistical significance. No moderation effects were observed across the tested characteristics, with the exception of contrast type, which significantly moderated the N400 effect. A comparative model further indicated that pattern-rate SSRs provided the most robust evidence of statistical segmentation. We discuss how our results inform the interpretation of these signatures as neural indices of statistical segmentation and outline directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Speech Onset Time at Home or in the Lab: The Role of Testing Environment and Experimenter Presence.
articles_hidden.authors: Giorgio Piazza; Natalia Kartushina; Christoforos Souganidis; James E. Flege; Clara Martin
articles_hidden.abstract: Psycholinguistic research has become increasingly reliant on online experimentation, which has also grown more attractive for studying speech production. However, concerns remain about data quality in online settings and the absence of experimenters to ensure participant engagement. In this pre-registered study, we used two tasks—picture naming and reading aloud—to test whether the lexical frequency effect (Low Frequency words > High Frequency words) on speech onset times can be reliably detected in online environments (run at Home), both with and without experimenter supervision. Participants completed the same tasks under four conditions, varying by Supervision (between-subjects: Supervised vs. Unsupervised) and Environment (within-subjects: Lab vs. Home): Lab-Supervised, HomeSupervised, Lab-Unsupervised, and Home-Unsupervised. Frequency effects emerged across all conditions except Home-Supervised for the reading aloud task, where the effect was in the expected direction but non-significant (~12 ms). All other conditions yielded consistent frequency effects (~17–38 ms), comparable to previous online and lab-based findings. Notably, participants were faster at home than in the lab (~10 ms), and unsupervised settings yielded the largest effect sizes, suggesting that experimenter presence may inadvertently dampen subtle effects, possibly due to increased self-monitoring or reduced comfort. These findings validate the use of online platforms for speech production research and highlight the nuanced influence of supervision on experimental outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Pre-Post Comparisons: A Comprehensive Effect Size Framework for Intensive Longitudinal Interventions via Time-Varying Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaohui Luo; Yue Liu; Hongyun Liu; Laura Francina Bringmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Intensive longitudinal interventions (ILIs), which deliver repeated interventions in people’s daily lives while intensively tracking their psychological states, offer unique opportunities for ecologically valid, real-time, and personalized support. However, there is a striking mismatch between the richness of the data these studies generate and the simplicity of the methods used to evaluate them: evaluations still rely largely on pre-post mean comparisons that collapse dozens or even hundreds of observations per person into a few summary statistics. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a comprehensive effect size framework based on Bayesian multilevel time-varying autoregressive (TV-AR) models within the generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) approach. The framework organizes effect sizes along four dimensions: subject level (population-average, individual-specific, and between-group), parameter type (mean level, autoregressive effect, and variance), temporal scale (integrated and time-specific), and study phase (active intervention and post-intervention decay). These metrics move researchers beyond whether an intervention works to when effects emerge, plateau, or fade, how the intervention reshapes the dynamics and stability of a process, and for whom it is effective. We demonstrate the framework with data from a mindfulness-based ILI targeting negative affect, in which an intervention and a control group were assessed before and during the intervention, and provide openly available annotated R code and a tutorial. Overall, the framework provides a practical and flexible toolkit for evaluating ILIs, supporting the broader shift toward a more dynamic, process-oriented, and personalized intervention science.

articles_hidden.title: Configurations of Mother-Child and Father-Child Attachment Relationships as Predictors  of Child Social Competence: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Or Dagan; Carlo Schuengel; Sheri Madigan; Glenn I. Roisman; Marian Bakermans-Kranenburg; Marinus H. van IJzendoorn; Marije Verhage; Robbie Duschinsky; Abraham Sagi-Schwartz; Jean-François Bureau
articles_hidden.abstract: Attachment theory posits that early child-caregiver relationships shape socioemotional development. Social competence has received particular attention both because it is theoretically expected to be shaped by early attachment relationships and due to its well-established associations with children’s mental health and adjustment. However, most research has examined a single child-parent relationship, typically the child-mother dyad, overlooking the simultaneous attachment relationships many children form with other significant caregivers. In this study, we used individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis to test whether mother-child and father-child attachment configurations uniquely predict children’s social competence. This pre-registered two-step IPD meta-analysis included studies that assessed child attachment relationships with both mothers and fathers using observational measures, and children’s social competence using parent, teacher, or observer reports. Effects computed for 16 studies, comprising 1,585 children, were synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Children with two insecure attachment relationships showed significantly lower social competence compared to those with one or two secure attachments (g = 0.20, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35]). No difference was observed between children with one versus two secure attachment relationships. We found no evidence that the number of disorganized attachment relationships predicted social competence. Across attachment configurations, mother-child and father-child attachment relationship quality did not differentially predict social competence. The presence of at least one secure attachment relationship, whether with the mother or father, may buffer against the risks of having two insecure attachments for children’s social competence. These findings add to the growing evidence that attachment relationships with mothers and fathers are similarly important in predicting key developmental outcomes. In contrast, organized versus disorganized attachment configurations were not reliably associated with social competence, raising both methodological and conceptual questions.

articles_hidden.title: Steering Generative AI Toward Developmentally Supportive Learning: The SCAFFOLD Framework and a Pilot in a School Setting
articles_hidden.authors: Olga Muss
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents are the fastest-growing users of Large Language Models (LLMs) and many LLM-powered toys are entering homes, transforming their environment. Yet these tools were not designed for their educational, emotional, and developmental needs. Children are particularly vulnerable because their skills are immature, knowledge limited and they are undergoing sensitive periods of development, when the foundations are being laid. Safe, developmentally and pedagogically grounded design for interactions with LLMs are therefore essential for limiting risks and harvesting benefits of this technology. This thesis presents the Steered Contextual AI Framework for Orchestrating Learning Dialogue (SCAFFOLD), which builds upon its technical framework, a layered reliability framework that surrounds LLM-generated text and speech with external verification, targeted repair, and safe fallback, to enable to steer LLM’s behavior towards its conceptual framework that operationalizes the knowledge from developmental psychology and neuroscience, science of learning, science of education and pedagogy and the science of human-computer interactions. Model-agnostic and privacy-preserving, SCAFFOLD helps educators to configure interactions with AI that support safety, learning and development, with transparency and modularity. The thesis includes a piloted minimal SCAFFOLD prototype tested in a classroom with 12–16-year-olds using an LLM-powered social robot in a multi-user co-creation task, where students collaboratively designed a mnemonic on a previously covered topic. Preliminary findings showed that, compared to a prompt-only LLM, the SCAFFOLD prototype elicited more student activity, engagement, and on-topic participation. Co-creation level was associated with post-test knowledge scores after controlling for prior knowledge. These findings provide initial evidence for SCAFFOLD's feasibility and potential to support engagement and learning in educational settings.

articles_hidden.title: COVID-19 Impacts and Child Psychological Distress: A Twin Direction-of-Causation Study
articles_hidden.authors: Mandeep Singh; Hongcui Du; Callie W. Little; Sara Ann Hart
articles_hidden.abstract: COVID-19 disrupted children's social, economic, and psychological circumstances, yet the causal direction of this association with child distress remains unresolved. We applied twin Direction of Causation (DoC) modeling to 579 twin families (183 MZ, 396 DZ pairs; grades 3–12) from the NatPAT COVID 2022 survey. COVID-19 impacts were modeled as a latent construct spanning social, economic, and COVID-specific stress domains; distress was indexed by anxiety and perceived stress. The two constructs showed different genetic and environmental influences: COVID-19 impacts were predominantly environmental, distress substantially heritable, yet were strongly associated (r = .706). Modeling favoured a unidirectional path from COVID-19 impacts to distress per our preregistered tiebreaker (β = .703, p < .001; ΔAIC = 0.29), although this small margin does not rule out a bidirectional relation. These findings suggest that reducing pandemic-related disruptions, rather than targeting stress responses alone, may help protect child mental health during future societal disruptions.

articles_hidden.title: When truthful innocent suspects become less forthcoming: Effects of memory constraints in SUE-based mock interviews
articles_hidden.authors: Helen Wyler; Martina Buchli; Flavia Zaidi-Tinner
articles_hidden.abstract: Past Strategic Use of Evidence studies found innocent suspects to be forthcoming, but usually implicitly assume that they can remember the critical details needed to provide evidence-consistent accounts. Building on Sukumar et al. (2018), we examined how encoding intentionality, retention interval, and type of critical detail affect forthcomingness in a mock investigative interview (S1; N = 193) and observers’ veracity judgements (S2; N = 402). Encoding intentionality had no statistically significant effect. The three-week retention interval substantially reduced forthcomingness among innocent suspects relative to immediate retrieval, although guilty suspects remained less forthcoming. Delayed innocent suspects were descriptively more likely to be judged as deceptive, but this effect was not confirmed by the preregistered interaction. Exploratory analyses suggested that incidental details were both most vulnerable to delay and associated with deception judgements. The findings highlight the importance of conceptualising forthcomingness as a function of both strategic information management and memory constraints.

articles_hidden.title: Towards a genetics of mental disorders as complex dynamical systems: A symptom-specific and symptom-interactive approach
articles_hidden.authors: Omid V. Ebrahimi; Michel Guillaume Nivard; Ludvig Daae Bjørndal
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychiatric genetics has largely mapped genetic liability onto diagnoses and symptom sum scores. Yet these disorder-level phenotypes are heterogeneous composites: individuals sharing a diagnosis may exhibit markedly different symptoms; the same symptoms recur across multiple disorders; and symptoms influence one another over time. Genetic analyses based on such aggregates may therefore obscure symptom-specific biological signals and overlook the dynamic processes through which genetic liability becomes expressed clinically. We propose a complementary symptom-specific and symptom-interactive framework that conceptualises psychiatric disorders as dynamic systems of mutually influencing symptoms. This framework distinguishes three forms of genetic influence: direct effects of genetic risk on individual symptoms; indirect effects propagated through symptom-to-symptom pathways; and examinations of how genetic risk moderates the strength, persistence, and activation potential of symptom interactions. We show how various genetic and psychometric methods can be integrated to investigate these processes. We identify four priorities for psychiatric genetics research that can be advanced by adopting this framework: improving symptom-level phenotyping; distinguishing disorder-specific and transdiagnostic symptoms; modelling mediated genetic effects across symptoms; and testing whether genetic liability shapes symptom co-activation and their temporal dynamics. Reframing psychopathology as systems of interacting symptoms could sharpen genes-to-phenotype mapping, clarify heterogeneity in illness trajectories, and align psychiatric genetics more closely with novel mechanistic theories of mental disorders and the goals of precision psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: The Functional Connectivity of Hallucinations in Psychiatric Disorders and Neurodegenerative Disorders: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Yifan Ren; Huyen Ngoc Pham; Xiong Xiong; Shun-Chin Jim Wu; Emilio Fernandez-Egea; John T. O’Brien; Graham Murray; John suckling
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Hallucinations span psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders, yet unified neurobiological or consciousness-based explanations remain uncertain. Functional connectivity (FC) provides a network-level view with highly heterogeneous findings.
Methods: Following PRISMA, we included studies with FC of hallucinations to ask whether it is sensitive to hallucinations, can distinguish different disorders, and if adopted theories are explanatory. 
Results: 198 studies were included, with far fewer studies in neurodegenerative (35) than psychiatric disorders (163). Across conditions, hallucinations consistently involved dysconnectivity among default mode (DMN), salience (SN), central executive (CEN), sensory systems, and subcortical circuits. Shared alterations included disrupted SN modulation of sensory gating, altered DMN-sensory coupling and within DMN coherence, limbic system involvement, and reduced CEN regulation of perceptual networks. Disorder‑specific patterns were evident: psychiatric hallucinations preferentially involved auditory-language networks, cortico‑striatal circuits, and salience hubs, whereas neurodegenerative hallucinations were characterised by visual and attentional network dysfunction, including dorsal and ventral attention systems and visual cortices.
Conclusions: FC is sensitive to hallucinations and shows different disorder-linked patterns while revealing shared mechanisms, supporting the transdiagnostic nature of hallucinations at the level of functional brain networks. Despite the involvement of multiple transdiagnostic networks, the current literature does not converge on a unified cognitive or consciousness-based theory of hallucinations, underscoring a critical theoretical gap and the need for integrative models.

articles_hidden.title: Can Large Language Models Simulate Child-Like Theory of Mind?
articles_hidden.authors: Anja Brand; Tobias Wingen; Oliver Christ
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified debates about the validity of using silicon samples, of artificial participants simulated by AI. This question is especially relevant for developmental psychology, where valid simulation requires models not only to solve tasks, but also to reproduce age-typical limitations in cognitive ability. We tested whether standard autoregressive models (e.g., OpenAI's GPT-4) and more advanced reasoning models can simulate such developmental trajectories in Theory of Mind (ToM). Six LLMs were prompted with child-age personas ranging from 2.5 to 6.0 years and completed classic false-belief tasks. Most models showed strong baseline ToM performance, and many also successfully downplayed their abilities in line with human developmental trajectories. However, performance varied substantially across model type, provider, and task. These findings suggest that silicon sampling may be promising for developmental research, but relying on silicon samples alone is not yet a valid method.

articles_hidden.title: Social influence and information cascades in experience-based decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Kiri Kuroda; Simon Kai Ciranka; Dirk U. Wulff; Ralf Kurvers
articles_hidden.abstract: Many consequential decisions are made in environments where outcome probabilities are not explicitly described but must be inferred from experience. In most modern environments, this information search takes place in the presence of others. Yet, the role of social influence in experience-based decisions has been largely overlooked, leaving it unclear how personal and social information combine to shape what people sample, when they stop searching, and what they finally choose. Here, we address all three decision stages. In a preregistered study, participants could freely sample two options before making a final choice, either alone (solo condition) or while observing the final choices of their group members (group condition). We developed a modeling framework and show that social influence left sampling unaffected but altered stopping and choice. Participants searched longer when the group was more divided and stopped earlier when the majority choice agreed with their own personal sampling information. Consequently, they drew fewer samples and encountered fewer rare events than solo participants. When choosing, group members copied others' choices only when their personal information was ambiguous. Comparing decision sequences in groups with a solo baseline, complemented with agent-based simulations, showed that this strategy gave rise to mild information cascades, with decisions in groups being more similar to each other than in a solo baseline. Our results reveal how social influence shapes search, stopping, and choice, and how these individual-level decision rules scale up to collective dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: The context-dependent evolution of structure learning and metacognition
articles_hidden.authors: Rochelle Kaper; Megan A. K. Peters
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans learn multiple probabilistic regularities at once, and often without feedback, which may be aided by metacognitive evaluations throughout learning. To understand this learning-metacognition relationship, we must first characterize how both capacities co-evolve as environmental structures are internalized, especially when feedback is unavailable. Here, participants learned a two-level probabilistic environment in which stimulus co-occurrences were embedded within a sequence, using unfamiliar fractals and familiar line drawings in a two-session, within-subjects design (N=63; N=50 completed both sessions). For each stimulus set, we measured learning across six repeating exposure-test cycles, using a cover task during exposure phases and forced-choice questions in test phases; test questions also included confidence judgments. Results revealed stimulus- and structure-dependent learning and metacognitive signatures. First, learning dynamics differed across stimuli: fractal sequence test accuracy outpaced co-occurrence accuracy, but vice versa for line drawings. Further, confidence increased across blocks, and was higher for line drawings as well as co-occurrences and first but not second sequence selections. Finally, both metacognitive sensitivity and test accuracy increased in successive exposure-test cycles for fractals, but metacognitive sensitivity remained stagnant for line drawings even as test accuracy improved. These results demonstrate that structure learning and metacognitive processes are highly context- and complexity-dependent rather than being completely generalizable. This study informs future directions for refining theories of learning without feedback, including how people evaluate their own learning and uncertainty and the interaction of both cognitive abilities with task design, stimuli, and environmental structures.

articles_hidden.title: Integrating science and design in the development of Detour: A mobile intervention for youth smoking cessation
articles_hidden.authors: Suhaavi Kochhar; Maartje Luijten; Ken Koontz; Hanneke Scholten
articles_hidden.abstract: Digital smoking cessation interventions for adolescents and young adults (AYAs) often either lack a strong evidence base or fail to engage their intended users. Integrating psychological science with design-based methods offers a promising route to interventions, yet the processes behind such integration are rarely reported in detail. In this paper, we describe the development of Detour, a mobile smoking cessation intervention for AYAs, redesigned from an earlier app (HitnRun) using the Bloombox Toolkit to integrate science and design throughout. We describe how six psychological mechanisms including smoking cue devaluation and delay discounting were translated into intervention components. We used an iterative, interdisciplinary process involving behavioural scientists, app designers, and an ongoing youth advisory board. Additionally, we included over 380 AYAs across focus groups, play tests, and qualitative questionnaires. We then reflect on our experience integrating design and science for intervention development and share practical challenges encountered, including budgeting for interdisciplinary teams, retaining youth participants, and regulatory delays. By reporting these processes and challenges transparently, we aim to support other researchers in designing digital health interventions that are both scientifically grounded and engaging for their target users.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial biases in Arithmetic: The Effect of Operation Order and Visual Spacing on Calculations
articles_hidden.authors: Martyna Sroka; Michał Obidziński; Krzysztof Cipora; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual layout is known to affect computational performance, yet its relation to response format and numerical proficiency remains unclear. This preregistered study examined whether spatial presentation modulates arithmetic problem-solving. We conceptually replicated Experiment 3 of Landy and Goldstone's (2010) study using the Precedence and Proximity Task in a forced-choice format. Additionally, we assessed arithmetic fluency using a speeded test. A total of 201 adults solved 200 mixed addition–multiplication expressions in which spacing either aligned or conflicted with order-of-operations rules. Operation order was also manipulated. Participants were faster and more accurate in congruent spacing conditions, whereas incongruent spacing increased operation-order errors, especially when problems began with addition. A subgroup of participants showed disproportionately poor performance under incongruent spacing, suggesting a prepotent susceptibility to misleading grouping cues. The spacing effect persisted despite differences in task format and response procedure compared to the original study, supporting its robustness. Higher arithmetic fluency was associated with higher accuracy and shorter reaction times in the Precedence and Proximity Task. These findings corroborate that visuospatial layout biases symbolic computation and that individuals differ in their susceptibility to it.

articles_hidden.title: Preparing the University for Generation Alpha: A Research Agenda for the Digital Transformation of Higher Education
articles_hidden.authors: Sandra Grinschgl; Malte Elson; Tina Hascher; Andre Klostermann; Etna Rosa Krakenberger; Adrian Ritz; Thomas Christian Sauter; Amanda Zurkirchen; Michael Schulte-Mecklenbeck
articles_hidden.abstract: Generation Alpha, a cohort growing up with smartphones and generative AI as ordinary features of everyday life, will soon enter a higher education system that is itself undergoing profound digital transformation. We argue that the central challenge of this transformation is not technological alone but human and that it is shaped by three fundamental tensions: upskilling vs. deskilling, autonomy vs. dependence, and individualization vs. collaboration. Developed by an interdisciplinary Community of Practice at the University of Bern (UniBE), we introduce the BRIDGE model, which conceptualizes the university as an ecosystem of three interdependent groups: students, academic (researchers and lecturers) and organizational support staff whose psycho-social, health, well-being, and performance competencies must be understood across the trajectory from school to working life. Building on this model, we propose a two-phase research agenda: systematic identification of competencies, expectations, and institutional processes through a multi-year, longitudinal research program spanning all three groups, followed by collaborative transformation of higher education through empirically evaluated interventions. This agenda provides what digital transformation in higher education currently lacks: an empirical basis for deciding where digital tools strengthen learning, work, and well-being--and where they undermine them--and tested interventions to shift that balance. It thereby operationalizes UniBE's Digitalization Strategy 2030 and responds to national as well as international calls for evidence-based, human-centered digital transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Normative and Maladaptive Personality Traits in Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative and Hierarchical Analysis of HEXACO and PID-5
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Weiß; Johanna Hepp; Katja Isabell Seitz; Yun-Loe Laura Lai; Nikolaus Kleindienst; Sylvia Steinmann; Katja Bertsch; Inga Niedtfeld
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of personality pathology invite the question of how normative and maladaptive trait systems jointly characterize borderline personality disorder (BPD). This study examined how the HEXACO model of personality and the DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders trait system, operationalized with the Personality Inventory for DSM–5, differentiate individuals with BPD from mentally healthy control (HC) individuals, both separately and jointly.
Methods: Data from two assessment waves of a large clinical research program were combined into a final sample of 575 participants (233 with BPD, 342 HC). A joint item-level PCA was conducted to examine seven- and eleven-component solutions, and a Bass-Ackwards principal components analysis was conducted to examine the joint hierarchical structure of HEXACO and PID-5 items. Both instruments were administered as self-reports. 
Results: Compared with HC, individuals with BPD showed lower HEXACO Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness, and higher Emotionality, as well as higher scores on all PID-5 domains, particularly Negative Affectivity and Disinhibition. In the combined domain model, low Extraversion and high  PID-5 Negative Affectivity, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism uniquely predicted BPD status. At the facet level, low Social Self-Esteem (HEXACO) and high Emotional Lability (PID-5) were especially discriminative. Joint item analyses yielded a sevencomponent solution in which six components corresponded closely to the six HEXACO factors and a dominant seventh component represented broad maladaptivity, with PID-5 items loading positively and HEXACO items largely loading inversely. Group differences were almost entirely confined to this broad component. 
Conclusions: These findings suggest that BPD is characterized by both a broad maladaptivity dimension and a more specific trait profile involving affective instability, interpersonal insecurity, irritability, and reduced behavioral control. The findings support integrating normative and maladaptive trait models in  the dimensional description of BPD, while indicating that the dominant joint dimension cannot be interpreted unambiguously as a substantive general factor of personality pathology.

articles_hidden.title: Translation and Validation of the Japanese version of the Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (J-APEQ)
articles_hidden.authors: Kaishu Iijima; Hiroto Yamamoto; Yuko Yotsumoto; Shuhei Iimura
articles_hidden.abstract: Picky eating is a multidimensional eating behavior that has been studied primarily in children, although it is also observed in adults. The Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (APEQ) was developed to assess multiple dimensions of picky eating in adults, but a validated Japanese version has not been available. The present study aimed to develop and validate a Japanese version of the APEQ (J-APEQ) (Researcher-led translation) and to compare it with a translation generated using generative artificial intelligence (AI-generated translation). The researcher-led translation was completed by 892 Japanese adults, with 210 participants completing the scale again after three weeks. A separate sample of 939 participants completed an AI-generated translation. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original four-factor structure of the researcher-led J-APEQ, and a second-order factor model also showed acceptable fit. The composite score showed adequate internal consistency, while reliability was lower for some subscales, particularly Meal Disengagement and Taste Aversion. Test–retest reliability was moderate, and correlations with food neophobia, disgust, and eating-attitude measures generally supported convergent validity. The AI-generated translation showed a factor structure and reliability broadly comparable to those of the researcher-led translation. Measurement invariance analyses supported configural, threshold, metric, and partial scalar invariance between the two versions. In the present study, however, the researcher-led translation was the version formally validated and established as the Japanese APEQ (J-APEQ), whereas the AI-generated translation was included for comparison. These findings support the use of the J-APEQ for assessing picky eating in Japanese adults and suggest that generative AI may be useful as a tool for psychological scale translation, although human review and validation remain necessary.

articles_hidden.title: Memory reactivation levels remain unaffected by anticipated interference
articles_hidden.authors: Nursena Ataseven; I. Efsane Algın; Duygu Yucel; Berna Güler; Lara Todorova; Keisuke Fukuda; Eren Gunseli
articles_hidden.abstract: Most daily tasks require frequent information exchange between working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM). However, the factors that modulate the reactivation of LTMs in WM remain to be explored. Here, we tested the effects of anticipated perceptual interference (in Experiment 1) and anticipated dual task interference (in Experiment 2) on reactivation of LTMs in WM using contralateral delay activity (CDA) in the EEG. On each trial, participants saw one or three previously studied or novel objects that were tested after a brief retention interval. In half of the blocks, the retention contained perceptual distractors (Experiment 1) or dual task interference (Experiment 2). In both experiments, the CDA prior to the interference period was similar regardless of the anticipated interference. Additionally, we measured contralateral alpha power suppression as an index of spatial attention. We found that spatial attention allocated to the memorized objects’ locations also was not modulated with anticipated interference. These findings indicate that anticipating interference does not influence the extent to which WM is engaged in representing information stored in LTM.

articles_hidden.title: Healthy attachment for the parents? An investigation on the association between attachment parenting and parental mental health.
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Schlier; Hanna Laura Meder; Mira-Pauline Grapentin; Nora Imlau
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction. Attachment parenting (AP) became popular for it promotes responsive caregiving, but has been criticized for over-extensively translating attachment research into challenging parenting standards, mirroring detrimental intensive-parenting beliefs that adversely affect parental health. Meanwhile, evidence on AP remains limited and assessments of AP-beliefs and AP-practice are lacking. This study aims to develop and validate an AP-questionnaire and test the associations between AP and parental mental health and explore the mediating role of intensive-parenting beliefs.
Methods. In a preregistered cross-sectional online-survey, 1664 parents (98.5% mothers) of children aged up to six years answered an extensive item-list assessing AP-beliefs and AP implementation into practice, an intensive parenting questionnaire, and mental health measures. Confirmatory factor analyses were used for AP-questionnaire validation and correlation- and mediation-analyses for exploring the association between AP and mental health.
Results. A 26-item AP-questionnaire was extracted that assesses AP-beliefs and AP- practice, both for the global AP-approach and seven individual core-principles. AP-indicators consistently showed small/minimal correlations with better mental health, whereas mediation analyses revealed parallel, opposing pathways: a positive, direct association from AP to mental health (possibly explained via parental fulfilment) and adverse indirect pathways through intensive-parenting beliefs (challenge-/self-sacrifice and essentialist-beliefs).
Conclusion. AP may be neither uniformly beneficial nor harmful. Rather, it can foster parental fulfilment which increases parental well-being, but also instil dysfunctional beliefs about sacrifice and unavoidable strain that increase parental-stress. To improve evidence-based personalized parenting-recommendations, longitudinal research is needed to disentangle when AP fosters positive parental identity and when it reinforces parental vulnerabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Material Life Satisfaction Increases Willingness to Engage in Costly Climate Action
articles_hidden.authors: Fabian Dablander; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles_hidden.abstract: Addressing climate change requires sustained public support for policies and willingness to engage in actions that may incur personal costs. Understanding the social conditions under which citizens are willing to support such measures is important for assessing the feasibility of ambitious climate action. Using data from a large, population-weighted survey of Dutch citizens (N = 22,749) and covariate adjustments informed by directed acyclic graphs, we estimate the effect of different facets of life satisfaction on willingness to contribute 1% of monthly household income to address climate change. We find a strong effect of material life satisfaction: individuals who are very satisfied with their material conditions are more than three times more likely to be willing to contribute than those who are not satisfied at all. In contrast, satisfaction with social life, physical health, and mental health show weak or negligible independent effects on willingness once material life satisfaction and relevant background variables are taken into account. We discuss the implications of our results for the design and acceptability of climate policies that are perceived as placing burdens on households.

articles_hidden.title: Human outcome-irrelevant value learning is insensitive to its monetary cost
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Noham Wolpe; Nitzan Shahar
articles_hidden.abstract: When learning from reinforcement, individuals should assign credit selectively to features of their actions that causally determine outcomes. Yet, even when explicit instructions and extensive experience clarify which action features predict reward, humans assign credit to outcome-irrelevant features, leading to suboptimal choices. Here, we use computational modeling to test if this suboptimal credit assignment can be controlled depending on the monetary cost at stake. Specifically, we tested whether higher payoffs can increase control over outcome-irrelevant credit assignment. Participants (N = 287) completed a multi-armed bandit task under low and high monetary stakes. Higher stakes increased the influence of outcome-relevant values on choice, but, strikingly, had no influence on outcome-irrelevant values, which influenced choices to a similar degree. These findings demonstrate the automatic nature of credit assignment to outcome-irrelevant features, suggesting that associations between features and reward are formed despite clear instructions and their detrimental consequences for monetary gains.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the effect of briefing modality on participant experiences, data quality, and data quantity in an experience sampling study
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Hutasoit; Milla Pihlajamäki; Ginette Lafit; Olivia J Kirtley; Inez Myin-Germeys; Gudrun Eisele
articles_hidden.abstract: The Experience Sampling Method (ESM) requires participants to repeatedly complete assessments in daily life, typically without direct researcher supervision. Participant briefing is therefore an important opportunity to prepare participants to follow the protocol independently, but the effects of different characteristics of briefings are poorly understood. This quasi-experimental study examined whether online versus in-person briefing influenced data quantity (compliance), data quality (careless responding), and participant experiences (participant burden, perceived briefing sufficiency). First-year psychology students (N=249) were assigned to an online (n=209) or in-person (n=40) briefing condition based on recruitment phase and completed a seven-day ESM protocol with 10 daily prompts. Results showed that briefing modality did not significantly affect mean levels of compliance, careless responding, participant burden, or perceived briefing sufficiency. However, the effect of briefing modality on compliance changed over time: initial compliance was higher and declined more steeply in the online briefing condition than in the in-person briefing condition, although both conditions reached descriptively similar compliance rates by the end of the study. No significant interactions with time were found for careless responding or momentary burden. These findings suggest that online briefing may be a viable alternative to in-person briefing in relatively short and straightforward ESM protocols. However, in-person briefing may support more sustained compliance over time. Future research should replicate these findings in fully experimental designs and examine whether briefing modality matters more in other samples or longer or more demanding ESM studies.

articles_hidden.title: Physical endpoint contact enhances visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback in virtual reality
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan George King; Guy Wallis
articles_hidden.abstract: When reaching for a visually defined target, sensory information not only guides the preparation and execution of the reaching response but also serves as a crucial source of error feedback. Research on visually guided reaching has typically emphasised the contribution of visual feedback to movement preparation and execution.  However, visually guided reaching also depends on non-visual sensory information. Here, we focus on the role of haptic endpoint feedback and visual hand feedback and how they interact to regulate behaviour. Thirty-six participants completed a rapid reaching task using a virtual reality head-mounted display, allowing us to manipulate endpoint haptic feedback and visual feedback of the moving hand. Participants completed a vibrotactile feedback condition, providing vibration feedback to the fingertip upon target touch, and a vibrotactile and physical contact feedback condition, providing additional physical surface contact. On 25% of trials, the virtual hand disappeared after movement initiation. The addition of physical contact led participants to initiate movement earlier, increase movement times, and spend proportionally more time decelerating, resulting in improved endpoint accuracy. Across kinematic measures, the effects of physical contact did not interact with visual hand feedback. Additionally, of six presence and embodiment items, only the item asking whether touch felt like one's own differed between conditions. Overall, these findings suggest physical contact improves visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback alone. However, this advantage appears to be selective, increasing the realism of touch rather than overall presence or embodiment and not compensating for a loss of visual feedback of the hand.

articles_hidden.title: The Unified Model Graph: Drawing the Statistical Models of Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Hsiu Ting Ting Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists describe their statistical models with diagrams. The conventions in use, path diagrams, multilevel panels, plate notation, and causal graphs, each grew inside one modeling tradition, and they disagree on basic symbols. As a result, one figure can stand for two different models. An ellipse with three arrows can show a factor model or a latent profile model. A labeled arrow can show a fixed slope or a person-varying slope. A mediation triangle can show a regression decomposition or a causal claim. This article introduces the Unified Model Graph (UMG), a notation built so that the figure identifies the model that was fitted. Three visual cues type every quantity: fill for observed versus latent, shape for continuous versus categorical, and outline for inferential role. Four edge types separate regression, covariance, deterministic, and mixture relations. Plates mark replication, and a badge states whether the figure makes a causal claim. Every well-formed UMG corresponds to exactly one family of distributions, and path diagrams, plate notation, and causal graphs are special cases; the formal results and proofs are in the supplemental material. The accompanying R package \pkg{} builds diagrams from code or from fitted lavaan, lme4, mirt, and brms objects, validates them, translates them to and from lavaan syntax, checks necessary identification conditions, derives testable implications, and generates model-implied data displays. A benchmark of eight R diagramming packages on ten representational features and ten operations locates what the notation adds. All materials, scripts, and outputs are openly archived.

articles_hidden.title: Time pressure modulates resource-rational planning in online chess
articles_hidden.authors: Ionatan Kuperwajs; Evan Russek; Lisa Schut; Yotam Sagiv; Wei Ji Ma; Tom Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Human planning is incredibly efficient. Even in complex situations with many possible courses of action, people are able to make good decisions. Recent proposals suggest that a primary contributor to this efficiency is the intelligent use of cognitive resources, but how people allocate these resources under time constraints is not fully understood. In this work, we conduct a resource-rational analysis of planning in a large data set of online chess games. We first demonstrate that players spent more time thinking when they had more time to do so, and that this effect was especially prevalent when computation was more valuable. Then, we show that additional time spent planning resulted in better selected moves when one existed, and highlight the role of expertise in this setting. Finally, we scale our analysis by showing that changes in move time, move quality, and move entropy as a function of time control setting correlate across board positions. Our results provide evidence that people make resource-rational choices when planning under time pressure.

articles_hidden.title: Hypothesis Spaces: How Structural Beliefs Shape Uncertainty in the Anxious Mind
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Benita Senfft; Ondrej Zika
articles_hidden.abstract: While uncertainty is ubiquitous, not all uncertainty is the same.
