In this review, we dissociate between uncertainty in aspects of known problem spaces (e.g. how long are hospital waiting times; “parameter uncertainty”) and uncertainty arising from unknown structure or even the nature of a problem (e.g. how do I get medical help in a new country; “structural uncertainty”). We suggest that much everyday uncertainty is structural: uncertainty about which model of the world applies in the first place. We bring research on uncertainty and structure learning together through the concept of hypothesis spaces - sets of candidate generative structures that an individual considers plausible, together with distribution of beliefs over their likelihood. We propose that properties of these spaces, including their size, complexity and entropy, provide a systematic framework for understanding structural uncertainty and may help explain characteristic features of anxious thought such as worry, overthinking, catastrophizing and overgeneralization. This perspective also offers a way to refine broad constructs such as intolerance of uncertainty by linking them to specific representational and inferential processes and their properties. We suggest that revisiting the role of uncertainty in anxiety from the viewpoint of structural inference holds the key for mechanistic understanding of clinical observations and closer alignment with fundamental research in cognitive neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Cue–Appraisal Learning in Organizations: A Theory of Conditioned Appraisal Meaning
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Umbra
articles_hidden.abstract: Employees often respond to recurring workplace cues as if those cues carry the meaning of prior experience. A performance review, complaint channel, supervisor phrase, meeting routine, or organizational space may be appraised differently across employees even when the formal cue is the same. This article develops a theory of cue–appraisal learning in organizations. The theory proposes that recurring organizational cues become psychologically consequential when employees repeatedly encounter them in episodes appraised in similar, concern-relevant ways. Over time, employees may develop conditioned appraisal meanings: learned relations between recurring organizational cues and specific appraisal meanings that become more likely to be activated when those cues are encountered again. This cue-level perspective explains how prior organizational experience can shape appraisal activation before a current event has fully unfolded. It also clarifies how learned cue meanings may influence workplace emotion and action tendencies through appraisal processes that remain sensitive to situational, regulatory, and behavioral constraints. The article defines conditioned appraisal meaning, distinguishes it from adjacent constructs, develops propositions concerning acquisition, appraisal specificity, generalization, discrimination, revision, and downstream response, and outlines implications for research and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic attribute activation explains gaze biases in choice.
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaozhi Taro Yang; Sudeep Bhatia
articles_hidden.abstract:
People tend to choose the options they look at more. Prior work explains this effect by assuming that visual attention increases preference for the attended option. However, it remains unclear why looking at an option increases its preference and when this relationship is
weakened. Using an experimental paradigm that combines eye-tracking and a think-aloud protocol, we provide evidence that visual attention shapes preference by activating attributes associated with the attended option. Critically, the content of these activated attributes
depends on contextual factors such as stimulus desirability and behavioral goals. In standard choice settings, where the goal is to choose the preferred option, visual attention primarily activates positive attributes. In contrast, when these contextual factors are incongruent, activated attributes become less positive, reducing the influence of visual attention on choice. To account for these patterns, we propose a new computational model of gaze-driven attribute activation. Our model subsumes existing theories as special cases, and uniquely predicts which attributes are brought to mind by gaze and how they shape downstream decisions. Together, our work offers a mechanistic explanation of a fundamental driver of choice as well as its boundary conditions.

articles_hidden.title: A Spanish-Language Version of the Emotion Reactivity Scale: Psychometric Properties, Measurement Invariance, and Criterion Validity in a Large Adolescent Sample
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua B Gilbert; Zachary Himmelsbach; Matthew Nock; Nicole R. DeTore; Randi M. Schuster
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS) is a widely used self-report measure of the sensitivity, intensity, and persistence of emotional responses. It has been translated and evaluated in Dutch, French, German, Portuguese, and Farsi samples, and has been separately adapted into a brief six-item short form in English. However, no validated Spanish-language version currently exists despite Spanish being the most common non-English language spoken in U.S. schools.

Methods: We provide a Spanish translation of the ERS and evaluate its psychometric properties using data from 522 Spanish-language adolescent respondents and a demographically matched sample of 522 English-language adolescent respondents drawn from a school-based survey. We use multigroup item response theory to test measurement invariance across survey language and regularized differential item functioning (DIF) analysis to identify specific noninvariant items. We evaluate criterion validity through association with the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4).

Results: Multigroup item response theory analyses support metric but not scalar invariance across survey languages, with intercept differences identified for four items, none of which appear on the short form. Despite this evidence of differential item functioning, its practical impact is negligible, as adjusted and unadjusted scores are nearly perfectly correlated ($r > .99$). ERS scores show strong and statistically equivalent criterion validity across language groups in predicting concurrent psychological distress on the PHQ-4.

Conclusions: Both the long and short forms of the Spanish ERS are reliable and criterion-valid measures of emotion reactivity for use with Spanish-speaking adolescents.

articles_hidden.title: Group One Session Treatment: A Feasibility Study in Highly Spider Fearful Youth
articles_hidden.authors: Raphael Gutzweiler; Lou Aberfeld; Léonie Rodon; Boris Tolstich
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: One Session Treatments (OST) represent an intensive and efficacious therapeutic modality for the treatment of anxiety disorders. To date, research has been predominantly focused on individual OST in adults. Research on group OST with children and adolescents is scarce. The objective of the present study is to examine the feasibility of a group OST for highly spider fearful children and adolescents, and to conduct an initial evaluation of this treatment.
Methods: A total of 19 children and adolescents (M = 11.95 years, SD = 2.66) participated in the group OST. We assessed fear of spiders using questionnaires, a clinical interview, and a behavioural approach task. Furthermore, an assessment of disgust sensitivity was conducted. Assessments were administered prior to, at the end of (post), and three months following (FU) the group OST.
Results: Participants reported a high reduction in levels of spider fear (Hedges' g = 2.00 (post), g = 1.7 (FU)), increase in behavioural approach, and full remission (in 84% of cases). Participants, their caregivers, and therapists rated overall moderate to high improvements. No effects were found regarding disgust sensitivity. Group OST effects remained stable during the 3-month FU-interval.
Implications: Group OST in spider fearful children and adolescents provided evidence for feasibility and efficiency.

articles_hidden.title: People make inferences from policy decisions regarding default options:  Replication and extension of McKenzie et al. (2006)
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaoru Teng; Ka Wai LAU; Tsz King Ng; Chan Ka Po; Yeung Wing; Siu Kit Yeung; Gilad Feldman
articles_hidden.abstract: Default effect refers to the phenomenon that people tend to choose the default option in a choice-set. McKenzie et al. (2006) showed that one mechanism for the effect is that defaults are perceived as an implicit endorsement and a recommended option by the policy makers that set the defaults. In a pre-registered experiment with a Prolific online sample from the United States (N = 602), we conducted replications and extensions of Studies 1, 2, and 3 from McKenzie et al. (2006). Across the nine target-article tests, the adjusted Cramer's V effects ranged from .24 to .86 with corresponding replication estimates ranging from .41 to .80. We concluded a successful replication of all three studies, with support for their findings showing that: 1) people who report willingness to be organ donors, and people who think others ought to be donors, are more likely to select organ donation as the policy default, and that in turn: 2) people make inferences from policymaker’s set defaults (Study 2: organ donations; Study 3: retirement plans) regarding the policymakers’ own preferences regarding enrollment, and their views regarding whether others should enroll. In our extension we added a control condition with no defaults, finding that 1) people still make inferences about choice architects’ attitudes, even when defaults were not set, and 2) that setting defaults to not act (not enroll) is perceived as closer to no defaults than setting defaults to act (to enroll). Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/E5K4J.

articles_hidden.title: How Meaning Shapes a Rule: Neural Signatures of Morphological Learning and Generalization
articles_hidden.authors: Marianne Azar; Alec Marantz
articles_hidden.abstract: Rule generalization is one of the most useful tools our mind uses to facilitate learning. In language, we apply it to connect what words mean to what they are made of, such as their suffixes. This is a morphosemantic relation, and it helps us process words we already know and easily acquire new words by composing their meaning. How is this relation acquired, and how does it manifest into generalization for understanding new words? In this study, we investigated the brain basis of these questions through an English-based artificial language study, where learners read sentences to learn a suffix-meaning relation of new words like “thinkle”. Words were either meaningful (places or things) or had no clear meaning. Each suffix family had majority and minority meaning words that participants had to keep track of for testing. For meaningful words in training, we found that higher performance scores predicted higher selective engagement in the left inferior frontal gyrus, specifically the pars triangularis and pars opercularis. In testing, both learned and generalized words, both increased lateral prefrontal cortex engagement. Meanwhile, words with no clear meaning had a much more diffuse brain engagement, recruiting bilateral temporoparietal regions. This resembles the processing of abstract words from previous literature. We found no difference between majority and minority meaning words, especially with the variance in participants’ performance strategies, but found differences in what predicted significant brain activity based on strategy difference. This study grounds itself in the reality of word and affixal semantics with previous research on language learning and universals. Ultimately, it lends a learning paradigm that resembles natural language learning across many languages to carefully investigate its brain basis, while addressing an understudied aspect of rule generalization: ambiguity.

articles_hidden.title: Theoretical Considerations of the Common Factor Model and its Alternatives
articles_hidden.authors: Danielle Siegel; Mijke Rhemtulla
articles_hidden.abstract: Accurate psychological measurement typically relies on the common factor model, which assumes observed items reflect an underlying latent construct plus measurement error. However, growing evidence suggests that the factor model is not appropriate for all psychological constructs, and applying it when its assumptions are violated can bias both the measurement and structural parameters in structural equation models (SEMs). The paper reviews the common factor model along with a range of alternative measurement approaches, including composite models with prespecified and estimated weights, psychometric network models, and models that treat individual scale items as unique predictors. We describe the theoretical assumptions, strengths, and limitations of each approach, with particular attention to recent methodological developments that all factor-based and composite-based models to be statistically compared within the SEM framework. Using a running empirical example from Milas et al., (2021), we illustrate how the choice of measurement model changes parameter estimates, model fit, and the substantive interpretation of results. We conclude that researchers should select a measurement approach based on the theoretical relations they hypothesize among their scale items rather than defaulting to the common factor model. We offer recommendations for evaluating and comparing candidate measurement models.

articles_hidden.title: Covariate Selection for Doubly Robust Double/debiased Machine Learning Estimators for Causal Inference
articles_hidden.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles_hidden.abstract: High-dimensional data create challenges for causal effect estimation because identifying the covariates needed for correct model specification becomes increasingly difficult. Double/debiased machine learning (DML) facilitates the use of machine learning (ML) for causal inference by mitigating regularization and overfitting bias, but comparatively less attention has been given to covariate selection in relation to the double robustness (DR) property possessed by some DML estimators. In particular, ML-based covariate selection may result in differential covariate selection or in misspecification of both models, thereby limiting the practical utility of the DR property. To address these issues, we propose using the union of the covariates selected by the propensity score (PS) and outcome ML models to re-estimate both models. Simulation results show that using the union consistently reduces more confounding bias than using separate selected covariate sets. The results also show that ML-based estimation does not uniformly outperform conventional DR estimation, even under conditions favorable to the Lasso, and that post-Lasso reduces more confounding bias than standard Lasso. These findings demonstrate that successful use of ML for causal inference depends not only on the ML algorithm but also on how the information obtained through covariate selection is incorporated into causal effect estimation.

articles_hidden.title: Within-Person Symptom Dynamics in Serious Mental Illness: Insights from Daily Self-reports and Audio Journals
articles_hidden.authors: Daiil Jun; Jeffrey M. Girard; Yoonho Chung; Scott L. Rauch; Einat Liebenthal; Justin T. Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding how clinical symptoms fluctuate within individuals is crucial for developing personalized treatment, yet these dynamics remain understudied. We examined whether daily self-reports and speech features from audio journals predicted monthly fluctuations in clinician-rated symptoms among 54 outpatients with affective and psychotic disorders. We identified seven within-person symptom dimensions: disorganized thinking, mania, social withdrawal, inexpressivity, affective depression, cognitive depression, and anxiety. Daily self-reports and speech features were summarized on a monthly level across different temporal windows highlighting 3, 7, 14, and 28 days of daily data prior to the clinical interview to assess the predictive value of emphasizing more or less recent daily histories. Bayesian multilevel models indicated that both the intensity and day-to-day variability of daily experiences and speech features tracked month-to-month symptom fluctuations. Daily Positive Affect and speech sentiment were the most broadly informative indicators of fluctuations across symptom domains. Greater Daily Positive Affect or more positive sentiment predicted increased mania, whereas lower levels tracked increased other symptoms except for disorganized thinking. Model comparisons across temporal windows showed that models using daily self-reports were generally robust to different windows, although social withdrawal showed improved performance highlighting longer daily histories. Models using speech features generally performed better with longer temporal windows, whereas mania and anxiety showed no clear temporal window preference. Overall, these findings demonstrate the utility of daily self-reports and audio journals for dynamic symptom tracking and showcase a data-driven approach to investigating the optimal length of daily history for developing personalized monitoring tools in psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Substance Use Disorder Treatment: From Brain Awareness to Brain Recovery Capital
articles_hidden.authors: Tara Rezapour; Alex Baldacchino; Andrew Dalley; Jamie Berry; Shweta Chilka; Marc L. Copersino; Ali Farhoudian; Jing Jin; Steven Powers; Timothy Grigsby
articles_hidden.abstract: Substance use disorders continue to affect millions of people worldwide, yet a striking proportion never receive treatment. Poor awareness, internalized stigma, and neurobiological changes in the circuits responsible for self-monitoring all contribute to this gap in ways that conventional psychoeducation has not adequately addressed. Recent advances in addiction neuroscience offer a more precise and less stigmatizing language for understanding these barriers, one that reframes addiction as a brain disorder rather than a moral failure and opens new possibilities for how we educate patients about their condition. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation, or NIPE, builds on this foundation. It integrates current addiction neuroscience into an educational program designed to improve insight, reduce shame, and strengthen motivation for treatment and recovery. This paper proposes a clinical stage-based NIPE framework organized around the Transtheoretical Model of Health Behavior Change, mapping specific educational content and delivery priorities to seven stages of the recovery trajectory. The goal is an approach that meets people where they actually are in both their motivational readiness and their neurobiological capacity to engage. An example of a NIPE package for recovery and future directions to deliver effective NIPE and promote brain recovery are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Getting the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 Ready for Clinical Practice: Population-Representative Norms That Embrace Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Johannes Zimmermann; André Kerber; Christoph J. Kemper; Katharina Weweck
articles_hidden.abstract: The Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5) is the standard measure of the maladaptive traits in the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders, but normative information for score interpretation has remained limited. Existing norms refer to the U.S. population, are not conditioned on age and gender, and report point values without any quantification of uncertainty. We derived norms for the facets, domains, and total scores of the full PID-5 and its abbreviated versions, referenced to the German general population and conditional on age and gender. A modular Bayesian pipeline combined a probability-based reference sample (N = 4,727) with three “donor” samples that completed the full instrument (N = 2,471), linked via 34 common items. The norm tables quantify uncertainty at two levels, with credible bands for every norm value and score-conditional intervals for every raw score, and can be applied through a free online scoring platform.

articles_hidden.title: The Quiet Window–Challenge Window Framework: A Conceptual Framework for Habit Formation During GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy
articles_hidden.authors: Holly R Hull; Melanie Rae Lenius Meister; Laura E Martin; Molly M. Fain; Sarah Crawford; Debra Sullivan; Alexandra R. Brown; Johanna G. Finkle
articles_hidden.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have transformed obesity treatment by producing substantial weight loss while altering appetite, food-related cognition, and eating behaviors. Although current clinical recommendations emphasize dietary quality, adequate protein intake, physical activity, and behavioral support during GLP-1RA therapy, they primarily focus on what behavior strategies should accompany treatment rather than when they may be most effective. Emerging evidence suggests that the cognitive and behavioral effects of GLP-1RA therapy are dynamic, creating periods during which healthy habits may be more readily established and later tested. We propose the Quiet Window-Challenge Window Framework, a conceptual model that reframes behavioral opportunity during GLP-1RA therapy as a dynamic process. The Quiet Window represents a temporary period of reduced food-related cognitive burden that facilitates habit acquisition, whereas the Challenge Window reflects increasing cognitive and environmental demands during which newly established habits are tested. A central hypothesis is that durable behavior change depends on the progressive transfer of behavioral regulation from pharmacologic support to resilient, self-sustaining habits through repeated practice, increasing automaticity, and subsequent testing under greater behavioral demands. We further propose that Quiet and Challenge Windows operate across multiple time points, including broader treatment phases and recurring weekly states within weekly dosing intervals. The framework generates testable hypotheses regarding food-related cognition, habit formation and resilience, and adaptive behavioral interventions. By conceptualizing behavioral opportunity as dynamic, this Framework shifts the focus from whether behavioral interventions should accompany GLP-1RA therapy to when they are most likely to promote durable behavior change.

articles_hidden.title: A Latent Oscillator Measurement Model to Simulate Emotional-Expression Score Dynamics in Video
articles_hidden.authors: Aleksandar Tomašević; Hudson Golino; Alexander P. Christensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Facial-expression classifiers convert video into multivariate time series of scores with measurement
error from classifiers, videos, and recording conditions. Empirical score series cannot establish whether
the score channels reflect a smaller set of latent expressive processes or whether an analysis would recover
those processes. We introduce the Latent Oscillator Measurement Model (LOMM), a data-generating
model that separates latent dynamics, time-varying activity, and a factor-analytic observation model.
The latent processes are damped, undamped, or amplifying linear oscillators. LOMM generates bounded
scores or continuous indicators. Study 1 used four-fold cross-fitting with scores from 100 MAFW videos
to calibrate LOMM and evaluate generated series on held-out videos. Median plausibility and coverage
were 0.970 and 0.920 for LOMM, versus 0.510 and 0.370 for a calibrated static logistic-normal generator.
Study 2 tested whether Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis (DynEGA), static EGA, GraphicalVAR,
and GIMME recovered a known dimensional structure from continuous indicators generated by LOMM.
At 100 observations per clip, with failed or timed-out fits counted as incorrect, correct-dimension
recovery was 0.939 for DynEGA, 0.884 for static EGA, 0.777 for GraphicalVAR, and 0.176 for GIMME.
Replacing the common fixed initialization with independent stationary starts for stable dimensions and
bounded independent starts for amplifying dimensions reduced recovery for DynEGA, static EGA, and
GraphicalVAR. The primary initialization was optimistic relative to this alternative. LOMM provides
a controlled test of whether an analysis recovers a specified latent structure before score patterns are
interpreted psychologically.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting More Behavior More of the Time: On the Behavioral Nature of Different Personality Trait Measures
articles_hidden.authors: Niclas Kuper; Simon Mats Breil; Katharina Utesch; Mitja D Back
articles_hidden.abstract: Most research focuses on self-reported global trait ratings to approximate behavioral individual differences. However, several alternatives exist. Average self-reported states from experience sampling are thought to be closer to behavior, but little evidence supports this. Further, other-report should rely more strongly on behavior. Here, we predict interpersonal behavior from different personality trait measures, highlighting type of aggregation (global vs. average state measures) and perspective (self- vs. other-report). We provide initial, exploratory evidence with a small multi-methodological study (N = 88) including six trait measures: global self-report, global informant-report, time-based self-reported states (fortnightly diaries), time-based peer-reported states, event-based self-reported states (after social interactions), and event-based peer-reported states. Measures were compared in the prediction of actual behavior in the laboratory one year later. We focused on four behaviors (warmth, expressiveness, self-confidence, nervousness) and corresponding global/state dimensions. Self-reported states were rarely incrementally predictive above global self-report and thus not as close to behavior as commonly believed. When based on multiple raters, other-report was more consistently linked to behavior than self-report. Other-reported states averaged across peers were predictive beyond global informant-report and self-reported states, representing an underused method potentially closer to behavior. We outline future directions to go beyond self-report in behavioral personality science.

articles_hidden.title: How does Sleep Restriction Therapy work? Testing the Triple-R theory as an explanation through computational modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Jill de Ron; Tessa F. Blanken; Denny Borsboom; Hans Gommers; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Jaap Lancee; Leonie Franziska Maurer; Jason Nak; Donald Robinaugh; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep restriction therapy (SRT) is an effective treatment for insomnia, one of the most prevalent mental disorders today. The Triple-R theory has been proposed to explain the efficacy of SRT based on three processes: restricting time in bed, regulating sleep and wake times, and reconditioning of the bed-sleep association. However, based on the verbal theory alone it is difficult to determine whether the proposed processes explain the efficacy of SRT. In the current paper we test whether Triple-R theory explains the efficacy of SRT through computational modeling. Building on the productive explanation framework we (i) define empirical phenomena in sleep diary data before and after SRT; (ii) formalize the Triple-R theory as a computational model; (iii) test whether the empirical phenomena are reproduced by the model. We show that our computational Triple-R model reproduces most data patterns observed in empirical studies. Therefore, we conclude that the Triple-R theory provides a partial explanation of the efficacy of SRT. Moreover, our proposed Triple-R model makes predictions that can guide new clinical trials and provides a better understanding of the mechanisms of SRT.

articles_hidden.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles_hidden.title: Mentoring Trainees with Lived Experience of Psychopathology: A Strengths-based, Cultural Humility Framework for Psychological Scientists
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Devendorf; Julie Cristello; Cassandra L. Boness; Irene Tung; Cecilia Hinojosa
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health difficulties are prevalent among psychologists, yet professionals in the field are often discouraged from disclosing their lived experience with psychopathology due to persistent stigma. For much of history, lived experience with psychopathology has been treated as a deficit within the profession. However, emerging research and perspectives are beginning to challenge this status quo by highlighting that lived experience can be an asset in psychological science and practice. Despite this shift, there remains little guidance on how to navigate this topic in mentor-mentee relationships. We outline a framework for strengths-based mentorship that is based on six pillars: 1) tenets of strengths-based mentorship; 2) foundational and functional mentorship competencies; 3) mental health literacy; 4) feminist principles; 5) cultural humility; and 6) ethical considerations. This framework can help improve mentor-mentee relationships, reduce stigma, and ultimately improve the professional development of mentees with lived experience. We apply this principle-driven framework to common professional scenarios: recruiting applicants, evaluating personal statements, and navigating situations when a mentee is distressed, requesting accommodations, or interested in leveraging their lived experiences in their work. By offering this framework, we aim to facilitate dialogue and provide actionable guidance for mentors seeking to support trainees with psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Dietary Modulation of Neurobiological Mechanisms Underlying Executive Function and Decision-Making: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Iveta Harris; Ian Evans; Jessica Bayes; Mansi Das Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Executive function (EF) and decision making (DM) are central to adaptive behaviour, yet evidence explaining how diet influences their underlying neurobiological mechanisms remains fragmented. This systematic review examined how dietary exposures influence the neurobiological mechanisms underlying EF and DM. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251173091). Of 12,952 records identified, 26 studies met the inclusion criteria, involving over 2,000 participants. Across the included studies, dietary exposures were associated with changes in metabolic, neurochemical, inflammatory, neural, and gut–brain pathways relevant to EF and DM. Behavioural effects were reported across all dietary domains but were less consistent than biological changes and varied according to intervention duration, task sensitivity, and participant characteristics. EF outcomes were more consistently modulated than DM outcomes, with effects most evident in working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. Although less frequently studied, DM findings showed that dietary exposures could shift complex choices—including risk-taking, temporal discounting, and social decision-making—alongside changes in metabolic state and neurotransmitter precursor availability. Notably, none of the reviewed studies specifically examined ultra-processed food exposure, identifying an important gap in the current evidence. Few studies examined when or how biological changes translated into measurable behavioural outcomes. Together, the findings suggest that dietary effects may emerge across biological systems before consistent changes in EF and DM become detectable, potentially explaining variability in previous behavioural findings. Longitudinal, mechanistically integrated studies that account for potential confounding factors, including hormonal status, background dietary intake, and participant characteristics, are needed to test this temporal sequence and determine when biological modulation produces cognitive and behavioural change.

articles_hidden.title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
articles_hidden.authors: Tai Kurosawa
articles_hidden.abstract: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a higher distribution of web surveys was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

articles_hidden.title: Canonical Correlation Analysis of Multidimensional Perfectionism and Mental Health Among Filipino Young Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano
articles_hidden.abstract: Perfectionism is a multidimensional personality trait that has been consistently linked to both negative and positive mental health outcomes. Yet recent research has increasingly reduced perfectionism to broad higher-order factors leaving specific dimensions underexamined. The present study examined how the six dimensions of Multidimensional Perfectionism according to Frost et al. (1990)—Concern over Mistakes, Doubts about Actions, Personal Standards, Organization, Parental Expectations, and Parental Criticism—relate to positive and negative mental health outcomes among Filipino young adults. Canonical correlation analysis was employed in a sample of 1,093 participants (Mage = 22.10, SD = 1.66) to capture the multivariate patterning of associations between perfectionism dimensions and four mental health indicators: stress, anxiety, depression, and life satisfaction. Two significant canonical functions emerged. The first function (Rc = .649, 42.1% shared variance between the two canonical variates) linked Concern over Mistakes, Doubts about Actions, Parental Criticism, Parental Expectations and Personal Standards to higher stress, anxiety, and depression, and lower life satisfaction. The second (Rc = .332, 11.0% shared variance between the two canonical variates) linked Personal Standards and Organization to greater life satisfaction and lower depression, with weaker associations with anxiety and stress. These findings highlight the value of examining individual perfectionism dimensions rather than broad higher-order factors. Parental dimensions, in particular, appear especially relevant in the Filipino context.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure and Convergent Validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) Among Filipino Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles_hidden.abstract: The Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP) distinguishes between striving for high yet attainable standards (i.e., excellencism) and the pursuit of rigid, inflexible ones (i.e., perfectionism). The current study examines the psychometric validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) among two samples of Filipino adults preparing for a licensure examination. Results from confirmatory factor analyses supported the two factor structure of the SCOPE. Convergent validity was supported through expected cross-sectional associations with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale as well as time-lagged associations with subjective well-being. Time 1 excellencism was positively associated with Time 2 life satisfaction and positive affect, whereas Time 1 perfectionism was positively linked with Time 2 negative affect. Overall, these findings provide support for the validity of the SCOPE and the assumptions of the MEP, suggesting that pursuing excellencism—rather than perfectionism—is associated with greater well-being during intense career preparation.

articles_hidden.title: ENDS-Motivational and Affective Picture System (E-MAPS): Development and validation of a contextualized vaping image database
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Wahlers; Jonathan Westlake; Oh-Ryeong Ha; Steven Seung-Suk Kang; Delwyn Catley; Seung-Lark Lim
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) use is reinforced by motivational and affective
contexts associated with repeated ENDS use. Yet, there are currently no standardized, validated
ENDS-related image cues that differentiate among motivational contexts. This study aimed to
develop and validate contextualized ENDS-related image cues.

Method
Electronic nicotine delivery system users between the ages of 21 and 35 in the United States
were recruited via Prolific (N = 253). Eighty ENDS-related images were presented. E-MAPS
(ENDS-Motivational and Affective Picture System) depicts ENDS use in four motivational
contexts corresponding to prominent vaping dependence mechanisms: positive reinforcement,
negative reinforcement, habit/automaticity, and cue-induced craving. Each motivational context
also depicts social and nonsocial ENDS use. Each participant rated 80 images on dimensions of
valence, arousal, and craving.

Results
E-MAPS images were classified consistently with their intended motivational context and ratings
of valence, arousal, and craving exhibited strong reliability within each intended category.
Several differences in valence, arousal, and craving emerged among motivational contexts,
highlighting the importance of accounting for cue-related motivational context. Regardless of
context, E-MAPS images elicited relatively high cravings while higher (vs. lower) reported
cravings were strongly associated with clinically relevant outcomes: greater vaping dependence
and reduced motivation and confidence to quit.

Conclusion
E-MAPS reliably distinguished among prominent dependence-related motivational contexts,
offering researchers tools to study the motivational mechanisms that sustain chronic ENDS use.

articles_hidden.title: An emic way of examining morality based on Moral Foundations Theory: development and validation of the Moral Foundations Patterns Questionnaire in Japan
articles_hidden.authors: Hideya Sanada; Yoshito Tan; Haruki Oka
articles_hidden.abstract: How should morality be measured in a cross-cultural context? Although Moral Foundations Theory combines etic (universal) and emic (local) concepts, existing measures are largely etic. Therefore, we proposed an emic approach for measuring etic constructs of MFT, introduced a new construct, Moral Foundations Patterns, and developed the Moral Foundations Patterns Questionnaire (MFPQ) in Japan. We conducted five studies to develop and validate the MFPQ (total N = 2,161), using two different sampling platforms to diversify sample characteristics. We showed MFPQ has adequate reliability and validity. Finally, we discussed how this emic MFPQ can be applied in cross-cultural research and argued that MFPQ can contribute to the stringent tests of the Moral Foundations Theory's key claims and support cross-cultural comparisons of its construct.

articles_hidden.title: Is the Useful Field all you need on the road? Hazard localization performance in a gaze contingent scotoma paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Zivli; Jiali Song; Benjamin Wolfe
articles_hidden.abstract: The Useful Field is a construct which describes a limited region of visual space around fixation, and is often misinterpreted in driving contexts as being the only portion of the visual field which supports drivers’ knowledge of their environment. This account ignores the likely contributions of peripheral vision, but this has not been studied in dynamic scenes. Studies with static scenes suggest that peripheral vision supports scene gist, but the world and road are not static. Taking inspiration from the driving literature, and using our corpus of near-collision dash camera video, we examined the separate necessity of central and peripheral information to drivers’ ability to localize dangerous objects in a rapidly-changing road scene, directly testing the strong interpretation of the Useful Field. In separate blocks, we approximated this strong interpretation of the Useful Field with a peripheral scotoma and, the reverse, a central scotoma condition, forcing observers to rely on peripheral vision alone. Blockwise, the visible or occluded region varied according to a 3-up/1-down staircase. This procedure allowed us to estimate the extent of occlusion observers could tolerate in each condition. We replicated the key findings from the static scene gist literature, extending them to dynamic scenes. Specifically, we showed that while the Useful Field can support this task, its occlusion does not render the task impossible, suggesting that we use information beyond this limited region of visual space to support task demands.

articles_hidden.title: Questionnaire Democrats? Reconsidering the Relevance of Abstract Democracy Support in the American Public
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Reel Panish; Ariel Malka
articles_hidden.abstract: The American public largely favors “democracy,” yet many citizens tolerate undemocratic actions and candidates. This raises doubts about the relevance of abstract democracy support to actual democratic commitment. In contrast, we argue that abstract democracy support is a normatively significant dimension of attitude variation among Americans. Using nineteen surveys fielded between 1995 and 2024, we show that a sizable segment of the public expresses only tepid support for democracy, and that a nontrivial minority expresses opposition. Moreover, commonly used abstract democracy support items converge on a single latent construct which displays high rank-order stability, but also meaningful within-person variation, over a two-year period. Abstract democracy support negatively predicts openness to a wide range of electoral and liberal democratic violations and is associated with greater likelihood of electorally punishing anti-democratic candidates. In panel data, positive within-person deviations in abstract democracy support precede negative within-person deviations in openness to authoritarian governance, suggesting that individual-level shifts in abstract support predict later change in substantive democracy attitudes. Overall our findings suggest that the value of ‘democracy’ is contested among Americans, with potential implications for democratic erosion. We recommend that efforts to understand the American public’s role in democratic backsliding and restoration treat abstract support as a distinct attitude construct, measure it with multi-item scales, and explore whether or not it possesses causal significance.

articles_hidden.title: How should Moral Motivation be Represented? The Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA)
articles_hidden.authors: Paul McKee; Gregory Russell Samanez-Larkin; Scott A. Huettel; Walter Sinnott-Armstrong
articles_hidden.abstract: Moral psychology has mostly asked which motives drive moral action, and rarely how moral motivation should be represented once several are active at once. Most theories represent it as a single dominant motive or as one continuum from bad to good. Both discard information: a person torn between strong competing motivations and a person who feels nothing occupy the same position. We argue that representational format is a testable empirical claim, not a modeling convenience, and propose the Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA), which represents moral motivation as four independent dimensions formed by crossing motivational direction (approach, avoid) with perceived moral valence (good, bad). MoMA does not specify which motives matter; it specifies the space in which they combine. We derive requirements for an adequate architecture, show that lower-rank representations necessarily collapse psychologically distinct states, and state predictions distinguishing MoMA from simpler alternatives.

articles_hidden.title: Methodological Diversity and Heterogeneity in Psychological Evidence Syntheses
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Alfons Edmar; Duco Veen; Irene Klugkist
articles_hidden.abstract: One of the fundamental problems of meta-analysis is the comparability of primary research studies and the absence of robust modes of generalisability such as formal sampling theory. The decision whether or not a set of studies ought to be mathematically pooled is therefore a complicated issue requiring both domain expertise and statistical knowledge, especially in psychological science where studies often target abstract constructs. The objective of this paper is to capture when a set of studies become so methodologically diverse that pooling the data is ruled to be inappropriate. A convergent mixed methods approach was used to combine two interdependent studies. We conducted a scoping review of current meta-analyses literature $(k = 27)$ and a qualitative content analysis of systematic reviews that decided against pooling data due to substantial methodological diversity $(k = 9)$. We find the distinction between poolable and unpoolable studies to be ambiguous. Furthermore, meta-research in psychology appears to place limited emphasis on heterogeneity and issues of generalisability. We argue that a renewed focus on generalisability through an assessment of the prototypical attributes of the scientific literature at hand would greatly improve the interpretability of meta-analytic inferences in psychology. Clearly and explicitly describing the generalisability of a review would enable authors to effectively communicate theoretically important ideas to a diverse readership. We propose the adoption of a comparability statement as a simple tool that enhances meta-research methodology without overhauling or complicating current practices in applied psychological science.

articles_hidden.title: Is virtual reality beneficial and for which outcomes? Comparing VR and 2D in higher education classroom learning
articles_hidden.authors: Mikko Haavisto; Johannes Halttu; Tomi Jaakkola
articles_hidden.abstract: The transition from hands-on experience to computer-aided design poses challenges for students’ understanding of 3D structures because traditional 2D computer screens limit spatial perception. Immersive virtual reality (VR) offers a potential solution but its effectiveness and feasibility compared to 2D screens in a classroom context are unclear. This experiment investigates to what extent VR affects learning, motivational, and perceived outcomes, and cognitive load compared to 2D screen environments in dental technology education. It also examines how individual differences, such as spatial ability and VR proficiency, influence these outcomes. First- and second-year dental technology students (n = 45) participated in a preregistered within-subject crossover experiment. Because participants had more than a thousand times more prior experience with conventional 2D screens than with VR, the intervention started with VR orientation lessons. Participants then studied framework partial dentures and dental bridges once in VR and once in a 2D screen environment. Data from pre- and posttests were analyzed with mixed-effects models to account for repeated measurements and individual differences. The results showed that VR increased presence/immersion, interest/enjoyment, and perceived competence, and produced a small nonsignificant advantage in 3D comprehension. In contrast, 2D screen learning led to higher factual knowledge performance and lower total cognitive load. Individual differences explained a large portion of variance in outcomes. The benefits of VR were mostly experiential and motivational, whereas 2D screens supported better factual learning with lower total cognitive load. Classroom VR may therefore be useful as an addition to conventional instruction.

articles_hidden.title: Context Sensitivity Underlies Emotional Intelligence and Flexible Emotion Regulation in Daily Life
articles_hidden.authors: Riley Leckie; Carolyn MacCann
articles_hidden.abstract: The effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies depends on situation factors, such that effective emotion regulation involves regulatory flexibility (flexibly matching the regulation strategies you use to the context you are in). Recent research shows that two emotional intelligence abilities (emotion understanding and management) predict regulatory flexibility. This connection is assumed to be based on individual differences in context sensitivity (which underpin both emotional intelligence and regulatory flexibility). The current pre-registered study tests this assumption, aiming to replicate the emotional intelligence/regulatory flexibility link while adding a novel measure of context sensitivity in daily life. Participants (N = 131) completed baseline assessments of emotional intelligence and up to 30 experience sampling surveys (n = 2,901) across five days. Surveys measured four emotion regulation strategies and five appraisals of emotionally relevant situational features. Variability in strategies and appraisals was used to derive regulatory flexibility and context sensitivity metrics both in each situation (between-strategy and between-appraisal variability) and across situations (within-strategy and within-appraisal variability). All prior effects linking emotional intelligence to regulatory flexibility were replicated and there were two new findings. First, both emotional intelligence abilities predicted higher context sensitivity in each situation (between-appraisal variability), but not across situations (within-appraisal variability). Second, higher context sensitivity predicted higher regulatory flexibility at both the within-person and between-person level. These findings support the assumption that context sensitivity underlies both emotional intelligence and regulatory flexibility. To refine proposed measures of context sensitivity in daily life, future research should look to disentangle general appraisals of pronounced changes in the objective characteristics of the world from sensitivity to more nuanced changes.

articles_hidden.title: They’re All Like That! The Universality Signature of Central Form
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper investigates how humans store information within the thousands of concepts that structure our beliefs, and which ultimately guide our actions. Form Theory proposes that every concept has a central form, a unitary representational structure that encodes a compressed subset of conceptual information, captures conceptual identity, and generates a set of strong default beliefs. This paper introduces and tests a further form signature: a default universality belief. Across two experiments, participants judged central form properties as universally true of all category members. They rejected this belief for properties that were highly prototypical or causally important if they were not encoded as part of the concept's central form. This effect held across both familiar and novel categories, and across domains including animals, artifacts, institutions, places, and events. These findings identify the central form as a domain-general representational source of universality judgments, with implications for stereotyping, trauma, and ideology. They also help explain how Form Theory’s compressed conceptual structure can support complex thought.

articles_hidden.title: Embracing a new era of skill training and transfer in sports: An adaptive interface reorganization (AIR) framework
articles_hidden.authors: Sicong Liu; Wangyang Xu; Fengewei Hao; Andrew Mark Williams
articles_hidden.abstract: The value of vision-based training in sport depends on whether it transfers to competition or not. The recent debate over the utility of general vision and perceptual-cognitive training has exposed the limits of near-versus-far terminology for sport, where the practical objective is usually not improvement in a decontextualized capacity but functional change from a specified training task (i.e., practice) to a specified target task (i.e., competition). In this conceptual review, we reframe transfer in sports as a problem of multidimensional specificity and system reorganization. We develop four linked arguments. First, treating transfer distance as a single continuum obscures the dimensions on which training and target tasks correspond. Second, technologies including extended/virtual reality, eye tracking, motion capture, psychophysiology, and artificial intelligence can increase experimental control and measurement sensitivity, but cannot establish transfer without theory-led design. Third, we extend the modified perceptual training framework into a design model—the specificity cube—that profiles stimulus, response, and skill correspondence, with the skill dimension further specified by athlete state, timescale, and performance criterion. Fourth, we propose the adaptive interface reorganization (AIR) framework to help conceptualize durable reorganization of brain–body–environment relations within an athlete–environment system as a mechanism that sustains transfer. AIR makes the hypothesized reorganization testable through six complementary sources of evidence, including information sampling, action coupling, state regulation, performance stabilization, mechanism-aligned biomarkers, and untraining. The specificity cube and AIR recast the generic question of whether vision training works as a target-relative, mechanism-oriented research program, and generate applied implications.

articles_hidden.title: The Interplay of Contextual Representations Dynamically Shapes Human Defensive Responses
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Tortora; Daniel Gromer; Mario Reutter-Dieker; Sabrina Gado; Marta Andreatta; Matthias Gamer
articles_hidden.abstract: Flexibly adapting behavior to complex environments depends on the ability to process and integrate contextual information into a coherent representation. Animal research highlights the interplay between elemental and conjunctive contextual representations in guiding behavior. Here, we examined how these two forms of encoding interact to influence human defensive responses using a virtual reality context-dependent fear conditioning paradigm. The virtual environment consisted of three distinctly furnished offices, each containing the same two lamps. First, participants (N = 54) explored all offices (context encoding). Then, they repeatedly visited two of them and in each office, one lamp (e.g., yellow) predicted an aversive electric stimulation, whereas the other lamp (e.g., blue) signaled safety. Critically, contingencies were reversed across contexts (context-dependent acquisition). In the final phase (behavioral test), participants freely re-explored the offices. Subjective ratings, autonomic responses, proxemic indices, and gaze behavior were recorded. Ratings, autonomic responses, and gaze behavior showed context-dependent threat–safety discrimination, indicating a dominant role of conjunctive representations. Reduced discrimination in the context in which cue contingencies were reversed revealed a contribution of elemental representations. Interestingly, despite accurate contingency knowledge, participants adopted a “better safe than sorry” strategy during the behavioral test, avoiding both lamps across contexts, suggesting a stronger influence of elemental encoding on spontaneous defensive behavior under uncertainty. These findings demonstrate that multiple forms of contextual representation mutually interact across defensive domains, highlighting the complexity of human threat processing. This framework may provide new insights into the etiology and maintenance of maladaptive defensive responses in anxiety-related psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Dynamic and Reciprocal Within-Person Relations Between Emotion Regulation and Affect at Work: A Continuous Time Modeling Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Cort W. Rudolph; Amelia Wilcox; Hannes Zacher
articles_hidden.abstract: Effective emotion regulation is an important antecedent of emotional wellbeing in general, and in specific contexts, including the workplace. The impact of emotion regulation strategies, such as cognitive reappraisal and behavioral suppression, on short-term experiences of positive and negative affect (e.g., across several days or weeks) is rather well understood. In contrast, we know far less about the longer-term processes (e.g., across several months or years) by which the use of these strategies influence affect and vice versa. Based upon theories of emotion regulation, reappraisal and suppression emotion regulation strategies and positive and negative affect are posited to dynamically influence each other through a continuous process that unfolds within- person and over time. Using 47 waves of longitudinal data collected across 53 months from a sample of n = 1,458 full-time employed individuals in Germany, we hypothesize and test two distinct reinforcing “cycles” between cognitive reappraisal and positive affect, and between behavioral suppression and negative affect, respectively, in the work context. Results of continuous time modeling suggest evidence for both a “virtuous” cycle, wherein cognitive reappraisal is associated with higher subsequent levels of positive affect, and vice versa, and a “vicious” cycle, wherein behavioral suppression is associated with subsequently higher levels of negative affect, and vice versa.

articles_hidden.title: Neurophysiological correlates of time estimation in delay discounting
articles_hidden.authors: Cornelis Henrico Stam; Frederik M van der Veen; Ingmar Franken
articles_hidden.abstract:
Steep delay discounting behavior is associated with detrimental life outcomes, like addictive behaviors. It has been suggested that differences in time estimation abilities could underlie these detrimental behaviors. The research question this paper investigates is whether an association exists between delay discounting behavior and neurophysiological indices of time estimation. 
This study includes a sample of 100 participants, balanced by gender. As they performed a sequential time estimation task of 4 intervals (2, 3, 6, and 9s), the EEG was recorded while performing an error monitoring paradigm. Based on a pseudo-error condition, trials were split into correct and incorrect trials. EEG measures in the time domain were ERN and Pe, and in the time-frequency domain, trial-averaged delta, theta, alpha, and beta oscillatory power.
Consistent with expectations, delay discount rate was associated with producing shorter time estimations. For the time-domain analysis, no association was found with the ERN or Pe. But the time-frequency analysis showed that frontal theta band power was negatively associated with delay discount rate, whereas beta power was positively associated with delay discounting. Furthermore, theta power was positively associated with relative error (coefficient of variation; SD/mean). Theta band and beta band power were positively correlated, but the connection was weaker at higher levels of delay discounting.
Taken together, the time-frequency EEG results present novel evidence for a weaker temporal error monitoring ability in individuals who exhibit steeper delay discounting behavior, through a theta-beta mechanism. These individuals overestimated their time productions. This weaker ability probably results from two neurocognitive processes: 1. attenuated theta power (cognitive control deficit) and elevated beta power (magnitude distortion in memory).

articles_hidden.title: Educational Neuroscience Outreach Programs for School-Aged Students: From Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation to Career Development
articles_hidden.authors: Arash Khojasteh Zonoozi; Benjamin Ostow; Sepehr Mortaheb; Steven Jillings; Shiva Sharifi; Hamed Ekhtiari; Ghazaleh Soleimani
articles_hidden.abstract: Educational neuroscience outreach programs promote neuroscience literacy, science interest, and brain health among school-aged students, ranging from neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to engagement for neuroscience careers. However, their implementation, delivery, and evaluation remain poorly understood. This chapter examined programs through three questions: (1) Where and in what institutional contexts were students targeted? (2) How were programs delivered? and (3) What neuroscience content was taught and what outcomes were reported. A PRISMA-guided review searched PubMed from inception to 2025 for empirical studies of neuroscience-based educational/outreach programs targeting students aged ~5–18 years. Eligible studies reported outcomes of structured neuroscience education in school/community settings. Data included characteristics, design, content, delivery, implementation, and outcomes, and findings informed a translational roadmap. Forty-three studies met the inclusion criteria. Publications increased substantially after 2019, with approximately 65% of studies published during this period. Most programs were conducted in the United States (67.4%), implemented in schools (76.7%), and targeted high school students (58.1%). Activity-based programs were most common (41.9%), often single-day interventions (44.2%), with teachers’ moderators (44.2%) rather than trained implementers (23.3%). Content most commonly addressed addiction (25.6%), cellular/molecular (23.3%), and cognitive neuroscience (20.9%). Knowledge gain (27.9%) and attitudes/interest toward neuroscience (25.6%) were frequently evaluated. The findings provide a foundation for applying neuroscience education to NIPE-oriented goals, including brain and mental health literacy, skills and competencies, and health-related decision-making, while also supporting STEM and neuroscience career engagement. The proposed translational roadmap emphasizes global access, developmental tailoring, stronger school–academic partnerships, sustainable implementation, and rigorous, standardized evaluation to guide future educational neuroscience outreach and NIPE-informed education.

articles_hidden.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Computational Models in Psychology: A Tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Valeria Epelbaum; Sophie Engels; Jill de Ron; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Shirley B Wang; Derek de Beurs; Denny Borsboom; Valeria Krzhizhanovskaya
articles_hidden.abstract: There has been an increasing interest in formal models in psychology, allowing researchers to betterunderstand and intervene on psychological systems. However, the methods and tools for understandingand analysing these models are rarely used in psychological research. This is not necessarily due to a lackof methodology, but rather due to them not being familiar in this field. This paper introduces one suchmethod from computational science that can be used to determine the influence of model parameterson an output variable: (global) Sensitivity Analysis (SA). We first discuss the main goals of an SA andpotential applications, such as determining which parameters are the most relevant for causing a changein a chosen model output, such as suicidal thoughts or frequency of panic attacks. We then presenttwo methods that can be used to conduct an SA: the variance-based Sobol SA and the density-basedPAWN. Both of them are demonstrated using an existing computational model in a tutorial-like fashion,provided by (annotated) code in R. The results are connected to empirical literature and implicationsfor model evaluations are discussed. Lastly, we aggregate the entire process into a workflow and codepipeline that can be easily applied to other models. Although this paper only demonstrates the basicapplication of SA, further extensions and purposes, such as model calibration, are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Negative Word Production in Bilinguals Triggers Inhibitory Mechanisms: Evidence from Mass Univariate Time-Frequency Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Rafał Jończyk; Marcin Naranowicz; Guillaume Thierry
articles_hidden.abstract: Semantic processing of negative content is attenuated when bilinguals read for comprehension in their second language (L2). This phenomenon, well studied in comprehension, has seldom been studied in production or the auditory modality. Here, we show that the dampening of negative emotional content also applies in a production context, albeit to a different extent in the visual and the auditory modalities, and likely entails inhibitory control when bilinguals translate negative words from L2 to L1. Polish–English bilinguals orally translated written (Experiment 1) or spoken (Experiment 2) negative and neutral words either from L2–to–L1 or L1–to–L2. Event-Related Potential results suggested differential processing of negative and neutral words only in the L2–to–L1 translation direction and only in Experiment 1, between 300–750 ms after stimulus onset. Hierarchical linear modeling of neural oscillation power over time revealed a two-step modulation of alpha power in the case of negative L2 words suggesting reduced sensitivity at the stage of stimulus integration (240–365 ms) and enhanced inhibitory control during the preparation of L1 production (620–800 ms). In Experiment 2, we found modulations of theta and alpha power by valence regardless of language of operation, which may be explained by evolutionary precedence of auditory over visual language processing and may be specific to the current production context. We thus show that data-driven time-frequency analysis reveals language-emotion interactions in the course of speech preparation and offers more sensitivity than traditional mean voltage amplitude approaches.

articles_hidden.title: Electrophysiological Correlates of Maladaptive Daydreaming: An Exploratory Resting-State EEG Study
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Atashrooz; Amir Sam Kianimoghadam; Reza Khosrowabadi; Hoda Doosalivand
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Maladaptive daydreaming (MD) is characterized by extensive and immersive fantasy activity associated with distress or functional impairment, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly understood. This study examined resting-state electrophysiological differences associated with probable MD.
Methods: Resting-state EEG was recorded from 42 participants (20 probable MDer, 22 screen-negative) during eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. Absolute and relative spectral power and sensor-level functional connectivity were examined using linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to demographic, imagery-related, and affective covariates.
Results: Participants meeting the MDS-16 cutoff for probable MD (≥50) showed greater posterior alpha power than screen-negative participants (pFDR = .015), with estimated between-group differences of 0.83 dB during eyes-open (95% CI [0.06, 1.60]) and 1.38 dB during eyes-closed rest (95% CI [0.60, 2.15]). Significant group × condition interactions emerged for frontal theta and theta/beta activity (both pFDR = .007), reflecting stronger eyes-closed-related modulation in probable MD. Relative-power analyses similarly showed greater proportional alpha activity (both posterior and frontal pFDR = .005), with corresponding reductions in several non-alpha bands. These spectral findings remained robust to demographic, imagery-related, and affective covariates. Exploratory analyses also suggested greater sensor-level wPLI connectivity in probable MD.
Conclusion: Probable MD was associated with greater posterior alpha power, condition-dependent frontal theta modulation, and preliminarily elevated functional connectivity. This pattern is consistent with a bias toward internally directed attention rather than heightened imagery vividness, but because ongoing thought content was not sampled during recording, and group classification relied on self-report rather than clinical diagnosis, these findings should be treated as an initial electrophysiological characterization rather than an MD-specific signature.
Keywords: maladaptive daydreaming; resting-state EEG; quantitative EEG; posterior alpha; frontal theta; internally generated cognition; functional connectivity

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Negative Bias: Disrupted Positive Valence Processing and Asynchronous Hot–Cool Development in Youth Internalizing Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Jiangli Wu; Xiaoxia Hu; Ruoyu Qiu; Guoling Zhou; Yuqing Jin; Fenfen Wang; Ye Cheng; Yudong Zhou; Jianfei Shi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective. Adolescent internalizing symptoms are traditionally attributed to negatively 
biased processing, leaving the developmental trajectory of positive-valence processing 
unclear. Using the hot–cool executive function framework, we examined whether hot 
(emotion-laden) and cool (cognitive control) systems diverge across development and 
differentially predict symptom severity. Method. A community sample of 1,042 Chinese 
students (elementary: n = 300, Mage = 10.3 years; middle: n = 434, Mage = 13.2; high: n 
= 308, Mage = 15.6; 606 boys) completed four computerized tasks assessing inhibitory 
control, cognitive flexibility, attentional bias, and emotional-word processing. Symptoms 
were indexed by developmentally appropriate measures (Children’s Depression Inventory
and Social Anxiety Scale for Children; Depression Anxiety Stress Scales–21). A clinical 
reference group comprised 43 hospitalized adolescents (Mage = 14.5 years). Results. 
Cool executive functions matured linearly across school levels (ps < .001), whereas hot 
attentional bias showed no developmental change (p = .579). In childhood, elevated 
symptoms were associated with broad-based deficits in speed and accuracy; by early 
adolescence this narrowed onto crisis-word stimuli (rs up to .219). Cognitive indices 
explained an additional 12.1% of variance beyond demographics (p < .001). Clinically 
referred youth showed a reversal of the positive-word advantage (+111 ms vs. −35 ms in 
community controls; p < .001, r = .162), indicating a breakdown in appetitive processing. 
Conclusions. Hot and cool cognition mature asynchronously, cool control improving 
while hot valence processing stagnates. Crisis-word hypervigilance and blunted positive?valence processing are partly dissociable risk indicators with distinct severity profiles, 
informing age-sensitive screening for youth internalizing problems.

articles_hidden.title: Why don't the victims of bullying seek help? The effect of underestimating bystanders’ defending intentions
articles_hidden.authors: Guanghui Chen; Zhang anyi; fan Wang; Li Chao; Pei Yongshun; Wei Cui; Wenxin Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Seeking help from others is an important strategy for coping with difficult situations; however, victims of bullying are often reluctant to seek help. Using a series of behavioral experiments with 968 primary and secondary school students, the present study examined individuals’ prediction bias regarding bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective, its association with willingness to seek help, and whether this bias could be modified through an information-based intervention. The results showed that participants reported significantly lower levels of bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective than from the bystander perspective, indicating a systematic underestimation of bystanders’ willingness to defend. This underestimation bias was robust across different types of bullying, genders, and educational stages. Greater underestimation of bystanders’ defending intentions from the victim perspective significantly predicted lower willingness to seek help. Positive contextual information cues significantly reduced the underestimation bias and increased willingness to seek help, whereas negative contextual information cues significantly increased the underestimation bias and decreased willingness to seek help. These findings provide a plausible explanation for victims’ reluctance to seek help and offer practical implications for enhancing help-seeking willingness in school bullying prevention and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Parent-reported strengths in children with ADHD, autism, and AuDHD
articles_hidden.authors: Lessa Madelief Schippers; Amy De Roubaix; Sander Begeer; Corina Greven; Martine Hoogman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Traditionally, research on neurodevelopmental conditions has focused on challenges, while strengths received less attention, despite relevance to clinical practice and well-being. To date, few studies have investigated strengths in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Moreover, no studies directly compared strengths of children with ADHD, autistic children, and children with co-occurring ADHD and autism (AuDHD), leaving open questions about specificity of strengths for these groups.
Method
For the current study, we used data from a large Dutch National registry study, In Kaart. We qualitatively investigated parent-reported data from Dutch children (n = 143) aged 5-16 years with (suspected) ADHD, autism or AuDHD. Parents reported on strengths related to the diagnoses of their child. We used content analysis to identify strengths in children with ADHD, in autistic children and in children with AuDHD.
Results
Across all diagnostic groups, parents reported a wide range of strengths. Children with ADHD and autistic children showed both overlapping and unique strengths, whereas the strengths reported for AuDHD children reflected a combination of both groups. Strengths fell within the categories of ‘Courage’, ‘Higher order cognitive skills’, ‘Humanity’, ‘Justice’, ‘Motor skills’, ‘Temperance’, ‘Transcendence’, ‘Wisdom’ and ‘Other skill’. For children with ADHD, creativity and zest were most prominent, whereas attention to detail and honesty were most prominent in autistic children. 
Conclusion
The variety and frequency of reported strengths suggest that positive aspects are not uncommon for children with ADHD and/or autism and may offer opportunities for a more balanced perspective on these conditions. Our results can feed strength-based approaches for use in clinical practice, assessment, and support, helping children with ADHD and/or autism flourish.

articles_hidden.title: Can We Really Leverage AI-Assisted Automatic Item Generation for Psychological Scale Development?
articles_hidden.authors: Xijuan Zhang; Deborah Laze; Kai Wen Zhou; Kentaro Suzuki
articles_hidden.abstract: With the emergence of large language models (LLMs), researchers can use chatbots such as ChatGPT to rapidly generate large numbers of items for psychological scale development. This study examines the quality of AI-generated items. Across four preregistered studies, we compared AI-generated items with human-generated benchmark scales in terms of factor structure, reliability, and validity. Items were generated by four LLMs using three prompting strategies for three diverse constructs: global self-esteem, mindfulness, and ``resolution,'' a newly proposed facet of cognitive fluency that reflects people’s desire for immediate and concrete outcomes. The initial item pools contained many low-quality items, including near-duplicates of existing items, semantically redundant items, and, most seriously, items tapping into unintended constructs. After these low-quality items were removed, the resulting AI-generated scales showed strong validity across all conditions, but their factor structure and reliability varied by construct. AI-generated self-esteem scales matched the human benchmark in terms of factor structure and reliability, resolution scales showed intermediate performance, and mindfulness scales performed worst. These findings suggest that LLMs can accelerate item generation but cannot replace expert screening and empirical validation. These limitations may arise partly because general-purpose LLMs are not fine-tuned to distinguish among closely related psychological constructs.

articles_hidden.title: Synchronised group singing enhances social bonding more than group conversation or recitation does: A Registered Report across 30 languages
articles_hidden.authors: Zixuan Jia; Yuto Ozaki; Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; jiawen huang; Emmanouil Benetos; Uswatun Khasanah; Sasha Calhoun; Gakuto Chiba; Yoichi Kitayama; Shinya Fujii
articles_hidden.abstract: The evolution of music, language, and prosociality has been debated since before Darwin. The social bonding hypothesis proposes that these phenomena may be interlinked: musicality may have facilitated the evolution of social bonding beyond the possibilities of spoken language. Although dozens of experimental studies have argued that synchronised rhythms can promote bonding, methodological issues including publication bias, sample bias, experimenter effects, and appropriateness of experimental controls make it unclear whether synchronous singing reliably and generally enhances bonding relative to speaking. Following a peer-reviewed Stage 1 Registered Report protocol, we collected data from randomized controlled in-person experiments with 1,017 participants singing and speaking in groups of 5-10 in 30 diverse languages (N = 901 participants after planned quality control exclusions).
