Our results strongly supported all three of our pre-registered confirmatory hypotheses (all Bayes Factors > 30): (i) synchronised group singing enhances self-reported social bonding (20.9% mean increase), a significantly greater increase than (ii) group conversation (12.9% increase) or (iii) synchronous recitation (15.2% increase). Unregistered exploratory analyses suggested that perceived synchronisation and enjoyment are key predictors of social bonding, results are not artefacts of expectancy or group size, and singing’s bonding effects may be stronger in non-Western than Western contexts. Group singing may serve as a better bonding activity than speaking activities in settings such as school or workplace orientation events. Our study provides strong cross-cultural empirical evidence that music is not merely “auditory cheesecake” that is “useless” compared with language (Pinker, 1997). All forms of vocal communication increase social bonding, but group singing bonds us together over 1.5 times more on average than spoken conversation does.

articles_hidden.title: Immediate reward reduces procrastination in a naturalistic multi-day task
articles_hidden.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Yijun Lin; Falk Lieder; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Procrastination is costly and pervasive, and delivering rewards immediately is a widely recommended intervention in self-help advice, yet this advice lacks experimental support. A key challenge in testing it is designing a paradigm that both mimics real-world environments where procrastination arises and permits experimental manipulation. Here we introduce the Multi-day Online Reading Task (MORT), which combines these properties and enables measurement of the full time course of work. In a preregistered experiment (n = 611), participants were given seven days to complete a self-paced reading task and received payment either immediately upon task completion or one day after the deadline. Immediate reward led all participants to start earlier and led those with high trait procrastination, who need help most, to complete work units and the overall task earlier across three reward-performance relationships. The benefits were mediated by motivation and did not come at the cost of task completion or persistence. These findings provide causal evidence that immediate reward reduces procrastination.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual awareness as an information-distribution problem
articles_hidden.authors: Renzo Carlo Lanfranco
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do some sensory signals enter conscious experience while others influence behaviour without being consciously seen, heard, or felt? Research on perceptual awareness typically combines objective decisions with reports of awareness, visual clarity, confidence, or some subset of these measures, yet these outcomes are usually analysed separately. We argue that perceptual awareness can instead be approached as an information-distribution problem: how is stimulus information organised across objective decisions and subjective reports? We develop a theoretical information-theoretic framework based on mutual information, conditional mutual information, and co-information to characterise these relationships at the trial level. Crucially, the interpretation of these quantities depends on what the subjective report measures, allowing the framework to distinguish content-specific awareness, perceptual clarity, and confidence rather than treating them as interchangeable. The framework also specifies how informational relationships can be tracked across stimulus strength, used to formulate conscious–unconscious dissociations, and linked to metacognitive sensitivity. When awareness and confidence are both collected, we further introduce Subjective Access Co-information, CoI(K;A;C), which quantifies the net redundancy–synergy balance in how the two subjective reports jointly relate to decision correctness. By complementing established psychophysical and metacognitive measures with an explicit description of behavioural information structure, this framework provides new experimentally testable targets for theories and neuroscience of consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: Developing Effective GenAI Users: The Missing Motivational System and Why It Matters for Equity
articles_hidden.authors: Kali Trzesniewski; Sarah J Gripshover; Allison Master
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) in education has largely focused on how much students use it and its impact on learning. This framing overlooks the motivational processes driving students’ choices. We propose broadening research to include the study of what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective GenAI users. We define effective GenAI use and propose a motivational model of how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and GenAI engagement choices, with attention to educational inequities that may emerge.

articles_hidden.title: On Power and Sample Size Calculation for Bayes Factors: A Tutorial on the BayesPower Package
articles_hidden.authors: Tsz Keung Wong; Samuel Pawel; Jorge Tendeiro
articles_hidden.abstract:
Power analyses and sample size justifications are increasingly encouraged and required by funding agencies across disciplines such as psychology and the biomedical sciences, highlighting the growing need for accessible sample size determination tools. The present article introduces BayesPower, an R package for conducting sample size determination, power calculation, and Bayes factor calculation in Bayesian hypothesis testing without simulation. The package supports a wide range of statistical tests commonly encountered in the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences, including standardized mean differences, correlations, linear regression and analysis of variance, and tests for one and two proportions. In addition to the traditional comparison of a point-null hypothesis with a
composite alternative hypothesis, BayesPower supports sample size planning for interval-hypothesis Bayes factors (i.e., equivalence testing). For most testing problems, sample size and power are returned almost instantly, enabling researchers to design informative and efficient studies rapidly. To reach a broader audience, the package provides a user-friendly Shiny application for researchers with little or no experience coding in R, in addition to command-line functions for more experienced users. The use of the software is illustrated through five empirical examples.

articles_hidden.title: Testing AI’s abilities at closed-loop psychology research
articles_hidden.authors: Wilma A. Bainbridge; Akram Bakkour; Yuan Chang Leong
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have both incredible promise and incredible risk in becoming major contributors to scientific discovery. Psychology especially is a field that could experience major transformation, as empirical experiments can be run in fully digital closed loops via crowd-sourcing platforms. As a result, LLMs can conduct every stage of the research process: generating research questions, pre-registering its research plans, coding experiments, analyzing data, and writing the manuscript of the results. This could have the potential to accelerate scientific discovery, but also alongside many risks (e.g., false information, monoculturization, high energy usage). Here, we test the degree to which ChatGPT 5.0 can conduct a psychological experiment from start to finish—specifically, testing the degree to which humans employ hexadirectional strategies in navigating a familiar conceptual space. We discuss the model’s successes and failures at each step of the research process, and provide advice on where LLMs shine and where they need extra human observation. Our work opens a discussion of what this means for the broader field of psychological research—as these models have both high potential, but also important drawbacks and ramifications to consider.

articles_hidden.title: Cooperative care as a candidate mechanism linking prolonged childhood and brain expansion in human evolution
articles_hidden.authors: Tobias Grossmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Two traits distinguish modern humans from all other primates: an exceptionally large brain and an exceptionally prolonged childhood. What mechanism produced this combination, and why are the two traits dissociated in other hominins? Standard models predict that brain size and developmental duration should co-vary tightly, yet the fossil record reveals that they do not: small-brained hominins at Dikika, Dmanisi, and Rising Star show slow development, while large-brained Neanderthals matured fast. Evolutionary simulations show that cooperative care can offer a coherent account of these dissociations. In Experiment 1, cooperative care extends childhood and, as an emergent consequence, enhances social learning independent of brain size (+32.5% childhood extension with no change in brain size), creating a knowledge–storage mismatch that generates selection pressure for brain expansion. In Experiment 2, when the metabolic ceiling is lifted through allomaternal provisioning, cooperative care populations show significant brain expansion (+34%) co-occurring with further childhood extension and enhanced social learning. In Experiment 3, when populations lacking cooperative care achieve equivalent brain expansion through dietary improvement alone, they instead mature faster, producing brain expansion decoupled from developmental prolongation. The simulation thereby identifies two emergent routes to large brains: a cooperative-care route producing coupled brain–childhood expansion, and a nutrition-only route producing brain expansion without developmental prolongation—a dissociation that parallels the comparison between modern humans and Neanderthals. These results suggest that the distinctly human developmental package may reflect not brain expansion per se, but the cooperative care system within which that expansion occurred.

articles_hidden.title: Which Comes First: Ideology, or Moral Values? Panel evidence from the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles_hidden.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Kevin Smith; Ingrid Johnsen Haas; John Jostes
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent work has called into question the longstanding intuition that differences in political orientation are attributable to differences in moral values; instead, people may change their reported values to justify their political preferences. To identify which most plausibly causes which, we conducted a three-wave panel study, using quotas to approximate a demographically representative initial sample of U.S. adults and measuring values in four different ways, with each measure grounded in a distinct theoretical framework. We found that: 1) Ideology and partisanship consistently showed greater cross-wave stability than values. 2) Within-subject wave-to-wave shifts in political orientation and values were rarely and weakly related in either direction. Between-subjects analyses replicated existing work: conservatives and liberals tended to value different things. But during these months, respondents did not tend to become more conservative or liberal depending on what they valued, or to come to value anything more or less because of their ideology.

articles_hidden.title: Lifespan accumulated differences in semantic memory structure contribute to increases in episodic false memories
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Henderson; Ryan McCurdy; Anika Bhatia; Hita Devulapalli; Sean Matthew Polyn; Audrey Duarte
articles_hidden.abstract: Semantic memory grows across the lifespan with experience, scaffolding episodic memory processes while potentially contributing to memory errors when memory representations overlap. Prior work has attributed age-related increases in false recognition memory to executive dysfunction, but little is known about how lifelong semantic knowledge accumulation affects these episodic errors. In the current study, we recorded EEG while younger (n = 36) and older adults (n = 41) completed an episodic memory task in which study list-lure similarity was systematically varied using distributional model-derived measures of semantic similarity. We found older adults’ endorsement of lures was less dependent on semantic similarity than those of younger adults. Older adults also demonstrated reduced coupling of neural similarity to model-derived semantic similarity, and reduced encoding-retrieval reinstatement for accurate lure rejections. Together, these findings suggest that age-related increases in false memory reflect both altered semantic representational structure and reduced source monitoring, highlighting how semantic knowledge accumulated across the lifespan may simultaneously support episodic memory while increasing susceptibility to semantically driven distortions.

articles_hidden.title: Frontal midline theta tracks negatively biased affective updating in social anxiety from adolescence to young adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Elise Kortink; Öykü Gürcan; Selin Topel; Leonie Koban; Melle J. W. van der Molen
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative self-beliefs are a core feature of social anxiety, yet the neurocomputational processes that translate social-evaluative feedback into biased self-beliefs remain poorly understood. Here we examined whether frontal-midline theta (FM-theta) - an EEG signature of performance monitoring – governs how performance-based prediction errors (PEs) are incorporated into updating self-feelings based on performance feedback (i.e., affective updating). A sample of 216 adolescents and young adults (174 female; mean age 18.4 years) participated in a speech performance task during which participants provided a short speech that was evaluated by three judges. After the speech, participants were asked to appraise their own performance on the same evaluative items used by the judges. After their appraisal on each item, participants were provided with the judge’s evaluation and were subsequently asked to indicate how they felt based on the feedback received. We found that participants updated their self-feelings more strongly based on positive than negative feedback, and that this positive affective updating bias weakened with age. As hypothesized, participants with elevated social anxiety displayed more negative affective updating, and social anxiety fully mediated the age-related decline in positive affective updating. Critically, in individuals with elevated social anxiety, the magnitude of negative performance feedback was associated with stronger FM-theta modulated negative affective updating. These findings corroborate previous positive affective updating biases in healthy individuals and furthermore underscore a key role of FM-theta oscillations in feedback-guided affective updating, potentially reinforcing negative self-belief in individuals with elevated social anxiety.

articles_hidden.title: Dyslexia Eye Tracking COrpus (DECO): First- and Second Language Book Reading in Adults with Dyslexia
articles_hidden.authors: Sam Boeve; Lore FranÃ§ois; Ella Salgado Salgado Figueroa; Esperanza Badaya; Louisa Bogaerts; Nicolas Dirix
articles_hidden.abstract: Openly available eye-tracking corpora have been indispensable for the progress of psycholinguistic theories of reading. Past corpus work extensively covered typical reading in a range of languages, but left reading difficulties relatively under documented. In this article, we present a novel corpus, the Dyslexia Eye Tracking COrpus (DECO). It includes eye-tracking data collected from 20 Dutch - English bilingual adults with a diagnosis of developmental dyslexia. They read an entire novel (almost 60.000 words), with one half presented in their first language (Dutch) and the other half in their second language (English). After each chapter the participants answered multiple reading comprehension questions. Additionally, all participants completed several measures of linguistic abilities, including vocabulary, spelling, a one-minute reading test and a language questionnaire. This corpus is the largest of its kind and is a direct extension of the existing GECO corpus of typical reading (Cop, Dirix, Drieghe & Duyck, 2017). In combination with GECO, it provides researchers with a unique resource to study naturalistic reading in dyslexia and its intersection with bilingualism. All data and materials will be made available upon publication.

articles_hidden.title: Predictors of suicide attempt in adolescents with a history of self-harm: a machine learning study combining psychosocial and actigraphy measures
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Sellier Silva; Bhavya Patwa; Dylan James; Martin Lepage; Lena Palaniyappan; Massimiliano Orri
articles_hidden.abstract:
Youth suicide attempt is an important clinical and public health concern, yet prediction of
suicide attempt among youth with a history of self-harm remains challenging. Disrupted states of
arousal may play an important role in the etiology of suicide attempt but have rarely been measured
objectively in prospective studies. In this study, we examined to what extent actigraphy-derived arousal
markers and questionnaire-based psychosocial measures collected at age 14 could predict self-reported
suicide attempt at age 17 in a population-based sample of 1,321 adolescents with a history of self-harm
from a United Kingdom cohort. We conducted both inferential analyses (univariable and multivariable
logistic regressions), and predictive (machine learning) modeling using nested cross-validation.
Cannabis use, peer problems, depressive symptoms, higher BMI, lower self-esteem, and sex emerged
as significant independent predictors of later reported suicide attempt. Machine learning models
achieved moderate predictive performance (AUROC = 0.65–0.67), with relatively high sensitivity
(0.71–0.81) but lower specificity (0.37–0.53). Peer problems and depressive symptoms were
consistently among the most important predictors across models. Although some actigraphy-derived
measures contributed to prediction in specific models, two-stage analyses suggested little incremental
predictive value beyond questionnaire-based measures alone. These findings highlight the importance
of cannabis use, interpersonal difficulties and depressive symptoms in predicting suicide attempt
among adolescent who self-harmed and suggest a limited additional contribution of actigraphy-derived
arousal markers for long-term prediction.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Open-Weight Large Language Models for Structured Depression Assessment from Clinical Interviews
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey M. Girard; Gaossou Youssouf Kebe; Louis-Philippe Morency; Fernando De la Torre; Einat Liebenthal; Justin T. Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: The administration of semi-structured clinical interviews for depression assessment is resource-intensive and susceptible to rater drift. While large language models (LLMs) offer potential for automated quality assurance, reliance on proprietary models creates data privacy barriers incompatible with secure clinical workflows. This study evaluates a privacy-preserving pipeline using open-weight LLMs to perform item-level scoring of the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) directly from interview transcripts. The sample included 541 video-recorded English-language interviews with 277 psychiatric inpatients diagnosed with diverse affective and psychotic disorders. Benchmarking 25 architectures, we found that an indirect scoring strategy, where models predict individual item scores that are subsequently summed, significantly outperformed direct total score prediction. This suggests that decomposing the assessment into intermediate reasoning steps improves performance. The best-performing models achieved “good” error rates and “excellent” correlations with trusted human labels, approaching established benchmarks for human inter-rater reliability. To determine the active ingredients of effective prompting, we conducted an ablation study. Results revealed that descriptive cues (scoring criteria) were the primary driver of performance, whereas few-shot examples provided negligible additional benefit, suggesting that zero-shot prompting is a viable, efficient strategy. However, error analysis identified a multimodal gap, where text-only models struggled more with items dependent on nonverbal behavior. We conclude that open-weight LLMs demonstrate strong potential to serve as secure “digital second opinions,” representing a promising step toward augmenting clinical decision-making without compromising patient privacy.

articles_hidden.title: A Computational Account of Approach-Avoidance Conflict in a Foraging-Inspired Search Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Usée; Christiane A. Melzig; Dirk Ostwald; Anne Collins
articles_hidden.abstract:
An approach-avoidance conflict (AAC) arises when the same action promises reward but also carries potential harm. Here, we examined how humans
initiate and sustain engagement under such conflict using an online foraging-inspired AAC task. Eighty-seven participants repeatedly encountered
visual search fields associated with four instructed reward-punishment states and decided whether to enter each field and how extensively to search it,
allowing us to distinguish passive avoidance as withheld entry from active within-field avoidance as early search termination. Participants committed to
search more often and explored more extensively when expected rewards were high and punishments were low. Agent-based behavioral modeling indicated that initial
and sustained engagement could be characterized at different levels of behavioral granularity: commitment to search was best explained by additive
reward-punishment evaluation with state-independent trial drift, whereas search extent was best captured by a click-wise stopping process inspired by the
marginal value theorem, a foraging account of when to leave a current patch for alternatives. These findings suggest that avoidance under conflict is
not a single decision, but unfolds across separable decisions about whether to engage, how long to persist, and when to leave.

articles_hidden.title: Therapeutic Alliance and Perceived Closeness in MDMA-Assisted Therapy for Social Anxiety Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph M. Diehl; Christina Chwyl; Liliana Kennedy; Jenna Lejeune; Jason B Luoma
articles_hidden.abstract: The therapeutic relationship is considered central to psychedelic-assisted therapy, yet little empirical research has examined how it changes during 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) or relates to acute MDMA experiences and clinical outcomes, particularly for social anxiety disorder (SAD). This preregistered secondary analysis examined therapeutic alliance and perceived closeness during an open-label pilot trial of MDMA-AT for SAD (N = 20; NCT-redacted-for-anonymous-review). Participants completed three preparation sessions, two MDMA dosing sessions, and six integration sessions. Therapeutic alliance and therapist closeness were assessed before and after each MDMA session using the Agnew Relationship Measure and Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale, respectively. Social anxiety severity was assessed with the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale at baseline and post-treatment, and self-transcendent experiences were assessed following MDMA sessions. Alliance was high after preparation and increased significantly following the first MDMA session, with evidence of ceiling effects later in treatment. Closeness increased significantly during each MDMA session and decreased during the subsequent nondrug interval. Greater MDMA-session closeness predicted lower post-treatment social anxiety, including after adjustment for corresponding pre-MDMA closeness. Self-transcendent emotions and connection-related experiences were associated with greater MDMA-session closeness, and pre-dosing closeness predicted greater self-transcendent emotions during the subsequent MDMA session. These findings distinguish more stable therapeutic alliance from more dynamic felt interpersonal closeness and suggest that closeness may be a particularly sensitive relational process in MDMA-AT for SAD.

articles_hidden.title: Two Wisdoms, Two Pathways to Well-Being: Locus of Control among Tribal and Non-Tribal Youth in Jharkhand
articles_hidden.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Locus of control is widely treated as a near-universal predictor of psychological well-being. Most supporting evidence comes from Western, individualist samples. Whether this link holds equally in indigenous Indian communities remains unclear. Objective: This study compared locus of control and psychological well-being between tribal (Adivasi) and non-tribal youth in Jharkhand, India, and tested whether community moderates the strength of the relationship between the two. Method: A cross-sectional comparative design was used with 500 youth (250 tribal, 250 non-tribal), stratified equally by employment status and gender. Participants completed a 24-item locus of control scale and Ryff's six-dimension Psychological Well-Being scale. Results: Non-tribal youth scored substantially higher than tribal youth on both locus of control, t(449.4) = 23.76, p < .001, d = 2.12, and psychological well-being, t(326.2) = 13.83, p < .001, d = 1.24, with the largest subscale gap on Environmental Mastery, d = 2.09. The correlation between locus of control and well-being was far stronger among non-tribal youth (r = .93) than tribal youth (r = .43), a difference confirmed by a Fisher z-test, z = 13.08, p < .001. Conclusion: Community identity shapes not only mean levels of agency and well-being but also how tightly the two are linked, suggesting tribal well-being draws on pathways beyond individual perceived control.

articles_hidden.title: Combined sleep deprivation and light therapy for depression in major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Bartholomeus Haarman; Stella Druiven; Jeanine Kamphuis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Combined chronotherapy, a combination of sleep deprivation and light therapy, offers a promising approach to accelerating improvement in depression. Therapeutic sleep deprivation can have a rapid antidepressant effect, while light therapy and regulation of sleep timing are intended to maintain the initial benefit. This review examines the evidence supporting further clinical evaluation of combined chronotherapy in major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD).
Methods. We examined literature identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Europe PMC and citation searching, with the latest search conducted on 9 September 2026. Narrative synthesis was used to examine speed and persistence of response, clinical applicability and tolerability. Controlled studies of combined chronotherapy, studies of individual treatment components and observational studies were considered separately, with repeated reports linked where identifiable. We interpreted outcomes in relation to treatment schedules, comparators and study limitations.
Results. Seven randomised trials in adult patients with a depressive episode evaluated early antidepressant effects of combined chronotherapy. Several trials found rapid improvement, with benefits extending into follow-up, and outpatient studies support feasibility beyond inpatient settings. The most recent trial, including 44 randomised adults with masked outcome assessment, found greater improvement from day 5 through day 12 and discharge. Findings were not consistent across studies: one trial found an advantage confined to the first week, while two found no significant benefit on their primary comparisons. Studies of individual treatment components and clinical cohorts provide additional evidence on maintenance, patient selection and delivery.
Conclusions. Combined chronotherapy is a promising adjunctive treatment for depression in MDD and BD, with evidence of rapid improvement and persistence of benefit in some trials. Findings vary across treatment protocols and settings, and the magnitude and durability of benefit remain uncertain. Further adequately powered randomised trials are needed to establish its clinical role.

articles_hidden.title: Barriers and enablers to implementing and using surveillance technology for suicide prevention in public places
articles_hidden.authors: Bethany Cliffe; Alex Dark; Ian Marsh; Penny Phillips; Andy Willis; Laura Joyner; Lisa Marzano; Peter Craig; Keith Hawton; Jay-Marie Mackenzie
articles_hidden.abstract: This research sought to understand the barriers and enablers of implementing surveillance technologies for suicide prevention in public spaces. To explore a range of professional stakeholders’ experiences of and attitudes towards surveillance technologies, we drew on ethnography of three public sites that have high suicide rates, and seven focus groups with 56 stakeholders working there. Framework analysis was used, and ethnography notes were triangulated with this. We learnt that there were four stages at which barriers and enablers exist: 1) decision making, 2) procurement, 3) implementation and 4) perceived effectiveness. During decision making, barriers included lacking specialist expertise to know what technology to implement and how to implement it, and the organisational and personal risks around assuming responsibility for suicide prevention. During procurement, the costs were a notable challenge, with stakeholders having limited budgets to purchase the technology and ensure its sustainability. Factors which enabled implementation of the technology were having a suitable response mechanism so that interventions could be delivered, and making sure the technology was appropriate for the location/context. Technology was perceived to be effective when it enabled identification of/ response to incidents, but not when it generated false alerts or carried risks like displacement to other locations.

articles_hidden.title: Non-word repetition in bilingual children: the role of language exposure, vocabulary scores and environmental factors
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Gianmatteo Farabolini; pasquale rinaldi; Maria Cristina Caselli; Alejandrina Cristia
articles_hidden.abstract: Assessing language development in bilingual children is challenging in geographical areas where bilinguals have different native languages. Lexical development measures are often used as a starting point to study linguistic abilities in bilingual children. Non-word repetition (NWR) has been found to be very informative in detecting variation. The present study contributes to the broader research aim of documenting bilinguals' language skills. In a sample of 19 Italian-speaking bilingual children with different native languages, correlations among performance on an Italian-like NWR and receptive vocabulary score (Italian PPVT-R), cumulative exposure, age of first exposure to Italian, current Italian exposure, maternal education, parental concerns and vocabulary in toddlerhood (MB-CDI) were calculated. NWR performances correlated with PPVT-R and parental concerns, but not with maternal education and language exposure measures. Neither NWR scores nor PPVT-R scores were related to Italian vocabulary size in toddlerhood (MB-CDI). We integrate our results with those of others and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of administering NWR to bilingual children, and more generally how to perform early bilingual language assessments.

articles_hidden.title: What are we measuring when we measure moral concern?
articles_hidden.authors: Matti Wilks; Bastian Jaeger; Paul Bloom
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding the factors that shape who we consider worthy of moral concern has become a focus of moral psychology. This research generally shows that we care most about our family and close others, and less about non-humans and the environment. However, these studies sometimes yield unusual or nonsensical results. We demonstrate that these findings can be somewhat explained by issues with the conceptualization and measurement of moral concern. Study 1 reveals that many studies do not define their construct. Study 2 demonstrates weak convergent validity among five existing measures of moral concern. Study 3 highlights that laypeople actively differentiate between facets of moral concern, granting greater rights to a murderer than an apple tree, while expressing greater care and compassion for a tree. These findings indicate that treating distinct constructs, such as rights, obligations, and care, as interchangeable may limit our measurement and understanding of moral concern.

articles_hidden.title: A Systematic Review of MDMA’s Effects on Social Cognition in Placebo-Controlled Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Burmester; David Nutt; Laura Aggett; Chloe Wong; Sofia Bonito; Sophie Leigh; Tessa Bo Watford; Dasha Nicholls
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) is associated with distinctive prosocial and empathogenic effects, yet the consistency and scope of its impact on social cognition in humans remain unclear. Although numerous placebo-controlled studies have examined MDMA’s acute social effects, findings vary widely across subjective and behavioural domains.

Methods
We conducted a systematic review of placebo-controlled studies investigating the acute effects of MDMA on social cognition in adults. Outcomes included self-reported social and emotional experience, task-based measures of social cognition and behaviour, and relevant physiological and neurobiological indices. Studies administering MDMA as the sole intervention were included.

Results
Across 75 studies, MDMA reliably enhanced subjective social experience, including feelings of sociability, emotional openness, closeness, and emotional empathy. In contrast, behavioural manifestations of prosociality, such as cooperation and trust in economic or performance-based tasks, were inconsistent and strongly context dependent. Behavioural and neuroimaging measures showed reduced accuracy in identifying negative social cues, including fear and anger, but no study used signal-detection metrics to discriminate genuine perceptual blunting from a shift in response criterion. Neuroimaging findings were from small, methodologically heterogeneous samples.

Conclusions
MDMA consistently alters how social interactions are experienced, but subjective changes do not reliably translate into observable prosocial behaviour. MDMA reduces accuracy in identifying negative social cues, particularly fear and anger, but whether this reflects a specific blunting of threat processing or a shift in response bias and salience detection remains unresolved. Clarifying these mechanisms has implications for understanding MDMA’s therapeutic potential in conditions characterised by heightened social threat and avoidance.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive evidence for a mediated association between childhood adversity and resilience: A reexamination of Suriano and Valentino (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix published by Suriano and Valentino, we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model linking adverse childhood experiences with resilience. We show that the reported pattern of associations can be reproduced almost exactly by a conceptually distinct latent-variable model that does not rely on the influencing ordering specified in the original study. In this alternative framework, adverse childhood experiences, resilience, positive humor, and tolerance for ambiguity are treated as indicators of a broader latent characteristic, namely core self-evaluation. The results highlight an important challenge in observational research: a single covariance structure may be consistent with multiple theoretical explanations. As a result, correlational evidence alone provides limited justification for privileging one explanatory account over competing models. Researchers should therefore evaluate plausible alternative specifications before drawing strong conclusions about psychological mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: MEMORY RECOGNITION IN AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER ACROSS LABORATORY AND MUSEUM CONTEXTS: AN EXPLORATORY STUDY
articles_hidden.authors: Bastien Cothenet; Nicolas Navarro; Nadine Ravel; Amandine Rey
articles_hidden.abstract: Episodic memory in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has primarily been investigated using laboratory-based paradigms. This exploratory study examined recognition memory across two distinct encoding contexts: an on-site museum visit and a controlled laboratory setting. Ten adults with ASD and 25 neurotypical (NT) adults completed recognition tasks following both contexts. Recognition sensitivity (d′), recollection judgments, and detail-based versus gist-based recollection were assessed. Recognition sensitivity differed according to group and context: ASD participants showed higher sensitivity than NT participants in the laboratory, whereas no group difference emerged following the museum visit. Recollection rates for correctly recognized items were similar across groups. However, following museum encoding, ASD participants relied more on detail-based recollection, whereas NT participants relied more on gist-based recollection. These findings suggest that episodic memory differences in ASD may concern the nature of information supporting recollection, highlighting the value of studying memory in real-world settings alongside traditional laboratory paradigms.

articles_hidden.title: Communicating causal effect heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Matti Vuorre; Matthew Kay; Niall Bolger
articles_hidden.abstract: Advances in experimental, data collection, and analysis methods have brought population variability in psychological phenomena to the fore. Yet, current practices for interpreting such heterogeneity do not appropriately treat the uncertainty inevitable in any statistical summary. Heterogeneity is best thought of as a distribution of features with a mean (average person’s effect) and variance (between-person differences). This expected heterogeneity distribution can be further summarized e.g. as a heterogeneity interval (Bolger et al., 2019). However, because empirical studies estimate the underlying mean and variance parameters with uncertainty, the expected distribution and interval will underestimate the actual range of plausible effects in the population. Using Bayesian hierarchical models, and with the aid of empirical datasets from social and cognitive psychology, we provide a walk-through of effective heterogeneity reporting and display tools that appropriately convey measures of uncertainty. We cover interval, proportion, and ratio measures of heterogeneity and their estimation and interpretation. These tools can be a spur to theory building, allowing researchers to widen their focus from population averages to population heterogeneity in psychological phenomena.

articles_hidden.title: Implementing an evidence-based 'identification-to-intervention' approach through school Mental Health Support Teams: A qualitative study of expected implementation determinants
articles_hidden.authors: Alice Rose Phillips; Rosie Underhill; Michael Larkin; Cathy Creswell; Rachel McGuire; Hollie Edwards; Catherine Gallop; Ian MacDonald; Falko Sniehotta; Tessa Reardon
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent in childhood and are associated with academic and social difficulties. Although effective early interventions exist, many children do not access support due to complex referral routes and limited-service provision. ‘Identification-to-intervention’ (i2i) approaches address these barriers by combining universal screening with a targeted therapist-guided parent-led online intervention. In England, Mental Health Support Teams (MHSTs) deliver evidence-based interventions in schools so may be well-placed to implement i2i approaches. We lack understanding of factors which might influence implementation of i2i for child anxiety problems in a routine practice context. 

Method: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with MHST staff (n=16), primary school staff (n=6), and parents/carers (n=6) across England. Interviews were guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR 2.0)’s implementation determinants and analysed using template analysis. 

Findings: i2i was viewed as a simplified and accessible route to early mental health support. Participants identified barriers to parents/carers accessing i2i, including stigma-related concerns, literacy or language challenges, and limited familiarity with MHSTs. MHST staff felt i2i aligned with their remit and current skillset. Although some school and MHST staff viewed i2i as timesaving, others anticipated workload increases. Usual referral and clinical data management systems would need adjustment to allow direct contact from parents and the collection of screening data. 

Conclusions: i2i approaches are considered acceptable and appropriate across parents/carers, school staff and MHSTs, but structural barriers associated with MHSTs would need to be addressed to optimise implementation.

articles_hidden.title: They’re All Like That! The Universality Signature of Central Form
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper investigates how humans store information within the thousands of concepts that structure thought, belief, and action. Building on recent work suggesting that each concept has a central form—a core representational structure that triggers strong beliefs when properties are encoded into it—this paper introduces and tests a new form-triggered belief: a default universality belief. Across two experiments, participants judged central form properties as universally true of all category members. They rejected this belief for properties that were highly prototypical or causally important, if they were not part of the concept's form. This effect held across both familiar and novel categories, and across domains including animals, artifacts, institutions, places, and events. These findings suggest a domain-general mechanism underlying universality judgments, with implications for theories of stereotyping, trauma, and ideology. More broadly, they help to explain how humans construct complex thoughts by reducing complex concepts down to a limited set of core properties, and they resolve a longstanding puzzle about why people assume universality despite its rarity in the natural world.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Gastric State on Perceptual and Attitudinal Body Image Dimensions and Their Moderation by Eating Pathology
articles_hidden.authors: Lucy Stafford; Alexandra Claire Pike; Catherine Preston
articles_hidden.abstract: Body image encompasses cognitive-affective attitudes and explicit and implicit body size perceptions. Although interoception is implicated in eating pathology, evidence directly linking gastrointestinal states to body image remains limited by caloric confounds, a dearth of research using perceptual measures, and narrow assessments of interoceptive facets. To address these gaps, this study (n=68) manipulated gastric state using the Water Load Test-II to evaluate how gastrointestinal sensitivity, over/unconfidence in sensitivity, and appraisal are related to baseline body image and disordered eating, and if gastric state can change body image and if this is moderated by disordered eating. At baseline, elevated hunger-fear and fullness-shame predicted heightened eating shame, dietary restriction/preoccupation, and reduced baseline body satisfaction, with fullness-shame uniquely predicting greater weight/shape concerns and restraint. Heightened gastrointestinal sensitivity predicted less certainty in judging an aperture as passable relative to body size, whereas underconfidence in gastrointestinal sensitivity predicted smaller waist size estimations and greater certainty in judging an aperture as passable. Controlling for baseline body image, fullness significantly decreased body satisfaction, increased the width required for an aperture to be judged as passable, and increased waist size estimations according to disordered eating severity. Eating disorder severity predicted lower certainty for aperture passability. During nutritional eating disorder recovery, where postprandial fullness is unavoidable, unaddressed negative appraisal, hypervigilance, and over/underconfidence in gastric sensitivity may directly trigger and perpetuate body image distortions and uncertainty. Eating to satiation, rather than complete fullness, may offer a behavioral goal for ongoing treatment once weight is stabilised.

articles_hidden.title: Reconceptualizing Individuals, Categories, and the Social Group: Self-Categorization Theory 2.0
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Skorich
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-Categorization Theory is a theory of the way in which human beings come to represent themselves cognitively as group members. In this paper, I present 5 critiques of Self-Categorization Theory, with the goal of further refining it: (1) categorization into equivalence classes is neither sufficient nor necessary for perceiving groups as entities; (2) the boundary conditions on self-categorization (vs. categorization) are underspecified; (3) the person level is relatively underexamined; (4) meta-contrast is implausible as a basis for entity formation; and (5) comparative and correlational relations are overemphasized. I propose as resolutions to these critiques that: self-categorization is the categorization of intentional agents; groups are holistic entities, perceptually triggered by cues to collective intentionality, and cognitively represented as “conceptual atoms” with an associated object file; group phenomena have person equivalents and vice-versa; and relations between intentional entities and between intentional entities and their properties are represented propositionally in a “language of thought”. Taken together these resolutions result in an updated Self-Categorization Theory 2.0 (SCT2.0). I discuss this expanded theory in general terms, and then further elaborate on the key mechanisms of salience, depersonalization, and prototypicality. I conclude by emphasizing the way in which SCT2.0 builds on the legacy of its predecessor.

articles_hidden.title: FEED your mind: The evolutionary roots of human food cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Raffaella I Rumiati; Annie E. Wertz; Carol Coricelli
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on food cognition has largely overlooked that our modern food environment strongly differs from the environment in which our ancestors lived. When foraging for food in wild environments, our ancestors had to distinguish edible food resources from myriad inedible and potentially toxic entities. In contrast, in most cultures today, many decisions about food are made during a trip to the grocery store or a meal at a restaurant, where we might ask ourselves: Is this item healthy? but certainly not: Is this item edible or poisonous? Here we argue that the scope of the problem humans faced with respect to food included navigating through wild environments to Find candidate food items, Excluding the costs of making a mistake and consuming a harmful food item, Evaluating the nutritional benefits of the potential foods and Deciding which food items to include in their diet. We call this the FEED problem and argue that it provides an organizing framework for thinking about the wide array of cognitive processes involved in human food psychology. The FEED problem can also be used as a generative theory to produce new testable empirical predictions about what cognitive mechanisms drive our modern food behaviors and provides a roadmap for future research in the field of food cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of peer victimization on prosocial behavior in adolescents: A reanalysis of Guo et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Guo et al., we reassessed the evidence supporting their mediation model relating peer victimization to lower levels of prosocial behavior among adolescents. We demonstrate that the empirical associations can be reproduced with high accuracy by an alternative latent-variable model that does not depend on the order of influence proposed in the original article. In this model, self-reported peer victimization, psychological capital, empathy, and prosocial behavior are conceptualized as indicators of a broader latent construct, namely core self-evaluation. The findings illustrate a fundamental issue in observational research: different theoretical models may account equally well for the same covariance structure. Consequently, correlational data alone provide limited grounds for favoring one specific explanatory mechanism over competing alternatives. Consequently, researchers should consider alternative specifications before drawing strong conclusions about underlying processes.

articles_hidden.title: What Predicts Psychotherapy Outcomes Across Disorders and Treatments: an Umbrella Review
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Jacobs; Tabea Jaleta; Kevin Hilbert
articles_hidden.abstract:
The objective of assigning patients to their most promising treatment has sparked considerable interest in 
contemporary research. Many studies develop models to predict treatment outcomes and stratify treatment 
allocation. Predictive accuracy of such models, however, has remained limited due to a lack of systematic 
information used for model training, given that variables included in such datasets are often selected due to their 
availability in routine care datasets. To increase systematic information in the data, the inclusion of promising 
candidate predictors, based on theoretical or empirical considerations, is crucial. Therefore, this study 
systematically searches for and summarizes the evidence on patient level variables that predict psychotherapy 
outcome. Since the literature to answer this question is vast, an umbrella review methodology (i.e., a review of 
reviews) was implemented. Searches in PubMed, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library with preregistered 
search strings yielded 5926 articles. Title and abstract screening implemented AI-based methods alongside 
human review. N = 51 papers were extracted and quantitative evidence was descriptively aggregated. We 
identified 69 potential predictors. Using post-hoc defined criteria, reliable and relevant predictors were selected. 
Some of these were known and frequently assessed predictors (e.g., symptom severity, diagnosis) while others 
are not frequently assessed in routine care. Among the latter were social support, executive functioning, 
therapeutic alliance and motivation for treatment. The identified variables represent promising candidate 
predictors, which can inform theoretical models of therapy success, guide clinicians, or, if included in future 
analysis pipelines, have the potential to increase predictive performance in psychotherapy studies.

articles_hidden.title: Social Coercion in the Shadow of Hierarchy: State-Mediated Coercive Mobilisation and Australians' COVID-19 Vaccination Compliance
articles_hidden.authors: Katie Attwell; Joshua Lake
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: This study investigates coercive (social) mobilisation to vaccinate in liberal democracies using evidence from Australia.
Methods: We analyse how government policies can prompt non-state actors to pressure the unvaccinated. We then analyse data on COVID-19 vaccination in a representative sample of adults (N=4208), investigating the prevalence and sources of coercive mobilisation and conducting regression analyses to identify associated factors.
Results: Conceptual analysis distinguished between state-led coercive mobilisation, where authoritarian governments rely on hierarchical structures to pressure citizens, and state-mediated coercive mobilisation, whereby liberal democratic governments generate social pressure through vaccine mandates that produce encourage stigmatisation, workplace expansion, and pressures associated with collective goals. Empirically, a quarter of people vaccinated reported being coerced, and more than half reported responding to some degree of social pressure. Social coercion was most common in New South Wales and Victoria. People were more likely to attribute vaccination to social coercion when they had lower political trust, or lower trust in friends and family as sources of vaccination information. Higher trust in social media sources and stronger community connectedness were associated with increased attribution to coercion. Higher education and socioeconomic status were associated with increased attributions of employer coercion, and education workers reported more social coercion. Younger people were consistently more likely to attribute vaccination to coercive mobilisation, with some evidence this was also true for women.
Conclusion: Findings extend research on coercive mobilisation beyond non-democratic settings, revealing similar dynamics shaping vaccination decisions in liberal democracies.

articles_hidden.title: What motivates support for mandatory vaccination? Trust as a moderator of relations between personal values and support for coercive policy measures
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua Lake; Uwana Evers; Katie Attwell
articles_hidden.abstract: Public debates about vaccination mandates often pit collective welfare against individual autonomy, yet little is known about how personal values relate to mandate support. In late 2025/early 2026 we surveyed adults in Australia (N=4,208), France (N=3,858), and Italy (N=3,973); personal values were measured with the Best-Worst Refined Values scale; vaccination trust with the Vaccination Trust Indicator; and attitudes toward mandatory vaccination with the Vaccination Mandate Attitudes Scale. We examined value-attitude relations by country for each of the 10 basic personal values, and the role of trust as a moderator. Vaccination trust moderated associations between values and mandate attitudes for 8/10 values in Australia, and 9/10 values in France and Italy. Across countries, when vaccination trust was high, growth oriented values (benevolence; universalism; self direction) and security values, were associated with increased mandate support, however when trust was low, they were associated with reduced support. Self enhancement values (achievement; power) and tradition values generally showed the opposite pattern of effects, while conformity values displayed a relatively stronger (positive) direct effect. Findings identify vaccination trust as a moderating factor in the attitudinal expression of value priorities, suggesting that future research on policy design and communication should examine how trust and value-congruent framing jointly shape public acceptability.

articles_hidden.title: Rescripting suicidal mental imagery in young people: A pilot study of feasibility, acceptability and safety
articles_hidden.authors: Lianne Schmaal; Georgie Paulik; Zamantha Munoz; Laura van Velzen; Pemma Davies; Martin Mitrevski; Eleanor Bailey; Phoebe Gleeson; Lisa Incerti; Samantha Galea
articles_hidden.abstract: Suicidal mental imagery – vivid, intrusive mental images of suicide or death - is common among young people experiencing suicidal ideation and may increase risk of suicidal behaviour, yet interventions directly targeting these images are lacking. We conducted a single-arm pilot study evaluating the feasibility, acceptability and safety of a brief, therapist delivered imagery rescripting intervention targeting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery in help-seeking young people aged 16–25 years with mood disorders and current or recent suicidal ideation. Fourteen participants were recruited; 12 were eligible for the intervention and 11 (92%) completed treatment and follow-up. The recruitment target (N=25) was not met, largely due to service disruptions and clinician capacity constraints. Acceptability and safety criteria were met: 73% reported that sessions were not distressing, none felt less safe following treatment, and no participant showed increased suicidal ideation from baseline to follow-up. Two serious adverse events occurred but were judged unrelated to the intervention. Exploratory analyses showed reductions in suicidal-image frequency, realness, compellingness, intrusiveness and distress, alongside a 52% reduction in suicidal ideation severity. Our pilot study indicates that directly rescripting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery showed encouraging short-term safety and acceptability signals in young people, supporting evaluation in a larger randomised controlled trial.

articles_hidden.title: Neural correlates and behavioral outcomes of aesthetic chills and their prosthetic augmentation
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Schoeller; Leonardo Christov-Moore; Ninette Simonian; NA; Yaya Shi; Abhinandan Jain; Adam Horowitz; Velu Prabhakar Kumaravel; Ben Zhang; Micah Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract: Aesthetic chills, psychogenic shivers elicited by emotionally charged stimuli such as music, offer a neurophysiological marker bridging subjective experience and measurable physiology. Although neuroimaging has localized chills to reward and interoceptive circuits and behavioral work has linked them to prosocial outcomes, their electrophysiological signature and its relationship to psychological change remain poorly characterized, precluding comparison with phenomenologically similar states induced by other means (e.g., psychedelics). Here we recorded 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG; n = 103) during validated chill-inducing music and examined spectral and complexity-based signatures of chills, their relationships to self-transcendence, psychological insight, emotional breakthrough, and prosocial behavior, and whether augmenting peripheral chill sensations with a custom thermal prosthesis modulates neural activity, phenomenology, and behavior. Chills carried a spatially distributed signature of attenuated theta power, elevated gamma power, and convergent increases across four independent complexity measures. Chills predicted self-transcendent phenomenology in a graded fashion across binary, frequency, and intensity operationalizations, yet predicted neither prosocial behavior nor schema change; both were instead predicted by the chills-locked neural signature, with distinct complexity measures tracking distinct outcome families. Thermal augmentation left the behavioral incidence of chills unchanged; in exploratory mediation models, however, it shifted chills-specific dynamics toward criticality and away from undifferentiated entropy, linking embodied augmentation to phenomenological, affective, prosocial, and schema outcomes. Aesthetic chills may therefore constitute an at least partially neuro-mimetic analogue of the psychedelic state, sharing its elevated signal diversity and a theta attenuation concordant with recent psilocybin electrophysiology, while gamma correspondence and the absence of psychedelic-typical alpha suppression remain unresolved.

articles_hidden.title: Unsupervised Careless Responding Detection: A Comprehensive Comparison between Model-based and Model-Agnostic Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Wenshuo Li; Carl F. Falk
articles_hidden.abstract: Careless responding (CR) is a major concern for data quality in the social sciences. It is common for researchers to attempt to detect and filter out CR at the respondent level. Though various choices are available, detection methods relying solely on response data have received much attention since they do not require the collection of additional information. Along these lines, model-based approaches to CR detection rely on specifying distinct measurement models for careful and careless respondents in a mixture model. In contrast, model-agnostic methods aim to identify thresholds of careless respondent indices, making classifications without reliance on measurement models. Although these two streams share some common assumptions for CR, these methods have been developed in parallel and have not been directly compared. To systematically compare these two streams of approaches, we conducted three large-scale simulation studies manipulating the number of items, proportion of reverse-coded items, contamination rates, carelessness types, presence of model misspecification, item properties, as well as sample sizes. To balance generalizability and realism, conditions for the first two simulations were inspired by real instruments from personality and health outcome measures, while the third simulation study explicitly manipulated item properties to de-confound naturally occurring variability induced under the first two studies. Generally, results indicate that model-based approaches are more specificity-focused and should be preferred under lower contamination rates and fewer items, while model-agnostic approaches are sensitivity-focused and outperform model-based approaches under other contamination rates and more CR types provided there are a sufficient number of items.

articles_hidden.title: Using reinforcement learning to explain psychodynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Zack Dulberg; Jonathan D. Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract: In this article we consider the use of reinforcement learning (RL) as a formal framework for understanding traditional psychodynamic phenomena. We show how RL can be used to provide new insights as well as normative explanations for key psychodynamic constructs, grounding them in principles of reward maximization and adaptation. We illustrate this by reviewing two recent studies in which simulations of adaptive agents offer new explanations for psychodynamic processes, discuss how RL could account for both similarities as well as individual differences in human psychological profiles, and outline possible future directions for this approach. We conclude that, by providing a computational foundation for psychodynamic concepts, RL may contribute to the development of a more rigorous science of psychological dynamics and their disruption in clinical conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Sincronicidad Facial y Contacto Visual en Telemedicina  mediante Visión por Computadora
articles_hidden.authors: Rodrigo Miguel Bermúdez Alemón; Daniela Carolina Rosero Córdoba; ivan arango; Lidia Márquez Márquez; Santiago Castiello
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introducción y Objetivo: La transición hacia la telepsiquiatría—una instancia de la telemedicina—ha generado interrogantes sobre cómo la mediación digital afecta la Comunicación No Verbal (CNV) y la consolidación de la relación médico-paciente. Este estudio tuvo como objetivo principal evaluar el impacto de la sincronía facial y el contacto visual mediado por computadora sobre la alianza terapéutica y la percepción de la calidad asistencial en pacientes adultos con trastornos de la personalidad.
Métodos: Se llevó a cabo un estudio observacional, descriptivo y transversal. La muestra consistió en 25 videograbaciones de teleconsultas psiquiátricas subsecuentes (N=25; n[fotogramas]>1,000,000) realizadas a través de la plataforma Zoom en el Instituto Nacional de Psiquiatría Ramón de la Fuente Muñiz (INPRFM). La alianza terapéutica se evaluó cuantitativamente empleando el Working Alliance Inventory en sus versiones para paciente (WAI-P) y clínico (WAI-T). Para el procesamiento biométrico, se utilizaron scripts personalizados y un software de visión por computadora. Este modelo extrajo series temporales de activación de Unidades de Acción (AU) faciales y vectores algorítmicos en grados de la dirección de la mirada, permitiendo modelar la Sincronía Facial Global y el contacto visual recíproco.
Resultados: No se encontraron correlaciones estadísticamente significativas entre la Sincronía Facial Global o el contacto visual y la alianza terapéutica (WAI-P y WAI-T). De forma homóloga, se observó una ausencia de correlación entre los reportes de alianza relacional del clínico y del paciente. Sin embargo, un análisis intrasesión detectó un aumento en la Sincronía Facial General al final de la teleconsulta. 
Conclusiones: Este estudio es la prueba de concepto para el uso de visión por computadora para analizar CNV en telemedicina. En sesiones de telepsiquiatría, la Sincronía Facial General y el contacto visual no se correlacionan con la alianza terapéutica en pacientes con trastornos de la personalidad. Investigaciones futuras deben considerar la dinámica temporal de la interacción durante la telemedicina. Aquí describimos el método para que unidades de telemdicina puedan llevar a cabo análisis de CNV mediante visión por computadora.

articles_hidden.title: Initial Development of the Hypomanic Tendency Scales (HTS): A Multidimensional Measure of Personality Dimensions Associated with Hypomania
articles_hidden.authors: Kasey Stanton; Jack D Burke; Helena Towne; Isabella Whitesides; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Noah N. Emery; Corinne Carlton
articles_hidden.abstract: A range of tools have been developed for assessing hypomania/mania risk and/or personality and temperament styles related to hypomania. These measures have utility in many ways, but they generally focus on yielding composite scores without providing multidimensional assessment of personality tendencies related to hypomania. A focus on broader composites potentially obscures assessment of heterogeneous aspects of personality that may show unique associations with hypomania history and other clinical variables, and we address this gap by conducting the initial development and validation of the Hypomanic Tendency Scales (HTS). We present data supporting the HTS’s utility as an efficient, 18-item measure including subscales of Elation, Agitation, Expansive Thinking, and Positive Urgency. Our measure development efforts include evaluation of internal structure, test-retest reliability, and multimethod validity associations across four samples and three studies, and we also discuss ways for enhancing assessment with the HTS in follow-up validation research.

articles_hidden.title: Genetic syndromes
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline G. Richter; Kaylie Burns; Phuong Ta; Wanqin Yu
articles_hidden.abstract:
•	Genetic syndromes are dynamic developmental conditions rather than fixed gene-to-behavior outcomes; genetic alterations set initial constraints that interact with health, learning, family, and educational contexts to shape probabilistic developmental trajectories.
•	Turner, Klinefelter, and Marfan syndromes show that a genetic diagnosis does not imply intellectual disability: selective cognitive, academic, or medical vulnerabilities can occur alongside broadly preserved general intellectual functioning.
•	Down syndrome and Williams syndrome are compared across etiology, medical comorbidities, motor skills, language, literacy, mathematics, executive functioning, sleep, social behavior, and adaptive functioning, revealing contrasting profiles.
•	Information-processing, neuroconstructivist, and dynamic-systems accounts, including cumulative risk-and-resilience and family-systems models, explain how syndrome-related profiles emerge through developmental cascades rather than being directly specified by genetic etiology.
•	Assessment and intervention should extend beyond IQ to component processes, longitudinal change, self-report from the individual, probabilistic prognosis, and modifiable environments and instruction, such as systematic phonics for reading.

articles_hidden.title: Achievement motives and anxiety are associated with persistence for delayed rewards
articles_hidden.authors: Avital Miller; Karolina Maria Lempert
articles_hidden.abstract: People vary in how long they are willing to persist for delayed rewards when the timing of those rewards is uncertain. Decisions about when to give up on delayed rewards result from a dynamic decision-making process in which people weigh the benefits of continued waiting against the opportunity costs of waiting. We hypothesized that individual differences in persistence might therefore emerge from differences in motivation, with approach motives (i.e., hope for success) predicting increased persistence and avoidance motives (i.e., fear of failure) predicting reduced persistence. In an online study, participants (n = 284) completed self-report questionnaires and a decision-making task optimized to capture individual differences in persistence. Hope for Success and Fear of Failure were assessed with the Achievement Motives Scale. Hope for Success was significantly positively associated with persistence, a relationship that was robust to controlling for relevant demographic covariates. Fear of Failure was negatively associated with persistence, but this association was only marginally significant after controlling for covariates. Reduced persistence predicted alcohol use intensity, replicating previous research. Finally, exploratory analyses demonstrated a significant association between anxious-depression and reduced persistence. Together, these findings suggest that persistence is linked to individual differences in motivational orientation and related psychological characteristics.

articles_hidden.title: Reduced theta-gamma coupling during real-world episodic encoding
articles_hidden.authors: Alireza Taheritorbati; Jane O'Connor; Tel Silito; Keva Klamer; Shaylyn Kress; Niayesh Allahdad; Jordyn Alicia Musial; Jared Rollingson; joshua Craig; Mary-Lou Gregoire
articles_hidden.abstract: Episodic memories are rarely formed under the controlled, simplified conditions typical of laboratory research. They are built from continuous, embodied experiences unfolding in real time and real space. We examined how theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC), a candidate neural signature of encoding demand, differs when an experience is encountered in a live setting rather than an approximately matched screen-based version. 62 healthy young adults encoded an identical narrative vignette, presented either as a live theatrical performance or as a two-dimensional (2D) video recording, while high-density EEG was recorded. Coupling between frontal theta and parietal gamma activity was computed during encoding as an index of this cross-frequency coordination, and free-recall memory was assessed immediately after. Real-world encoding was associated with significantly lower frontal theta to parietal gamma PAC than 2D encoding, even though recall performance did not differ between conditions. PAC positively predicted recall only in the 2D condition, with no equivalent relationship emerging for Real-world encoding. In the Real-world condition, PAC was negatively correlated with general cognitive ability, suggesting that higher cognitive functioning requires less cross-frequency coordination during naturalistic encoding. Together, these findings position theta-gamma PAC as a compensatory neural mechanism, recruited more heavily when the encoding environment provides less external structure. This suggests that real-world experiences may place a lighter coordination burden on the encoding brain, consistent with a compensatory account of theta-gamma PAC.
