articles_hidden.title: Not All Spiritual Bypass Is the Same: Divergent Network Roles Across Spirituality, Forgiveness, and Psychological Resources
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastian Binyamin Skalski-Bednarz; Jacek Prusak; Paweł Dudzik; Edyta Charzyńska; Jon R. Webb
articles_hidden.abstract: Spiritual bypass, the use of spiritual beliefs and practices to sidestep unresolved psychological difficulty, comprises two dimensions, psychological avoidance and spiritualizing, which may relate differently to psychospiritual constructs. This chapter used a network approach to examine how these two dimensions, alongside three dimensions of spirituality (ritualistic, theistic, existential), three dimensions of dispositional forgiveness (self, others, uncontrollable situations) plus feeling forgiven by God, and three additional positive resources (hope, gratitude, self-compassion), are organized as a set of direct, facet-level associations rather than as broader, undifferentiated domains. A regularized partial correlation network was estimated in a sample of 1,750 individuals from a US college community, with node centrality and bridge centrality used to identify the most embedded facets and those bridging distinct construct clusters. Psychological avoidance was closely aligned with ritualistic spirituality, whereas spiritualizing occupied a highly central but predominantly negative position in relation to spirituality and positive psychological resources, a pattern supported by bootstrapped difference testing. Positive resources occupied a comparatively peripheral position, though feeling forgiven by God and self-compassion emerged as strong connectors across spirituality, forgiveness, resources, and spiritual bypass. These findings suggest that spiritual bypass is not a homogeneous construct and that its associations vary across dimensions of spirituality and other positive psychological constructs.

articles_hidden.title: Measurement factors influencing caregiver involvement in child health studies: A mixed-methods study
articles_hidden.authors: Moira Duffy; Laoise Kelly; Eibhlín Looney; Dimity Dutch; Brittany J Johnson; Lucy Porter; Sarah Redsell; Karen Matvienko-Sikar
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. How outcomes are measured in studies can influence recruitment, retention, and data quality. This study examined characteristics of outcome measurement instruments influencing caregivers’ data provision in child health studies. 

Methods. An online mixed-methods cross-sectional survey including 22 closed-ended and one open-ended question(s) about outcome measurement instrument related factors influencing data provision in child health studies. Quantitative data were descriptively analyzed; qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis. 

Results. The survey was conducted with 490 caregivers of a child ≤12 years. The most important characteristics influencing caregivers’ provision of data were potential risk or discomfort to their child, ease of data provision, and perception of potential benefit to others. Caregivers ranked online data provision as their highest preference (M 1.23, SD 0.53; lower score indicates higher preference). Caregivers’ highest preferences were for healthcare professional data collection (M 2.50, SD 1.29), providing data in their own time (M 1.68, SD 1.27), and in their own homes (M 1.38, SD 0.88). Qualitative data indicated that trust, time and ease, perceived research value, and child comfort and safety were important to caregivers.   

Conclusions. Enhancing child comfort/safety, caregiver understanding/trust, and ease of data collection in child health studies is vital to maximize data provision and quality. Doing so, can improve evaluation of treatments and interventions, and improve child health outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Brain and Muscular Signatures of Local and Global Temporal Dynamics in Facial Expressions
articles_hidden.authors: Rafal Marcin Skiba; Patrik Vuilleumier
articles_hidden.abstract: Natural facial expressions are inherently dynamic events governed by precise temporal coordination between facial features, yet the neurobiological mechanisms integrating kinematic timing, facial mimicry, and emotional evaluation remain poorly understood. Here, we combined event-related fMRI with simultaneous continuous facial electromyography (EMG; corrugator supercilii and zygomaticus major) and behavioral psychophysics in 27 healthy adult participants to examine how temporal global synchrony versus analytic asynchrony (8% and 18% onset lags between upper and lower facial features) across two dynamic speeds (1.5 and 3 sec.) shapes emotional processing. Naturally unfolding synchronous expressions distinctively engaged bilateral primary motor cortices, supplementary motor area (SMA), and primary somatosensory cortex. In contrast, kinematically disrupted expressions preferentially recruited the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), fusiform gyrus, and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG). Parametric modulation analyses revealed a clear dissociation between somatic and cognitive tracking: trial-by-trial facial muscle mimicry engaged a distributed sensorimotor simulation network that severely fractured or collapsed during asynchronous kinematics. Conversely, subjective intensity evaluations of unnatural asynchronous expressions triggered an extensive recruitment of the bilateral amygdala and the entire longitudinal axis of the right STS, pointing to heightened computational demands for resolving perceptual ambiguity and social conflict. These findings demonstrate that natural temporal synchrony is a prerequisite for automatic motor-affective embodiment, whereas kinematic temporal disruptions shift processing toward lateral social-perceptual networks to analytically resolve fragmented communicative signals.

articles_hidden.title: Social prioritization of others can be explained by representational  closeness to the self
articles_hidden.authors: Meike Scheller; Georgios Velimachitis; Gabrielle Foster; Greesha Yadav
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual cognition is shaped not only by sensory input, but also by social relevance. While self-related information is processed preferentially, similar advantages extend to close others. How prioritization rapidly extends to others, however, remains unclear. We propose a framework of ‘representational closeness’, whereby individuals cognitively represented closer to the self, benefit from more efficient processing. Devising three markers – closeness, boundary imprecision, overlap – in a reanalysis of Scheller & Sui (2022, n = 43) and a new experiment (n = 78), we show that this framework explains processing benefits across two domains: friends over strangers, and more over less attractive strangers. Faster and more accurate responses, reduced response variability, and increased self-other confusion tracked representational closeness. These findings suggest that prioritization reflects a general organising principle of social perception through which cognitive resources are dynamically allocated according to social relevance, linking visual processing to the structure of social representation.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the control bottleneck: cognitive control reconfigures its neural and computational architecture to meet task demands
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo; Francisco Barcelo; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive control enables flexible adaptation of behavior, but it has associated costs: task rules must be held in memory and updated when they change. It remains unclear whether these costs arise from a unitary control bottleneck or from the interaction of multiple computational processes, and how such processes are implemented in the brain. Here we recast rule maintenance and switching within a computational model based on probabilistic (active) inference, which we apply to trial-by-trial behavioral and EEG data from a cued task-switching paradigm. Behavior showed a speed–accuracy dissociation, with slower responses during rule repetition and reduced accuracy during rule switching. We identified three separable model parameters as necessary to explain behavior: context stability, cue sensitivity and action precision. These parameters were dynamically reweighted across task contexts, with context stability predominating during rule maintenance and cue sensitivity during rule updating. They also influenced behavior through dissociable routes: higher action precision selectively improved accuracy without slowing responses. Using hierarchical Parametric Empirical Bayes with out-of-sample cross-validation, we related these latent parameters to electrophysiological signals, revealing both context-invariant and context-specific mappings: parietal P3b latency tracked cue sensitivity across conditions, whereas frontal beta latency and the frontal P3a indexed context stability in a context-dependent way. The neural implementation of context stability reorganized with task demands, shifting from frontal beta during switching to frontal theta during maintenance. Together, these findings move beyond the bottleneck view, suggesting that cognitive control is best understood as an adaptive computational architecture that integrates endogenous and exogenous information while reconfiguring its neural implementation according to task demands.

articles_hidden.title: The Social Prioritisation Gradient: Gender, Age and Personality Shape the Relative Salience of Self, Friends, and Strangers
articles_hidden.authors: Meike Scheller; Naomi Lee; Jie Sui
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do people differ in how they prioritise social information? Enhanced processing of self-relevant information is among the most reliable effects in social cognition, but individuals vary considerably in how strongly different social identities are prioritised. The present study asked where along the self–friend–stranger gradient individual differences emerge. We combined data from eight experiments using the shape-label matching task with Big Five personality questionnaire measures. At the group-level, participants showed a robust gradient of social prioritisation, with self-associated information processed most efficiently, followed by friend- and stranger-associated information. Despite this consistency, substantial inter-individual variation was evident, reflected in the malleability of processing of others rather of the self: Gender, Openness, and Extraversion emerged as the most robust predictors of social identity processing performance: gender and Extraversion were particularly associated with friend-related processing, and Openness with the separation of strangers from socially closer identities. Age moderated several personality-related effects across the social gradient, though less consistently and in a young-skewed sample. Together, the findings suggest that individual differences in social prioritisation appear to arise less from how strongly the self is prioritised than from how socially close and distant others are weighted around it.

articles_hidden.title: The Benefits of and Motivations Behind Large-Team Coordination in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Sajedeh Rasti; Krist Vaesen; Daniel Lakens
articles_hidden.abstract: To increase coordination in science in areas where this would be beneficial for knowledge generation, collaborative work needs to offer clear benefits to individual researchers. This study investigates the motivations for initiating large-team papers and the potential benefits of these projects in psychology. By qualitatively analyzing 500 papers, we find that large-team collaborations are most often instigated to deal with the practical challenges  inherent to complex research questions, but can also be motivated by broader social and or strategic factors. The results from quantitatively analyzing 1,699,513 papers published between 1975 and 2024 indicate that large-team collaborations are more likely to be cited and to appear in higher-ranked journals. Furthermore, their immediate impact on the field, as measured by citation counts within the first 2 years after publication, is on average higher than individually-authored papers. This suggests that contributing to collaborative projects in psychology will likely increase the number of high-rank journal publications to the resume of researchers. Overall, our findings indicate that large-team collaborations can be rewarding for individual researchers both by enabling early scientific impact and by contributing to stronger publication records.

articles_hidden.title: Mood stability and change map onto distinct insula-centered networks
articles_hidden.authors: Noa Danan; Michal Ramot; Hanna Keren
articles_hidden.abstract: Mood is changing continuously even when external events are minimal. These spontaneous mood dynamics may reveal how the brain maintains and modifies affective states. Yet mood is typically studied in response to external input, leaving the neural basis of spontaneous mood changes largely unknown. Here, we combined repeated mood sampling with functional neural connectivity across two resting-state fMRI sessions separated by several weeks to identify the neural systems associated with different spontaneous mood dynamics. Our most robust finding was that stronger insula-striatal connectivity was associated with greater mood stability. Additional analyses revealed that stronger connectivity within an insula-cingulo-frontal network was associated with greater spontaneous mood decline, while reduced insula-frontal connectivity was associated with higher depressive symptoms. Together, these findings suggest that distinct insula-centered functional networks are differentially associated with affective stability and affective updating and change, providing a neural framework for spontaneous mood dynamics and their relation to depressive symptoms.

articles_hidden.title: The more, the better? Behavioral and neural correlates of frequent and infrequent vowel exposure
articles_hidden.authors: Sho Tsuji; Paula Fikkert; Yasuyo MINAGAWA; Emmanuel Dupoux; Lucas Filippin; Maarten Versteegh; Peter Hagoort; Alejandrina Cristia; Alex Eguiluz
articles_hidden.abstract:
A central assumption in the perceptual attunement literature holds that exposure to a speech sound contrast leads to improvement in native speech sound processing. However, whether the amount of exposure matters for this process has not been put to a direct test. We elucidated indicators of frequency-dependent perceptual attunement by comparing 5-8-month-old Dutch infants’ discrimination of tokens containing a highly frequent [hɪt-he:t] and a highly infrequent [hʏt-hø:t] native vowel contrast as well as a non-native [hɛt-hæt] vowel contrast in a behavioral visual habituation paradigm (Experiment 1). Infants discriminated both native contrasts similarly well, but did not discriminate the non-native
contrast. We sought further evidence for subtle differences in the processing of the two native contrasts using near-infrared spectroscopy and a within-participant design (Experiment 2). The neuroimaging data did not provide additional evidence that responses to native contrasts are modulated by frequency of exposure. These results suggest that even large differences in exposure to a native contrast may not directly translate to behavioral and neural indicators of perceptual attunement, raising the possibility that frequency of exposure does not influence improvements in discriminating native contrasts.

articles_hidden.title: The mental health of trans and gender-diverse populations: an umbrella review of systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: M.O.S.A. Elsawy; Zhuoli Zheng; Baudewijntje Kreukels; Anke Boukje Witteveen; Pim Cuijpers; Sara Fatima; Ralph de Vries; Marit Sijbrandij
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background Trans and gender-diverse (TGD) populations face significant mental health challenges. This umbrella review aimed to assess the prevalence of mental disorders, suicidal behaviors, and substance use among adult TGD populations by synthesizing findings from existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
Methods A systematic review of reviews and meta-analyses was conducted by searching bibliographic databases PubMed, Embase.com, APA PsycInfo (Ebsco), CINAHL (Ebsco), Web of Science (Core Collection), Scopus, and Cochrane Library (Wiley) from inception to December 18, 2025, and LILACS from inception to May 26, 2026. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses (SRs/MAs) of cross-sectional or longitudinal designs were included if they reported prevalence data on mental health disorders, substance use, or suicidal behaviors in adult TGD populations. Two independent reviewers conducted the study selection, quality assessment (using AMSTAR-2), and data extraction.
Results Twelve SRs met the inclusion criteria. Only two systematic reviews used structured clinical interviews, while the rest relied on a mix of diagnostic interviews and self-report measures. The review found elevated prevalence of mood and anxiety disorders, suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts among TGD populations compared to the general population. Substance use, including tobacco and illicit drug use, was prevalent. Quality assessments of included studies ranged from 2.5 to 7.0 on AMSTAR-2, with a mean score of 4.8, indicating variable quality.
Conclusion This umbrella review highlights the mental health burden in TGD populations, including high prevalence of mood and anxiety disorders, suicidal behaviors, and substance use. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously due to variability in study quality, assessment methods, and lack of comparison groups. The review underscores the need for inclusive, gender-responsive care and further high-quality research to better address TGD mental health needs.

articles_hidden.title: If you try hard but still fail to help, regulating others’ emotions will take an emotional toll
articles_hidden.authors: Zachariah Yung Weeks; Hester Xiao; Carolyn MacCann
articles_hidden.abstract: Existing evidence conflicts as to whether trying to regulate another person’s emotions is depleting (makes the regulator feel worse) or replenishing (makes the regulator feel better). Research suggests that different mechanisms produce different effects for the regulator: greater regulatory effort predicts higher negative affect, whereas greater perceived efficacy predicts lower negative affect. However, research has not yet tested how effort and efficacy combine to influence regulator outcomes. The current studies test whether the regulator’s positive and negative affect are predicted by: 1) their regulatory effort, 2) their perceived regulation efficacy, and 3) the effort-by-efficacy interaction. Study 1 (N = 119) used experience sampling (5 days, 30 occasions), and Study 2 (N = 120) used twice-daily reports over 10 work days. Multi-level models clustered occasions within persons. Across both studies: 1) effort predicted greater negative affect at both within- and between-person levels; 2) efficacy predicted less negative affect at both within- and between-person levels and greater positive affect at the within-person level; and 3) there was a significant effort-by-efficacy interaction on negative affect at the between-person level only (effort predicted greater negative affect more strongly at lower perceived efficacy). Results demonstrate that the costs of regulating others’ emotions are due to effort and the benefits are due to perceived efficacy which has practical implications for contexts that require sustained regulation of others (such as family carers and healthcare roles). Future research should use experimental designs to investigate causality.

articles_hidden.title: Remaking “The Unconscious” Paradigm, Act I: …The Gap” Between Subliminal Processing and the Unconscious “Mind…
articles_hidden.authors: Myron Tsikandilakis; Persefoni Bali; Roland Erich Uriko; Mohammad Eskandari; Victoria-Maria Pasachidou; Romina Toranzos; Konrad Szczesniak; Ivona Dömischová; Pierre-Alexis Mével; Christopher R Madan
articles_hidden.abstract: The notion of subliminal processing often refers to perception that takes place below the threshold of conscious visual awareness. This is suggested to lead to behavioural and emotional changes with spontaneous and actionable evolutionary-survival and/or social-adaptation response value. Therefore, it has been suggested that the presentation of imperceptible visual elicitors can lead to responses, such as skin-conductance and heart-rate, and facial-emotional, and participant behavioural and self-report changes without conscious awareness. In a series of experiments, we disproved this theory. We showed that individually-adjusted, truly imperceptible elicitors did not induce any of these changes, when using null-hypothesis-testing, and, furthermore, provided evidence for null responses, when using Bayesian analyses. We proceeded to a series of novel and exploratory experiments on unconscious theory. We tested whether behavioural and emotional responses were reported to precede conscious awareness using overt presentations of visual-emotional elicitors. We showed evidence that the experience of physiological-emotional responses was reported to precede conscious awareness of a perceived visual-emotional content. These early responses were automatic and involuntary; they did not involve or require conscious access, or accessibility, and deliberation, and could not be physiologically restrained by conscious instruction for inhibition. We proposed that responses that can be termed unconscious, but not subliminal, are preceding, spontaneous and conditionally uninhibited experiential components of exposure to perceived, but not imperceptible, emotional elicitors. We extended that they involve genuine evolutionary-survival and social-adaptation value, compared to so-called subliminal processes, because they enable spontaneously-occurring, and progressively-intentional and intended behavioural and emotional adjustments, and readjustments, and adapting refinements.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity trajectories using random forest classification in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
articles_hidden.authors: Özde Sönmez; Hyun Ruisch; Jan Buitelaar; Christiane Thiel; Andrea Hildebrandt; Andrea Dietrich; Pieter Hoekstra
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Despite well-established genetic and environmental risk factors for attention deficit–hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), it remains unclear why children show different developmental trajectories from mild to severe levels. This study aimed to investigate distinct developmental trajectories of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores and identify predictors of these trajectories from childhood to adolescence in a community-based sample.
Methods: Data were drawn from the longitudinal Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development dataset (n = 11,875) with yearly measures from baseline to wave 3 (ages 9-10 to 12-13). Growth mixture models were applied to the inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity items of the ADHD subscale of the Child Behavior Checklist to identify trajectories. Random forest classification models were then trained to predict these trajectories using familial, demographic, behavioral and genetic variables, previously linked to ADHD. Logistic regression analyses were conducted to determine the direction of associations.
Results: Three trajectories were identified for inattention (non-affected, moderate, and persistent-high), and four for hyperactivity-impulsivity (non-affected, worsening, improving, and persistent-high). Key predictors for both domains included male sex and higher externalizing problems, family conflict, and polygenic risk scores of ADHD, distinguishing affected from non-affected children. Additional distinguishing factors were less secondary caregiver acceptance (inattention) and lower family income (hyperactivity-impulsivity). Further, a persistent-high inattention trajectory was associated with negative school experiences and more internalizing problems, while worsening and persistent-high hyperactivity-impulsivity trajectories were linked to slower pubertal development.
Conclusion: This study supports the distinction between inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity trajectories, which may be shaped by domain-specific factors. Nevertheless, at its core, both ADHD domains appear to be associated with shared factors, including biological and environmental, in the distinction between non-affected youth and those with ADHD symptomatology.

articles_hidden.title: Potential Agency in the Absence of Actual Motor Control? Ownership-dependent Judgments in the Rubber Hand Illusion
articles_hidden.authors: Hélène Vanborren; Fleur Touzard; Matthew Longo; Loïc Paul Heurley; Brouillet Thibaut
articles_hidden.abstract: We define potential agency as the explicit judgment that one could have made an artificial hand move had one intended to do so. We asked whether participants would report potential agency for an artificial hand they had no means of controlling, and how such reports varied with body ownership. In a within-subject static rubber hand illusion (RHI) paradigm, 104 participants received synchronous and asynchronous visuo-tactile stimulation while their real hand remained hidden; neither the real nor the artificial hand moved, and no sensory consequences of voluntary action were available. After each induction, participants rated ownership of the artificial hand and potential agency towards it; proprioceptive drift was also measured. Synchronous stimulation produced the expected RHI pattern, with higher ownership and greater proprioceptive drift than asynchronous stimulation. Potential agency ratings were also higher following synchronous stimulation. Across conditions, ownership was positively associated with potential agency, but this association was stronger under synchronous stimulation. In the synchronous condition, ownership accounted for 56% of the variance in potential agency. Critically, on the −3 to +3 scales, the model-estimated probability of positive endorsement (mean potential agency rating ≥ +1) increased from 10% at ownership 0 to 88% at +3. Reanalysis of a comparable static RHI dataset showed a convergent ownership-dependent pattern. These findings extend the study of the ownership–agency relationship beyond executed actions and their sensory consequences: even in the absence of actual motor control, experienced ownership was closely related to whether the artificial hand was judged to be available for voluntary movement.

articles_hidden.title: Dense-Sampling the Menstrual Cycle Using EEG in a Single Case Study: Relating Markers of Cognitive Control and Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Nijboer; Federica Lucchi; Erik J. Giltay; Peter Putman; Ellen de Bruijn
articles_hidden.abstract: Introduction. Women may show menstrual cycle-related susceptibility to depressive and anxiety symptoms during estradiol (E2) and progesterone (P4) fluctuations. Electrophysiological (EEG) markers, including the error-related negativity (ERN) and resting-state theta/beta ratio (TBR) index cognitive control processes and are emerging biomarkers of adverse mental health outcomes. Methods. Using a proof-of-principle, hypothesis-generating approach, we intensively tracked one healthy, naturally cycling woman in her late twenties for 30 days. We collected daily salivary E2 and P4, mental health data, and EEG. We provide a descriptive case study to showcase a dense-sampling and dynamic time warping (DTW) combination. Results. EEG markers varied considerably across the menstrual cycle. The ERN was larger around ovulation, coinciding with an E2 peak. Around midluteal phase the ERN was smaller, coinciding with a P4 peak. TBR varied most during the early-follicular phase. The DTW networks suggested the ERN was related to TBR, that TBR was related to positive and negative affect, and to response bias on a Go/No-Go task.  Discussion. Our descriptive, hypothesis-generating results suggest that cognitive control markers can vary across a menstrual cycle, and that they can be important targets for further study regarding women’s mental health and precision medicine. Cognitive control markers exhibited considerable daily variability, underscoring the importance of accounting for such fluctuations in research.

articles_hidden.title: From social input to social attention: Parental mood predictability is related to the development of gaze cueing
articles_hidden.authors: Dimana V. Atanassova; Marlene Meyer; Sabine Hunnius
articles_hidden.abstract:
Gaze following is a fundamental developmental milestone for social cognition. Adults’ attention is reliably cued by gaze shifts but less is known about how gaze cuing emerges in early childhood or what shapes its developmental trajectory. Reduced sensitivity to social input—such as gazes—and differences in the early social environment can affect the development of gaze cueing but the role of these factors remains untested.
We explored the developmental trajectory of the gaze cueing effect (GCE) and the factors shaping it in a large longitudinal sample from the YOUth cohort (N=1928; 5 months, 10 months, 3 years, 6 years). Using static facial stimuli, we found no conclusive evidence of gaze cueing in the first year of life. By 3 years, an early form of the GCE was detectable, with children making more errors on gaze-incongruent trials. By 6 years, the effect was robustly established, yet remained sensitive to characteristics of children’s early social environment.

Contrary to our expectations, reduced social sensitivity indexed by higher callous-unemotional traits did not attenuate the GCE at any age; instead, at 3 years, it was associated with faster overall target detection. Parental mood unpredictability, indexing exposure to an inconsistent social environment, was associated with attenuated gaze cueing at 6 years. In contrast, greater parental mood negativity was associated with slower disengagement from gaze-incongruent targets.

Together, these findings map the developmental trajectory of gaze cueing across early childhood and highlight the role of the parental characteristics as a key factor in shaping early social-cognitive development.

articles_hidden.title: The influence of audience presence in expert classical piano performance: Reliable reproduction with greater expressive variability
articles_hidden.authors: Emily A. Wood; Rory Kirk; Cameron J Anderson; Martin Alejandro Miguel; Laurel Trainor
articles_hidden.abstract: How the presence of an audience shapes skilled performance has been studied for over a century, largely through laboratory tasks testing whether being watched improves or impairs. Music offers a richer test case: a demanding skill performed for others in which how the performance changes can be measured, not only whether it improved. We compared an expert pianist’s performance of the same six-piece programme alone in a private rehearsal and a public concert, measuring her motion, beat-level timing, sound intensity, and pedalling. The two performances were remarkably similar, with the pianist reproducing her expressive interpretation with high fidelity across every feature. Further, the passages she had marked as most expressive in the score were no more affected by the audience than the rest. Despite this overall consistency, audience presence introduced small but reliable changes: greater variability in her motion, timing, and soft pedal use, and at the least intense moments in the music (as rated by listeners) she drew out the tempo and shaped the quietest passages more with the soft pedal in concert. For this performer, an audience did not impair her performance but facilitated it, supporting a faithful execution of her prepared interpretation while increasing expression through enhanced variability.

articles_hidden.title: Randomized Trial of AI-Powered Mental Health Support  Embedded in University Academic Infrastructure
articles_hidden.authors: Julie Youko Anne Cachia; Xuan Zhao; Wenxi Pu; Chi Liao; merel Keijsers; Julian De Freitas; Peter Cornish; Rebecca Fortgang
articles_hidden.abstract: Realizing digital mental health’s promise in low-resourced settings requires a tool that works in real-world systems and that people engage with. We report a preregistered 6-week randomized controlled trial (N = 1,137) of Flourish, a scalable AI-powered mental health intervention, at a university in the Canadian province with the lowest psychologist supply. The intervention was introduced through academic infrastructure rather than offered as an opt-in wellness service. Participants were randomized to app access or care as usual. Flourish protected against declines in positive affect, resilience, and flourishing over the academic semester, and accelerated reductions in loneliness, extending prior evidence to a resource-constrained context and informing the emerging literature on whether purpose-built AI can improve well-being. Engagement was high: 95% activated the app within 2 weeks, and average use was 3.2 days per week. Embedding AI-powered well-being tools in institutional infrastructure may extend support where clinical capacity falls short of need.

articles.title: Defining Nature for Policy and Practice
articles.authors: Patricia Soranno; Stephen Posner; Courtney DeLoatch-Hill; Emerson Conrad-Rooney; Katie Arkema; Meena M. Balgopal; Gillian Bowser; Monika M. Derrien; Kevin C. Elliott; Tessa Francis
articles.abstract: What counts as "nature" is increasingly central to public policies, investment decisions, and scientific assessments, yet the term is often left undefined or implicit. Because nature is a complex, value-laden concept, a universal definition is unlikely to serve all uses, creating problems for comparability and auditability of claims. When users document what counts as nature and disclose the basis for their claims, measurement becomes more comparable, and accountability improves. We present a framework that pairs a concise definition with its purpose, context, and boundary rules, and apply it to develop a definition of nature that can reveal how benefits, harms, and stewardship responsibilities are distributed across people and places. Definitions should be treated as public commitments: articulating both a definition and a replicable process for revision makes governance more transparent, auditable, and open to legitimate contest.

articles.title: Learning to Speak Green: The Production of Green Conformity in European Cultural Policy
articles.authors: Vânia Rodrigues; Catarina Santos-Silva; Olga Solovova
articles.abstract:
Ecological vocabulary is nearly absent until 2021, when greening became a cross-cutting programme priority, and rises abruptly thereafter. Green, climate and sustainable increasingly appear together as an interchangeable signal of commitment. Sustainable also retains its earlier organisational meaning, binding ecological claims to claims of institutional survival. Modernisation dominates the coded projects, framing sustainability as innovation, capacity-building and better practice. Transformative elements persist only as traces, and the vocabularies of degrowth, commoning and ecological justice are absent or residual across the whole corpus. The programme's explicit greening guidance appears to supply the very terms in which compliance is demonstrated.
The article argues that this narrowing is anticipatory and sincere, which makes it harder to contest than greenwashing. It contributes to debates on travelling cultural policy and multilateral cultural governance by showing how a transnational green idiom, composed largely in English, carries a sustainability paradigm across Europe while constraining the ecological futures cultural institutions can meaningfully articulate.

articles.title: Uncovering the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth:  an interdisciplinary review and research agenda
articles.authors: Franziska Cooiman; Julia de Groote; Isabell Stamm; Jan Ole Krieg
articles.abstract: Given the centrality of entrepreneurial activity to the accumulation, reproduction, and legitimization of wealth – and conversely, of wealth in the form of capital to foster entrepreneurship – it might be reasonable to expect a plethora of research on the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth. However, as we demonstrate in our interdisciplinary literature review, a surprising lack of engagement exists with regard to this relationship. Sociological studies of wealth inequality rarely address entrepreneurship, and entrepreneurship research rarely addresses wealth. We systematically review, discuss, and synthesize the discourse in the leading journals of both fields. In the sociological discourse on wealth, we find that entrepreneurship is seen as one of many sources of income and wealth, and as a means of legitimizing its accumulation. However, the social practices, actors, and institutions that mediate the concentration of wealth through entrepreneurship, as well as the structural power of wealth in entrepreneurial activity, are rarely addressed. Similarly, in entrepreneurship research, we show that considerable attention is paid to the role of family businesses, transgenerational wealth, and non-financial wealth (“socioemotional wealth”), whilst the fundamental role of these factors in fostering wealth concentration more broadly remains largely unremarked upon in the literature. We therefore suggest future research that systematically engages with how entrepreneurial activity shapes wealth accumulation, and how wealth, in turn, structures entrepreneurial opportunities and outcomes. With this review, we contribute to advancing debates on inequality, social mobility, and economic development.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Unbundling Support for Political Violence
articles.authors: Sam Fuller; Jack T. Rametta; Alexa Federice
articles.abstract: Measures of support for political violence (SPV) vary drastically across what violence they describe, who performs it, against whom, and the stated justification. We argue that these measures are not interchangeable operationalizations of a single latent attitude but rather represent correlated, distinct subdimensions of SPV. Across three studies, we iteratively develop and validate concise batteries that 1) differentiate between actor-target combinations and reactive versus proactive violence and 2) vary across justification and the response's severity. We find that SPV is a multidimensional concept: levels of reactive support are remarkably higher than proactive; support for state-on-mass and mass-on-state violence are only weakly correlated, with Republicans supporting state-on-mass and Democrats supporting mass-on-state violence at significantly higher rates; common SPV measures correlate with proactive more than reactive; and we find mixed evidence that survey disengagement influences SPV. Our findings contextualize disparate and conflicting literatures, offering measurement strategies tailored to specific research questions.

articles.title: Homeschooling as Racial Retreat: The Impact of School District and Leadership Diversity
articles.authors: Maranda Joyce
articles.abstract: What explains the decision to homeschool? This study examines whether local racial context influences families’ decisions to homeschool their children. I argue that many white parents exit public school systems due to concerns about the distribution of school resources to racial out-groups, particularly in racially diverse and resource-constrained districts. I conduct a state-representative survey of over 30,000 respondents to describe the homeschooling population in the United States. Then, using data from Virginia that link student and district leadership demographics (school board members and superintendents) to district-level homeschooling rates, I examine how racial composition and leadership diversity shape educational exit. I find that higher levels of non-white students and certain kinds of leadership diversity are positively associated with increased homeschooling, especially where resources are limited. By showing that homeschooling is often motivated by perceived racial threat, this study informs debates about the regulation and public subsidization of homeschooling.

articles.title: Quo Vadis, Digital Accessibility? A Prerequisite for Democratic Equality
articles.authors: Tânia de Jesus Vilela da Rocha; Gonçalo Cruz
articles.abstract: Digital participation channels may widen access to public decision-making, but formal availability does not ensure substantively equal opportunities for political voice. This paper asks how accessibility conditions across a digital consultation journey may shape participation costs and what their potential implications are for political equality and procedural legitimacy. It conceptualizes digital accessibility as democratic infrastructure and integrates technical accessibility, journey analysis, socio-technical evaluation, and democratic interpretation. The analytical strategy distinguishes observed conditions, plausible participation risks, and demonstrated outcomes and traces a chain from observed condition to required resource, participation cost, recovery route, and potential democratic relevance. A bounded exploratory pilot applies the strategy to the publicly accessible, logged-out segment of ConsultaLEX, the Portuguese government portal for legislative and regulatory consultations. The pilot covers discovery, orientation, and authentication and assesses the availability of an entry point to expression and feedback. It identifies enabling conditions in programmatically named controls, structured consultation information, exact dates, and alternative authentication routes. Potentially constraining conditions involve relative deadlines, scripted navigation, registration and identity requirements, and human verification. Because no live commenting process was available, expression and feedback could not be inspected. The study therefore supports mechanism-level inferences rather than claims about participant exclusion or platform-wide conformance. These findings support treating accessibility as a necessary but insufficient condition for equal participation. The paper contributes a proof of concept connecting accessibility evidence to democratic analysis and identifies disability-led participant testing, live-process observation, and cross-platform comparison as priorities for future research.

articles.title: Specific Support, Diffuse Trust: Central Banks and the Mass Politics of Unconventional Monetary Policy
articles.authors: Björn Bremer; Jeffrey Chwieroth
articles.abstract: Central banks relied for a decade on unconventional monetary policies (negative interest rates, large-scale asset purchases, and forward guidance) that carry significant distributive consequences and became intensely politicized. Yet little is known about the mass politics of central banking, or whether contestation over specific instruments threatens central banks' broader legitimacy. We provide evidence from two pre-registered survey experiments in Germany and the Netherlands. A conjoint experiment shows that citizens strongly oppose negative interest rates, the most penalized levels in the design, and are skeptical of unconditional asset purchases. A framing experiment shows support for negative rates responds to both egotropic and sociotropic arguments, with pocketbook concerns resonating most strongly. Exploiting a within-respondent measure of trust in the European Central Bank (ECB), we show that these same frames shift citizens' specific support for the policy without eroding their diffuse trust in the ECB, a highly insulated, technocratic, non-elected institution.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: How Intergenerational Closure Shapes Parental Aspirations in a Highly Differentiated Educational System: Evidence from Germany
articles.authors: Monja Schmitt; Kerstin Schörner; Felix Bittmann
articles.abstract: According to James Coleman's theoretical considerations, intergenerational closure, defined as social ties among the parents of children's peers, is a crucial factor in the formation of educational inequalities. Empirical studies report positive associations between intergenerational closure and academic success, while indicating that these associations cannot be understood in isolation from the social contexts in which closure is embedded. Nothing is known about its impact on parental aspirations that precede the children's educational success. From the perspective of the Wisconsin Model, aspirations are not only precursors of educational attainment but are themselves shaped through social interactions with significant others. Educational systems structure the social contexts in which children and parents form networks and become significant to each other, and the extent to which educational outcomes, including educational aspirations, are shaped by the degree of educational stratification. Germany represents a highly differentiated educational system with secondary school tracks that differ in their student composition and educational opportunities. No study has examined whether parents of classmates function as significant others for parental educational aspirations, nor whether this role varies across school tracks. Using unique data from a National Educational Panel Study (n = 6,162), we examine whether intergenerational closure is associated with parents’ realistic and idealistic aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. Results from linear probability models indicate that intergenerational closure significantly increases realistic aspirations only among parents with children in intermediate educational tracks, suggesting that significant others shape realistic aspirations primarily as models providing information and resources, rather than through normative mechanisms.

articles.title: Harnessing Human–AI Interpretive Difference: Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism
articles.authors: Emmanuelle Poncin
articles.abstract: Recent debate over GenAI in qualitative inquiry centres on concerns that computational participation reinforces postpositivist dominance. Critical analysts propose excluding it, out-theorising it, or continuously inspecting its entanglements. In parallel, a growing body of work builds architectures to accommodate human-AI collaboration in interpretive inquiry. While most of this work relies on postpositivist assumptions, an emerging strand develops collaborative architectures grounded in interpretivism, an approach this article adopts. I propose that for computational interpretation to be part of interpretivist inquiry without being granted reflexivity or interpretive authority, it must be deliberately structured into an accountable, productive relationship alongside human interpretation. To that end, I outline Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism, an epistemological position resting on five propositions. First, productive epistemic non-equivalence holds that human and computational interpretation need not share an epistemic basis for their difference to be structured as a resource. Second, interpretive co-construction grounds computational interpretation in meanings negotiated between researcher and participant, rather than a decontextualised corpus. Third, productive divergence treats non-alignment between human and computational interpretations as a potential source of analytic insight. Fourth, interpretive traceability refers to the capacity to see the grounds upon which human and computational interpretations are made, rendering them accountable structurally. Fifth, reflexive engagement holds that computational participation can create occasions for the researcher to interrogate her relationship to her subjectivity. This position is operationalised through Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA). LICA deploys computational interpretation to anchor interpretive insights to the empirical material. It integrates explicit interpretive co-construction between participant and researcher in interviews, scrutinises divergence between researcher and computational interpretations, renders analytic reasoning traceable, and embeds the researcher's subjectivity into the computational process. Together, these features create the conditions for new insights to emerge from the interaction between human and computational interpretations.

articles.title: Do genes modify earnings trajectories following job loss?  Gene-environment interactions with endogenous and exogenous forms of job loss
articles.authors: INVEST Flagship; Arno Van Hootegem; Henri Salokangas; Gaia Ghirardi; Henrik Dobewall; Laura Jernström; Maria Vaalavuo
articles.abstract: Job loss is a disruptive event that results in long-term economic scarring, though effects vary across social groups. This study explores a new potential source of inequality in the impact of job loss by examining whether genetic traits can amplify or attenuate earning declines following job loss. To address bias from gene-environment correlations, we compare interactions between polygenic indices (PGIs) and both endogenous job loss (individual unemployment) and exogenous job loss (plant closures). We focus on PGIs for depression, educational attainment, and risk-taking. Using Finnish population register data linked to genetic information for approximately 10,000 individuals observed over ten years, we apply a difference-in-differences design. We find persistent earnings losses following job loss, with larger declines for endogenous unemployment spells. Genetic moderation is observed only for plant closures: individuals with higher depression-related PGIs experience greater earnings declines. No comparable interactions emerge for endogenous job loss or the other PGIs.

articles.title: Automated Creativity in the Imagined Network: Creative Writer's View on Generative AI
articles.authors: Tianyu Zhao
articles.abstract:
As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies reshape the creative sector, understanding their implications for writers becomes increasingly vital. The study addresses a significant research gap by the impact of GenAI on creative writers in the United Kingdom, focusing on their perceptions and interactions within professional networks. The research explores two primary questions: how UK creative writers perceive and interact with GenAI technologies in their professional network, and what factors shape these perceptions and interactions within the creative industry. Employing a qualitative approach, the study conducts in-depth interviews with members of the Writers' Guild of Great Britain to gather rich, contextual qualitative response.

Key findings reveal the complex relationship between writers' self-identification within their professional networks and the integration of GenAI technologies. The study also uncovers writers' concerns about potential displacement by AI and examines the interplay between GenAI and capitalist forces in the creative industry. By centring the voices of creative writers, this research contributes to the ongoing discourse on technology and creativity, advocating for a more nuanced understanding of the sociotechnical dynamics in the creative industry. The study informs future discussions on the ethical use of AI in creative fields and provides an STS perspective on the evolving relationship between technology and creative professionals.

articles.title: A Rough Revised Estimate of Exclusive Breastfeeding at 6 Months in England Based on the 2024 Infant Feeding Survey
articles.authors: Emily H Emmott
articles.abstract: The 2024 Infant Feeding Survey likely overestimates exclusive breastfeeding prevalence at 6 months in England. Roughly correcting for probable selection and attrition bias, true prevalence is more plausibly in the region of 4–17%, with an upper bound estimate of 21.4%. More precise estimates would require individual level data, which would allow formal modelling and direct estimation of differential attrition by feeding status.

articles.title: Localizing the Sustainable Development Goals through Digitally Visible Initiatives: An Exploratory Study in Brazil
articles.authors: Cecilia Kotzias; Tamer Uzun; Hans Michael van Bellen; Roberto Pacheco; Cinthya Mônica da Silva Zanuzzi; Paulo Maurício Selig
articles.abstract: Community-based and other sustainability-oriented initiatives across Brazil address problems central to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), yet their contributions may be less visible within formal SDG monitoring because they are distributed across numerous small actors and often expressed in local rather than SDG terminology. This study frames the challenge of making the contributions of such initiatives legible within SDG localization as a knowledge-translation problem and develops an exploratory digital mapping and classification procedure for identifying and interpreting digitally visible sustainability-oriented initiatives in relation to nationalized SDG targets. An iterative snowball mapping procedure on Instagram identified 2,328 publicly visible profiles, from which 256 sustainability-oriented initiatives were classified in relation to nationalized SDG targets (230 assigned a primary SDG). A documented subset of 50 initiatives, including 47 examined using additional public sources, was analyzed in depth. Coding followed a transparent codebook, and an independent second coder recoded the documented subset, yielding moderate intercoder reliability (Cohen's κ = 0.57), followed by negotiated adjudication of disagreements. The findings indicate that many initiatives address SDG-relevant problems without using SDG terminology, that assigning a single primary SDG entails interpretive loss when representing multidimensional local practices, and that fewer than one quarter of the initiatives in the in-depth subset are directly recognized in Brazil's official civil society registry. The study introduces a transparent and auditable mapping-and-classification procedure grounded in this framing and provides empirical insights into both the analytical potential and the interpretive limits of translating situated local narratives into classifications aligned with nationalized SDG targets.

articles.title: No Reform, No Election: CHADEMA's Campaign and the Legacy of Incomplete Political Reform in Tanzania, 1991–2025
articles.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles.abstract:
On 23 March 2025, the Chama cha Demokrasia na Maendeleo (CHADEMA) launched its “No Reform, No Election” campaign in Mbeya City, demanding substantive electoral and political reforms as a condition for participation in Tanzania's forthcoming general election. Although the campaign emerged in the immediate aftermath of the 2024 local-government elections, its political rationale was rooted in a much longer history of incomplete institutional reform dating from the Nyalali Commission of 1991. This article examines the campaign within the historical trajectory of Tanzania's major presidential commissions and reform initiatives, including the Nyalali Commission, the Warioba Commission on corruption, the Kisanga Committee, the Warioba Constitutional Review Commission, and the Presidential Taskforce on Multiparty Democracy chaired by Professor Rwekaza Mukandala.
The article argues that Tanzania's reform trajectory is characterized by a recurring gap between the identification of institutional problems, the production of reform recommendations, and their comprehensive implementation. This article conceptualizes this phenomenon as the reform implementation gap and argues that its cumulative effect has generated a reform expectation gap between citizens' and political actors' expectations and the institutional outcomes delivered by successive governments. The 2025 CHADEMA campaign should therefore be understood not simply as an electoral boycott strategy but as a political claim concerning the relationship between electoral participation and institutional legitimacy. The article further examines the 2023–2024 electoral and political-party legislation, CHADEMA's invocation of President Samia Suluhu Hassan's “4Rs” philosophy, and the opposition's increasing reliance on digital mobilization in a constrained political environment. It concludes that democratic consolidation in Tanzania requires not merely additional reform initiatives but credible implementation of existing recommendations, stronger institutional independence, and political conditions capable of sustaining meaningful electoral competition.

articles.title: The Growing Transatlantic Sanctions Divide
articles.authors: Anton Peez
articles.abstract: Multilateral cooperation on sanctions is a key determinant of their success, yet transatlantic collaboration on sanctions is steeply declining. This transatlantic sanctions divide is a symptom of increasingly divergent US and EU foreign policies. Sanctions are likewise best terminated multilaterally to effectively wield them as leverage. Here too, trustful US-EU collaboration is increasingly difficult to imagine. Nonetheless, strong public support for sanctioning Russia in both the EU and US offers a basis for continuing forceful Western sanctions as Russia escalates its war of aggression against Ukraine.

articles.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles.title: Explaining the Decline of impal Marriage among the Karo: An Epidemiological Approach
articles.authors: Geoff Kushnick; Sam Passmore; Fikarwin Zuska; Karmila br. Karo; Daniel M.T. Fessler
articles.abstract: The Karo of North Sumatra, Indonesia, have long expressed a preference for matrilateral cross-cousin (impal) marriage, yet the practice has declined sharply over the past century. To identify the demographic and sociocultural factors underlying this change, we applied an epidemiological approach to cultural evolution, using a case-control design coupled with structural equation modeling (SEM). Ethnographic data from 176 married individuals across 62 villages were analyzed to assess the effects of demographic, alliance, religious, cosocialisation, and modernisation variables on the likelihood of impal marriage. The model fit was strong (CFI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.04), revealing significant direct and indirect effects. Marrying an impal was positively associated with the number of marriageable impal and with arranged or strategically motivated unions but negatively associated with reported religious conflict between spouses. Indicators of modernisation such as schooling and infrastructure were non-significant. These results indicate that the decline of impal marriage reflects demographic contraction and the weakening of alliance-based strategies rather than a rejection of the cultural norm itself. Framed within an epidemiological model of cultural transmission, the findings demonstrate how social practices may fade when the ecological and demographic conditions sustaining them erode, even as their normative value persists.

articles.title: Generational Imprinting: How Political Events Shape Cohorts
articles.authors: Turgut Keskintürk
articles.abstract: Contemporary narratives of generational politics propose that formative experiences produce shared political opinions across an age cohort. In this article, I advance a theory of cohortization to challenge that view, arguing that large-scale political events produce differentiation within cohorts as much as differentiation between them. I investigate the implications of this framework through the killing of George Floyd and the subsequent Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, analyzing attitudes toward law enforcement among non-Hispanic White Americans from 2016 to 2024. Using survey data from Cooperative Congressional Election Study, American National Election Study, and the Nationscape, I show that younger and older cohorts diverged after the event, but this differentiation was driven exclusively by young Democrats and Independents. The end result was not a unified generation, but one internally divided along party lines. This finding qualifies theories of generational politics, emphasizing that formative experiences may intensify existing political divisions within cohorts.

articles.title: Mapping the Discourse Network of Cervical Cancer Screening on Reddit: A Topic-Network Approach
articles.authors: Qiyao Peng
articles.abstract: Online health communities are a primary venue where the public interprets cervical cancer screening, yet how peer discourse, which has no editorial authority, bundles screening concerns remains unclear. Drawing on network agenda setting (NAS), this study treats a peer community as a collective agenda-setter and asks how it organizes screening topics. This paper analyzes 9,851 posts and comments from seven women's-health subreddits (August 2025 to January 2026) using Latent Dirichlet Allocation and the Analysis of Topic Model Networks, with Spearman topic-loading similarity filtered to a significant backbone. Thirteen topics form three communities: a diagnostic-information agenda, an embodied exam-experience agenda, and a narrative-and-support agenda. Embodied, temporally anchored concerns hold them together: timing and bleeding, pelvic pain, and access carry the highest betweenness. Sentiment follows network position, with support positive and cancer risk negative. These findings extend NAS to agenda-less, peer-driven settings and map how health agendas emerge from the bottom up.

articles.title: Generative AI and Society
articles.authors: Laura K. Nelson; Daniel Karell; Thomas Davidson
articles.abstract: For sociologists, generative AI inherits the legacy of earlier computational technologies: it is an advancement of machine learning already adopted as a methodology, and it intervenes in a society already shaped by algorithmic systems. Yet it also has a dimension that distinguishes it from previous computational methods, and one that makes it inherently sociological: its interactivity. In this review, we conceptualize the interactivity of generative AI and introduce a framework for understanding how it operates across individual, organizational, and institutional life. Specifically, the framework specifies how generative AI expands users, functions as a proxy for society, and expresses power, both in sociological practice and in society. We conclude by suggesting three dynamics driven by generative AI that sociology will face in the near future: the transformation of scientific practice, the reorganization of social interaction, and the acceleration of algorithmic governance.

articles.title: Able but unwilling? Mapping citizens’ political GenAI use through the lens of Expectancy-Value Theory
articles.authors: Michael van Straelen; Christopher Starke; Patrick van Erkel; Jessica Piotrowski; Nils Köbis
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise and risk for democracy, yet little is known about how
citizens evaluate and adopt it for political purposes. Drawing on Expectancy-Value Theory
and Uses & Gratifications Theory, this study offers an initial account of political GenAI
adoption, mapping how citizens' cost-value perceptions and expectancy beliefs cluster into
distinct profiles. We investigate how these ‘expectancy-value profiles’ shape political GenAI
use. Using cross-sectional survey data from 947 Dutch respondents, we conduct a latent
profile analysis, identifying four profiles: optimists, cautious pragmatists, sceptics, and
indifferents. Profile differences stem largely from differing cost-value perceptions rather than
expectancy beliefs, suggesting the question is less about whether people feel able to use
GenAI, and more about whether they feel it is worth using. Across all profiles, cost
perceptions are high and political use is low, though optimists report significantly more use
than others. Individuals’ political dispositions predict usage but not profile membership and
among technological dispositions, trust in GenAI and belief in the machine heuristic predict
being an optimist. Findings raise concerns about uncalibrated trust among adopters.

articles.title: The Power of “We” in Science Funding and Publication
articles.authors: Lijian Peng; Wenwen Li; Yi Bu; Hao Peng
articles.abstract:
Linguistic communication supports all stages of scientific innovation. However, we have limited understanding of rhetorical strategies for facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science. 
Drawing on prior literature on the importance of personal pronouns in inter-personal communication, we examine the unique role of first-person plural pronouns (``We'' words, including ``we'', ``us'', ``our'') in science funding and publishing. 
Our study leverages the full sample of 13K grant proposals submitted to the Novo Nordisk Foundation and 47K research papers submitted to BMJO and ICLR between 2011 and 2024. 
We find a strong and universal positive association between ``we'' words and success rates even after accounting for important confounding factors related to content, novelty, and author impact.
Specifically, a one percentage point increase in the percentage of ``We'' words used in the full text is associated with a 36-51% increase in the odds of success for grants and papers.
Furthermore, we find that the effect of ``We'' is applicable to both editors and reviewers of BMJO papers that used the single-blind review and is predictive of more positive and engaging review feedback for ICLR papers that employed the double-blind review.
Crucially, a large-scale LLM-assisted computational experiment that replaces ``We'' words with demonstrative pronouns provides robust causal evidence of ``We'' words on paper acceptance.
Lastly, our causal mediation analysis shows that ``We'' words can lead to more acceptance mainly because they can increase the perceived teamwork, credibility, significance, and robustness in research evaluation.
By revealing the unique strength of ``We'' in facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science, our study highlights the importance of small but mighty linguistic choices in promoting knowledge discoveries and breakthroughs.

articles.title: Constructing Methodologically Robust Subnational Estimates from Survey Microdata: A Methods Review
articles.authors: Kailas Venkitasubramanian
articles.abstract:
Constructing estimates for a custom, county-defined region from survey microdata is constrained by
the geography at which respondents are identified. In the American Community Survey (ACS) Public
Use Microdata Sample (PUMS), that geography is the Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA), which
does not nest into counties and is periodically redrawn. This review surveys the state of the art in
producing methodologically robust subnational estimates under these constraints, organized into four
method families — crosswalk and allocation-factor methods, consistent-geography harmonization, areal
interpolation and dasymetric and structure-preserving methods, and model-based small-area estimation.
Each family is assessed against a reference baseline: a population-weighted allocation-factor pipeline
with Successive Difference Replication variance estimation. The review pays particular attention to the
within-zone compositional homogeneity assumption that limits direct reweighting, to the harmonization
of geographies across boundary revisions, and to the rigor of uncertainty quantification. It restricts
attention to methods implementable with publicly available data. It serves both as a standalone reference
and as the methodological foundation for a companion analysis.

articles.title: Demographic Segregation in Online Information Ecosystems
articles.authors: Burak Ozturan; David Lazer
articles.abstract:
Concern about online echo chambers rests on the premise that the internet sorts people
by politics. Research on online ideological segregation has accordingly measured partisanship
almost to the exclusion of other social divides, and has measured it mostly within news, which
is a small share of online activity (Allen et al., 2020; Muise et al., 2022). Whether partisan
segregation is distinctive has therefore rarely been tested against demographic segregation on
equal terms. Using a 1.6-million-user Twitter/X panel linked to voter file records (July 2018 to
May 2023), we measure age, gender, partisanship and geography with a Theil index, and race
more briefly alongside them. First, partisanship is not the dominant division of online attention.
When measured across Democrats, Republicans and Independents, partisan segregation over
general sharing behaviour is roughly a third of demographic segregation, and age separates users
more sharply than party even within news, the content category where partisan segregation is
strongest and where the existing literature has looked almost exclusively. Second, segregation is
built at the article level rather than the outlet level. People who differ on any social divide we
measure converge on the same outlets and diverge on which stories they select from them, which
places segregation downstream of the outlet choices that most audience-level research observes.
Geography is the exception and segregates at the outlet level, as local news would predict. Third,
the five-year decline in demographic segregation is produced by different mechanisms for different
divides. Gender’s decline reflects almost entirely who left the platform, partisanship’s reflects how
people changed, and age’s is an even mixture, so parallel aggregate trends can rest on unrelated
causes. Online attention is segregated along social lines that are largely not political, at a level
of granularity that outlet-based measures cannot observe. Existing estimates of partisan echo
chambers describe a narrower and less distinctive phenomenon than the polarisation literature
has assumed.

articles.title: Economic Growth and Working-Class Representation: Evidence from Brazil
articles.authors: Jamil Civitarese
articles.abstract: Economic growth may lead to more resources for the working class to solve collective action problems and demand political representation, but not all instances of economic growth do unequivocally reduce economic inequality. When productivity gains accrue disproportionately to economic elites and political parties lack durable ties to labor, it may instead deepen class-based political exclusion. I test this argument using a novel panel that identifies the occupational background of every city council candidate in Brazil from 2004 to 2020, a period of economic growth led by agribusiness productivity increases. Within municipalities, increases in GDP are associated with a smaller share of campaign funding going to working-class candidates and a lower share of elected councilors from working-class backgrounds. Leveraging individual-level data on career trajectories of incumbents, I confirm these results. Additionally, I study the scope conditions for my theory, showing that non-leftist parties and rural areas drive my results. A qualitative comparison design reveals that discretionary choices by party leaders serve as a channel through which unequal growth can reinforce exclusion in political representation.

articles.title: The effects of childhood family disruption on sexual attitudes, experiences and well-being
articles.authors: Yucheng He; Yao Ma; zhuofei lu
articles.abstract: More than 40% of children in the representative UK Millennium Cohort Study experienced a risk of family disruption (i.e., not living with both biological parents by age 14), a circumstance widely recognized as shaping the early developmental environment. Yet the longer-term implications of family disruption for offspring’s sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being remain surprisingly underexamined. Drawing on 10,624 respondents from the most recent wave (2010–2012) of Natsal-3, and combining weighted OLS and logistic regression models, this study yields several novel findings. First, individuals who experienced family disruption by age 14 face elevated risks of non-volitional sex. Family disruption is also associated with more permissive sexual norms and greater involvement in boundary-testing sexual practices. Moreover, it is linked to slightly poorer sexual functioning and more frequent symptoms of low sexual mood. Taken together, these results provide new evidence that childhood family disruption has enduring consequences for sexual attitudes, experiences, and sexual well-being, underscoring the need for greater attention to interventions supporting children who experience family disruption.

articles.title: Automated Suspicion: Algorithmic Workforce Surveillance and the Erosion of Internal Legitimacy in the Metropolitan Police Service
articles.authors: Paul Ford
articles.abstract:
Abstract
This article examines the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) pilot deployment of Palantir analytics for internal workforce monitoring, announced in April 2026 as part of the force’s post-Panorama standards programme. The force defends the deployment as lawful, since it brings together data it already holds; this article argues that defence repeats a known mistake in policing legitimacy research, treating legal compliance as the ceiling of consent rather than its floor. Drawing on procedural justice theory (Tyler 2006), the dialogic and twin-track models of legitimacy (Bottoms and Tankebe 2012; Tankebe 2013; Bradford and Tankebe 2014), Beetham’s (1991) account of institutional legitimacy, and the author’s earlier work (Ford 2021, 2026), it audits the deployment against the four pillars of procedural justice and finds it deficient on voice, neutrality, respect, and trustworthy motives.
