It argues that the pilot inverts Sherman’s (2007) power-few hypothesis, fails the targeting—testing—tracking discipline of evidence-based policing (Sherman 2013), substitutes a technical fix for what Heifetz (1994) calls an adaptive challenge, and entangles culture reform with surveillance in ways that risk delegitimising Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) work and, through a mirroring effect, damaging public-facing encounters. A subsequent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, including the pilot’s Data Protection Impact Assessment and Equality Impact Assessment obtained in redacted form, tests these claims against primary evidence: it confirms an algorithmic yield of 2.6 million flags with a further-action rate of 0.075 per cent, corroborates self-acknowledged risks to trust and equity in the MPS’s own equalities analysis, and shows the force cannot establish what became of the cases its own system flagged. The article closes with implications for chief officers, police and crime commissioners, and professional standards leads.
Keywords: algorithmic management, workforce surveillance, police legitimacy, officer self-legitimacy, procedural justice, psychological safety, organisational culture, EDI, Palantir, Metropolitan Police Service.

articles.title: Thoughtforms in the Fog: Liminal Warfare and the Defense of Human Agency
articles.authors: Michael Paul Ross
articles.abstract:
Cognitive warfare is commonly framed as a contest over perception and decision-making. This
article argues that its most consequential leverage often appears during liminal periods, when
established identities, meanings, and institutions no longer provide sufficient orientation. It
introduces the thoughtform as a functional analytic construct with a long, heterogeneous
genealogy in initiation, ritual, and esoteric reflection, but does not rely on metaphysical claims.
A thoughtform is defined here as a recursively sustained symbolic formation that organizes
attention, emotion, identity, interpretation, and action across people, media, institutions, and
machines. A six-stage Liminal Thoughtform Cycle explains how threshold disruption can
produce either adaptive integration or cognitive capture. The article then advances liminal
security and Cognitive Aikido as agency-centered defenses, treating mental health and well-
being as capacities for sustaining meaning, relationships, reality orientation, and action under
pressure. The objective is capacity rather than control: preserving reflective freedom, relational
coherence, and meaningful action under persistent influence.

Keywords: cognitive security, cognitive warfare, liminality, thoughtforms, influence operations,
agency, resilience

articles.title: Rol de la Iglesia católica como aparato ideológico durante la dictadura de Trujillo, 1930-1961
articles.authors: Alfredo Antonio Pérez Sánchez
articles.abstract:
La presente investigación analiza el rol de la Iglesia católica como aparato ideológico durante la dictadura de Trujillo, 1930-1961. El estudio parte del interés por comprender la relación establecida entre la Iglesia y el Estado, así como la influencia que dicha vinculación ejerció en la legitimación del régimen y en la difusión de valores, prácticas y discursos orientados a fortalecer el poder político durante la Era de Trujillo. La investigación se desarrolló desde un enfoque cualitativo, mediante un estudio histórico-documental sustentado en el análisis crítico de documentos oficiales, legislación, publicaciones periódicas, correspondencia, obras historiográficas y otras fuentes primarias y secundarias relacionadas con el tema. El análisis realizado permitió establecer que la Iglesia católica ocupó un lugar importante dentro de la estructura ideológica del régimen, al ejercer una influencia significativa en los ámbitos educativo, moral y simbólico de la sociedad dominicana. Además, se observó que esta relación no permaneció estática, ya que en los años finales de la dictadura comenzaron a manifestarse diferencias entre la jerarquía eclesiástica y el poder político, motivadas por el incremento de la represión y el deterioro de la situación nacional. En ese sentido, la investigación ofrece una interpretación histórica que amplía la comprensión de las relaciones entre religión, poder e ideología durante el trujillato y aporta una visión integral sobre este proceso de la historia dominicana.

Palabras clave: Iglesia católica; dictadura de Trujillo; aparato ideológico del Estado; legitimación política; ideología.

articles.title: The Accountability Gap in Sub-Sovereign ESG Finance: A Case Study of Police Administration Oversight in Chiba Prefecture, Japan
articles.authors: Takashi Miyazawa
articles.abstract: This paper examines a critical vulnerability in the methodology of sub-sovereign ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) ratings, utilizing Chiba Prefecture, Japan, as a primary case study. While global ESG frameworks increasingly evaluate local government bonds, rating agencies predominantly rely on macro-level socioeconomic indicators and overarching policy frameworks, creating a significant "measurement gap." We demonstrate how this macro-dependence obscures micro-level governance failures—specifically, the indefinite suspension of complaint processing and the systemic non-creation of official records within police administration. By applying an axiomatic approach grounded in administrative law and corporate governance principles, this study empirically documents the existence of a structural "Accountability Gap" at the operational entry point. The findings highlight the critical need for institutional investors and ESG rating agencies to discount the reliability of sub-sovereign sustainability representations when auditable management evidence is structurally absent.

articles.title: Rethinking Children’s Family Complexity: A Multi-Conceptual Approach with Dynamic Sequence Analysis and Fixed Effects Models
articles.authors: Carla Rowold; Martin Gädecke; Zachary Van Winkle
articles.abstract:
Objective: The association between a wide range of family complexity indicators and children’s educational outcomes was assessed. 

Background: Previous research documented a negative impact of disadvantageous family transitions and family instability on children’s educational outcomes. However, there is a theoretical and empirical debate surrounding the most appropriate measure of family complexity during childhood.

Method: Numerous theoretically conceptualized sequence-based complexity measures are applied to parents’ life history data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, which were linked to children’s test scores in the National Pupils Dataset. Average within-child change in boys’ and girls’ math and English tests scores following change in mothers’ and fathers’ family complexity were estimated with fixed-effects regressions.  

Results: Family complexity measures were largely found to be negatively associated with children’s academic performance, however with differences across indicators. The number of transitions as well as the uncertainty and sum of disadvantage indicators were most tightly associated with children’s test scores. In addition, results varied by parents’ and children’s gender. For example, family complexity for fathers was often positively associated with children’s educational outcomes and associations were often stronger for boys compared to girls.

Conclusion: Findings highlight the importance of theoretically derived measures of family complexity. In this study, measures associated with family instability and parental absence were shown to be most strongly linked with children’s educational outcomes.

articles.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles.title: Maximizing Recruitment via Respondent-driven Sampling
articles.authors: Mariel Leonard; Julian B. Axenfeld; Hannah Bethge; Julia Witton; Carina Cornesse; Sabine Zinn
articles.abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS), a network-based method of sampling has become increasingly popular as a means of developing subgroup samples, particularly in web-first or web-only design (webRDS). WebRDS can reduce participant burden as well as increase the potential size and geographic scope of the sample, allowing for development of national samples with greater generalizability. However, webRDS can also introduce technical challenges as it requires all RDS processes to be mediated through internet-communication technology. In this paper, we focus on the challenges of engaging participants and reducing burden following a request to participate in webRDS. We present the results of two studies in which we tested several design features for their effects on webRDS recruitment success. We use social exchange theory as a lens through which to improve webRDS recruitment by maximizing benefits of participation and reducing burden. Based on our findings, we present recommendations for webRDS implementation.

articles.title: Digital media and social inequality : a primer in the context of Swiss digital society
articles.authors: Moritz Büchi
articles.abstract: Digital media innovations are used differently by people from different social groups and have varying consequences. Research has not found that these divides are narrowing. On the contrary, individuals who are socially better positioned appear to benefit more from digital media transformation. At the societal level, there is a need for a transparent negotiation of the values underlying the digital media infrastructure - values that can guide democratic governance.

articles.title: ‘My spiritual path is Belonging’: Belonging as a valued and sought after affective state for spiritual but not religious individuals.
articles.authors: Kathryn Diane Ford; Sotirios Kolios; Lora Adair; Matthew Michel Gervais; Aiyana Koka Willard; Michelle Ann Kline
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objective: Spiritual but not religious (SBNR) beliefs are often characterised as hyper individualistic and lacking community. This study explores concepts of belonging and community among spiritual seekers to assess these claims. 
Methods: This study entailed 30 semi-structured interviews of SBNR individuals combined with long term ethnographic research in Glastonbury UK, a small town with a reputation as a spiritual hub. 
Results: Thematic analysis of participant interviews highlighted the importance of affective belonging to participants. Participants left social contexts where they experienced a lack of affective belonging. Participants invested time and effort into finding sources of affective belonging and in creating sources of affective belonging for others.
Conclusion: Affective belonging is important to SBNR individuals. Prior research suggesting that spiritual but not religious do not value belonging is due primarily to miss-measurement and a lack of conceptual clarity. 
Key words: Spiritual but not Religious, Belonging, Community, Glastonbury, Belief, Qualitative, Interviews

articles.title: Dynamic Social Vulnerability Index (DSVI): A Mobility-Adjusted Measure of Community Vulnerability
articles.authors: Owais Gilani; Elena Khusainova; Talha Ali; Abby Flynt; Paul Christine; Simon Urbanek; Michael J. Kane
articles.abstract:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) serves as a useful tool to identify vulnerable communities in order to meet their needs before, during, and after disasters, infectious disease outbreaks, and other public health emergencies. Additionally, the SVI is widely used in social science research as a proxy measure of social disparities and as a measure of a community’s social determinants of health.
 
We argue that social vulnerability, assessed in terms of a community’s access to different resources, is not solely determined by residential location but also by the locations that its residents frequent throughout the day, as determined by their movement. Building on the concept of activity spaces for individuals, we propose the idea of an ``activity space for communities'', which is an aggregate measure of the activity space of all individuals who consider that community their ``home''. In aggregate, residents of different communities will tend to have very different movement patterns, and hence different activity spaces. Using large-scale cell-phone telemetry data for the United States in 2019, we quantify this activity space for communities at the census tract level and apply it to SVI to develop a mobility adjusted measure of community vulnerability - the Dynamic SVI (DSVI). 

By incorporating mobility patterns into SVI, we move toward a relational and dynamic model of vulnerability,
where risk is understood not just as a product of fixed geographic location, but also as shaped by daily
movements, access to transportation, and the spatial distribution of critical resources and services. A web application to explore and download the DSVI for 2019 is available at https://mobility.science/dsvi.

articles.title: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF BUDGET RATCHETING ON OWN-SOURCE REVENUE AND REVENUE SHARING FUNDS' EFFECT ON CAPITAL EXPENDITURE
articles.authors: NA; Akmal Huda Nasution; Edy Zulfiar; Mariana; Anhar Firdaus; Rulyanti Susi Wardhani
articles.abstract:
Objectives:      This study aims to analyze the direct effect of Local Own-Source Revenue (PAD) and Revenue Sharing Fund (DBH) on Capital Expenditure, as well as to examine the mediating role of Budget Ratcheting in these relationships.

Methodology: The research employs a quantitative approach with multiple linear regression analysis, utilizing time-series cross-sectional data from 23 regencies/cities in Aceh Province over a five-year period (2018–2022). Data were obtained from audited Local Government Financial Statements (LKPD), covering PAD, DBH, Capital Expenditure, and Budget Ratcheting variables. The analysis was conducted using SPSS version 25, with classical assumption tests applied to ensure model validity.

Findings:         The results show that PAD does not have a statistically significant effect on Capital Expenditure (p = 0.234), suggesting the presence of contextual influences such as governance quality and fiscal policy implementation. Conversely, DBH demonstrates a significant positive impact on Capital Expenditure (p = 0.000), consistent with prior studies emphasizing its role in enhancing local government investment capacity. Mediation analysis reveals that Budget Ratcheting strengthens the relationship between PAD and Capital Expenditure despite the initial insignificance (p = 0.015). Moreover, Budget Ratcheting mediates the relationship between DBH and Capital Expenditure with a notable negative adjustment effect (p = 0.005).

Conclusion:     The study highlights the critical role of revenue-sharing mechanisms and adaptive budgeting practices in supporting regional development. Strengthening fiscal management and enhancing budget flexibility are recommended strategies to maximize the effectiveness of local revenue streams in driving capital expenditures.

articles.title: One Policy, Many Publics: Central Bank Communication and the National Politics of Trust
articles.authors: Björn Bremer; Lucio Baccaro
articles.abstract: Central bank decisions have become politically contested. In response, central banks communicate more with the public, since their effectiveness rests on public trust. Yet whether they reach ordinary citizens is largely unknown. We exploit the European Central Bank’s unexpected announcement of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) during the fieldwork of a March 2020 survey in Germany and Italy. Our results show that the same decisive intervention was rewarded only where it aligned with the perceived national interest: in Italy, trust in the ECB rose, strongest among news-followers and the left; in Germany, trust in the ECB did not move at all, even as trust in national institutions surged. Preferences for central bank goal independence moved in neither country. Citizens thus notice exceptional monetary policy decisions, but their responses are mediated by national interests and discourses, with asymmetric consequences for a central bank that makes one policy for many publics.

articles.title: When Aging No Longer Means Turning Right: Evidence from Swiss Panel Data
articles.authors: Lena Ajdacic; Matthias Enggist; Reto Mitteregger
articles.abstract:
By adopting a generational lens, research has increasingly documented political and electoral
transformations in Western Europe. In parallel, many researchers have pointed to the
crucial relevance of the formative years to understand attitudinal development.
However, these approaches often dismiss that generations’ formative years can differ,
with newer generations marrying later, having fewer children, and completing education
later in life. Using data from the Swiss Household Panel (1999-2022), we analyze
whether different generations in Switzerland show diverging age effects regarding
political ideology. Find-ings from an interaction analysis of age and cohort show that
while previous generations consistently tended to become more right-wing as they aged,
members of Generations Y and Z remain largely stable in their ideological orientation
over the life course. We find that this pattern is not explained by changes in
demographic and socio-economic compo-sition between cohorts. The results of this study
not only have important implications for future studies analyzing age-period-cohort
effects, but also enhance our understanding of opinion formation in transforming postindustrial
societies.

articles.title: From Networks to Mission Platforms: A Graded Architecture for Interdisciplinary Research at Institutional Scale
articles.authors: Jesus Marco de Lucas; Victoria Moreno-Arribas
articles.abstract:
Large multidisciplinary research organisations face a well-documented tension: their breadth is
precisely what makes them suited to complex societal challenges, yet their disciplinary structure
(centres, areas, evaluation panels) makes interdisciplinary work costly to initiate and hard to sustain.
This paper presents a longitudinal institutional case study of the approach adopted by the Spanish
National Research Council (CSIC) — Spain’s largest public research organisation, with more than
1,500 research groups in around 120 institutes — to address that tension without restructuring the
institution. From 2018 onward CSIC developed a graded set of three collaboration instruments:
Conexiones (light, bottom-up thematic networks), Interdisciplinary Thematic Platforms (PTI: mission-
oriented, three-year, challenge-driven platforms with an ESFRI-derived design questionnaire) and
Extended Platforms (PTI+: large-scale platforms with a four-line work structure, a consortium-
agreement style governance and centralised financial management, created to absorb investments
above C10M). The design principles of each instrument, the formal texts that implemented them and
the governance rules are presented (dual coordination across centres, assembly/executive-committee
model, two-thirds quorum, individual veto, VICYT ratification, Team Science and Open Science
recommendations). Publicly available documentary evidence on outcomes up to 31 August 2026
is then compiled for the best-documented platforms and networks, including the PTI Salud Global
response to COVID-19, the QTEP quantum ecosystem, SusPlast pilot plants, the IPCC Interactive Atlas
delivered under PTI Clima, the Conexiones cohorts created in 2023 and 2025, and the 2026 migration
of the Teledetect remote-sensing platform into the EarthWatchHub Conexión. The documentary record
supports four observations: (i) a pre-existing platform template enabled unusually rapid institutional
mobilisation during COVID-19; (ii) the platform architecture and its core governance principles were
adapted to an increase of roughly two orders of magnitude in financial scale; (iii) a graded portfolio
allowed organisational migration between instruments instead of simple termination; and (iv) different
instruments generated documented joint activities and outputs. The instruments were subsequently
formalised, not discontinued, by the administration that succeeded the one that created them. A set
of transferable design propositions is derived from the case, and the limitations of a documentary
analysis without a counterfactual are discussed. The contribution is a longitudinal institutional case
showing how a large disciplinary research organisation can superimpose a graded set of transverse
collaboration structures on its existing organisational backbone without dismantling it.

articles.title: Do Voters Blame the Opposition for Losing in Electoral Autocracies? Evidence from Turkey
articles.authors: Jonas Draege; Philipp Lutscher
articles.abstract: How do voters in autocracies evaluate opposition performance after defeat? We study this question with an exploratory online survey of 1054 opposition voters six months after Turkey's 2023 presidential and parliamentary elections. Although the opposition operated under structural disadvantages typical of electoral autocracies, nearly two-thirds of opposition voters blamed the opposition for the loss. Open-ended responses reveal three sources of dissatisfaction: criticism of the presidential candidate, frustration with intra-coalition conflict, and discomfort with the ideological breadth of the alliance. While these concerns often reflected genuine weaknesses in the opposition campaign, several were also intertwined with constraints imposed by the authoritarian context. To capture this tension, we introduce the concept of the authoritarian double bind: opposition parties are constrained by the regime in ways that produce the very weaknesses for which voters hold them accountable. Our findings show how electoral autocracies can simultaneously constrain opposition performance while voters continue to hold the opposition accountable for electoral failure.

articles.title: Inhabiting a flammable landscape: wildfire, human (im)mobility, and the ambivalent role of neo-rural settlers in central Portugal.
articles.authors: Michele Dalla Fontana
articles.abstract: Wildfires are increasingly reshaping human mobility. Yet research treats the relationship as one-directional — mobility as an outcome of fire, or as its precursor — and looks mainly to North America and Australia. The depopulating interior of Southern Europe, where the fire regime is itself a product of past rural out-migration, has drawn far less attention. Drawing on immersive fieldwork and 25 semi-structured interviews conducted in 2024 in the Serra do Açor, central Portugal, seven years after the 2017 fires, I examine how wildfire and human mobility co-constitute one another, and find them bound recursively rather than causally. The fires did not deter in-migration but appear to have lowered barriers to it, while driving a slower out-migration among traumatised newcomers and owners of unrebuilt second homes. Place attachment and voluntary (im)mobility sustain an explicit, locally transmitted doctrine of staying to defend, even as the year-round settlement of isolated quintas (dispersed smallholdings) by newcomers inverts a historical logic and produces new spatial vulnerability alongside dense grassroots adaptation. Neo-rural settlers thus emerge as agents of vulnerability and of adaptation at once, and repopulation is best understood not as the reversal of a depopulation-driven fire regime but as its next chapter.

articles.title: Framing the Border as a National Security Threat: Fox News Immigration Coverage in the 2016 and 2024 Election Cycles
articles.authors: Jenny Xu
articles.abstract: While previous scholarship has established the existence of U.S. right-wing ideological media framing and its evolution over time, there is limited research exploring how influential outlets like Fox News have framed immigration across two critical election cycles: 2016 and 2024. These years represent key moments in recent American history, extreme-right-wing media narratives, and how that shapes public perception of emotionally charged topics, such as that of “illegal immigration” in the United States. This research paper explores the question: How has Fox News framed the U.S.–Mexico border and immigration policy during election cycles, particularly in 2016 and 2024? It argues that Fox News strategically frames immigration as a national security threat during the 2016 and 2024 election cycles. I conduct a content analysis of the language, guests, and visuals used on Fox News programming, such as Hannity, to highlight how Fox News deliberately intensified its framing of the U.S.–Mexico border as a national security threat to influence public perception and invoke fear. This paper contributes to the fields of media studies and political communication by providing a multi-year analysis of threat-based storytelling that Fox News uses to shape public opinion. It deepens our understanding of the interplay between media bias, national security threats, and commercial incentives.

articles.title: Demographic Decline and Economic Challenges in East Asia: A Comparative Analysis of the Republic of Korea, Japan, and China
articles.authors: Piyush Shrestha
articles.abstract: Although the Republic of Korea, Japan, and China are experiencing similarly rapid fertility decline and population aging, the socioeconomic consequences of these changes differ considerably across the three countries. Population decline does not operate through a single mechanism; rather, its effects are shaped by the structural conditions of households, labor markets, and local economies. Unlike Korea, where demographic anxiety is heavily concentrated in the overheated metropolitan housing market, Japan absorbs its aging burden primarily through a bifurcated labor system. China complicates this regional narrative further. Despite a shrinking national population, the slowing domestic economy is paradoxically struggling to absorb a record influx of university graduates. Across the three countries, unpaid care work remains unevenly distributed between women and men, adding to the pressures surrounding employment, marriage, and family formation. These differences imply that demographic policy cannot rely on a uniform set of incentives. Therefore, policy interventions are more likely to be effective when they respond to the particular institutional and socioeconomic constraints operating within each country.

articles.title: Ecological Sensemaking as a Recursive Process of Indigenous Climate Adaptation: Evidence from the Santal Community of Bangladesh
articles.authors: Sourav Paul Chowdhury; Syed M. Ali Reza; M. Nasim Reza; Dhanno Saha; Solaiman Chowdhury
articles.abstract: Climate adaptation research has focused more on adaptive capacity, technological innovation, and resilience, and less on the interpretive processes that lie before adaptive action. In this study, ecological sensemaking is investigated as a factor influencing agricultural decision-making among the Santal indigenous community in Barind region, which is prone to drought in Bangladesh. The research employed an interpretivist paradigm using thematic analysis of 25 semi-structured interviews. The findings indicate that adaptation starts with the ongoing process of interpreting ecological cues in a way that is negotiated through indigenous ecological knowledge, lived experience, scientific information, and social interaction. Four interrelated themes account for the process of the construction of ecological meanings, their translation to agricultural and livelihood practices, and how they are constrained by structural conditions. The study goes beyond organizational contexts to describe and explain ecological sensemaking, reconceptualizing indigenous ecological knowledge as a process of environmental meaning-making, and proposes a process-based conceptual model for climate adaptation in the face of ecological uncertainty. The study extends Weick's Sensemaking Theory by conceptualizing ecological sensemaking as a recursive, relational, and structurally mediated process operating within Indigenous socio-ecological systems, thereby offering a theoretically grounded understanding of climate adaptation beyond organizational settings.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Rising Life Satisfaction in Russia Amidst War: The Role of Perceived Socioeconomic Status Before and During the Ukraine War
articles_hidden.authors: Pavel Vlasov
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research has firmly established life satisfaction within the Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS) as a reliable measure for assessing perceived quality of life within Russia. In this paper, we present perceived socioeconomic status (PSS) within the RLMS as a latent measure introduced to help examine levels of life satisfaction in Russia before (prewar 2018-2019) and during the Ukraine war (wartime 2022-2023). Using exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and structural equation modelling (SEM), the findings indicate that PSS is a robust measure that increases the explanatory power of prewar and wartime models and positively predicts life satisfaction in both periods. Contemporary wellbeing research consistently supports the view that a key mechanism in shaping life satisfaction lies in how certain demographic conditions are psychologically interpreted. Drawing on appraisal theory, the study thus suggests that subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position provide meaningful information for understanding wellbeing that cannot be captured by demographic characteristics alone. Moreover, in the RLMS, overreliance on demographic indicators is shown to obscure the subjective mechanisms through which individuals living through wartime conditions evaluate their life satisfaction and interpret their social positions. Overall, the paper emphasizes that future research on the RLMS should consider incorporating PSS in their analyses and further developing on how subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position capture aspects of life satisfaction that are simply immeasurable in demographic only models of the RLMS. Emphasis should be placed on the major social, economic, and political disruption caused by the war that become normalized over time.

articles_hidden.title: The Changing Gender Training Gap - A Systematic Review of Evidence from Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Marco Seegers
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on gender differences in non-formal job-related further training in Germany has produced inconsistent findings, leaving unclear how gender inequalities in training have developed and whether divergent findings reflect training forms or conceptual and meth-odological differences. This systematic review synthesised quantitative evidence from studies published between 1990 and 2026. Web of Science, Scopus, and FIS Bildung were searched in June 2026 and supplemented by backward citation searching. Forty-two stud-ies yielded 160 finding-level records, which were integrated using a structured narrative synthesis. The evidence indicates a weakening of the earlier male advantage in overall training participation, with later evidence increasingly showing no statistically detectable gender difference or higher participation among women. This convergence was weaker for employer-supported training, while population-level convergence coexisted with life-course-specific inequalities. Conceptual and methodological differences shaped the com-parability and empirical visibility of gender inequalities but did not systematically ac-count for the broader historical pattern, which remained visible under more restrictive comparisons. Overall, gender inequality in further training appears to have been recon-figured rather than eliminated or simply reversed, with inequalities remaining conditional on institutional and life-course contexts.

articles_hidden.title: How bibliometric indicators align with REF 2021 peer review across disciplines
articles_hidden.authors: Junjie Shen
articles_hidden.abstract: Bibliometric indicators are increasingly used to approximate expert peer review, but how well they do so varies across disciplines in ways that remain poorly understood. Existing analyses of the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) have largely correlated metrics with individual article quality scores, within single fields and using restricted-access data. This study takes a complementary approach based on publicly available data: institutional REF 2021 output GPA is correlated with a consistent set of citation-based and journal-based indicators for all submitting institutions across fifteen Units of Assessment (UoAs). Comparing the two types of indicators side by side reveals a continuum of evaluation cultures. At one end, Physics tracks citation impact far more closely than journal rank (correlations of 0.85 versus 0.42, based on the share of outputs in the top 10% of each measure). At the other end, Business and Management Studies shows the reverse (0.59 versus 0.92), among the strongest journal-based correlations across all fields examined. Of the fifteen UoAs, nine correspond best with journal-based indicators and six with citation-based indicators, a divide that cuts across the usual STEM/non-STEM boundary. Indicator validity is therefore not a property of the metric alone but of the discipline’s evaluation culture, and research assessment should choose and interpret metrics field by field.

articles_hidden.title: Modeling Network Dynamics with Overlapping Cohesive Subgroups
articles_hidden.authors: Stepan Zaretckii; Tom A.B. Snijders; Marijtje A.J. van Duijn; Christian Steglich
articles_hidden.abstract: We introduce a longitudinal extension of the latent membership stochastic actor-oriented model (LM-SAOM) for analyzing the co-evolution of network ties and actors’ memberships in overlapping cohesive subgroups. The model treats group memberships as latent and time-evolving, giving actors frequent opportunities to update their memberships while a strong \emph{membership cohesion} effect favors membership choices that place actors in the same groups as their network contacts, thereby keeping the inferred cohesive subgroups aligned with the evolving network. In an application to a friendship network, we find evidence that students are more likely to have ties with peers with whom they share cohesive subgroup membership, beyond what is captured by dyadic and triadic effects. Goodness-of-fit assessments indicate that incorporating group-level dependence improves the representation of selected meso-level network configurations.

articles_hidden.title: Global Trends in Widowhood Prevalence, 1970–2020: The Role of Population Ageing, Mortality, and Union Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Elder Lara-Castaneda; Zachary Van Winkle
articles_hidden.abstract: Widowhood is the predominant marital status at older ages, especially among women. Although population ageing is expected to increase widowhood, evidence on this trend remains scarce or fragmented across countries. This study contributes to the global understanding of widowhood by addressing two questions. First, how has widowhood prevalence changed among women and men across countries and world regions between 1970 and 2020? Second, to what extent are changes in overall widowhood prevalence attributable to changes in population age structure rather than to changes in age-specific widowhood prevalence, i.e. mortality and union dynamics. We gathered marital-status tabulations from censuses, registers, and nationally representative surveys covering 222 countries and territories, and trace crude and age-standardized widowhood prevalence from 1970 to 2020. A Kitagawa decomposition separates change between 1980 and 2010 in 135 populations into age-structure and age-specific-prevalence components. Widowhood prevalence declined globally and in most regions, especially among women. Although population ageing contributed to increasing widowhood prevalence, changes in age-specific prevalence more than offset this effect. An ageing world is not necessarily one in which an increasing share of people are widowed, but it may still be one in which large, socially vulnerable populations live with the consequences of spousal loss.

articles_hidden.title: Why Do Immigrant Girls Participate Less in Organized Leisure Activities? The Role of Parental Influence Across the Transition from Adolescence to Adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Mia Stenbro Lorenzen; Frank van Tubergen; Hans-Peter Y. Qvist
articles_hidden.abstract: Research documents immigrant-native gaps in girls’ participation in organized leisure activities across Western Europe, particularly among Muslim immigrant-origin girls. While parental characteristics are often assumed to shape these gaps, less is known about which parental factors matter most and how their influence unfolds from adolescence into adulthood. Using German longitudinal data from CILS4EU and CILS4EU-DE, we address these questions by examining participation gaps among non-Muslim and Muslim immigrant-origin girls relative to native girls across the transition from adolescence to early adulthood.In doing so, we estimate a structural equation model that distinguishes between initial parental effects in adolescence, path-dependent effects linking adolescent and adult participation, and persistent parental effects in early adulthood. Differences in parental participation andsocioeconomic resources explain a substantial share of theimmigrant-native participation gaps, whereas parental gender values explain comparatively little. Although participation gaps narrow over time, they persist, primarily through path-dependent processes, as lower participation during adolescence is carried forward into adulthood. Persistent parental effects remain but are comparatively modest. While participation gaps are larger among Muslim immigrant-origin girls, the underlying mechanisms are broadly similar across immigrant-origin groups. The findings highlight how family-based inequalities shape participation trajectories and contribute to the production and reproduction of participation gaps across the life course.

articles_hidden.title: Long-Term Health Financing in Chile: A Historical Analysis of the Segmented System, 1981–2024
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Camilo Cid Pedraza
articles_hidden.abstract: The objective of this article is to present the results of reconstructing the historical series of health expenditure in Chile from the creation of the segmented model in 1981 to 2024, and to briefly analyze its evolution in historical context. To this end, data were collected and digitized from primary sources: the Statistical Bulletins and Public Accounts of FONASA (1989–2016; 2020–2024), the Statistical Series of the Isapre System (SUPER, 1990–2024), and the Public Finance Statistics of DIPRES (2004–2025). The results show accelerated growth in private spending until the 1990s, followed by a sustained increase in public health expenditure associated with higher fiscal contributions and mandatory contributions. However, the long-term analysis reveals periods of slowdown in public spending coinciding with the expansion of private infrastructure, revealing the persistence of a segmented and unequal financing system. The trajectory of Chilean health expenditure shows significant variation in proportions and pace, conditioned by political and economic contexts. Alongside this analysis, we make the complete series used available to researchers in open access.

articles_hidden.title: What’s Worth Dreaming of? The Gendered and Classed Logics Behind Occupational Aspirations
articles_hidden.authors: Diego Strassmann Rocha; Marie Labussière
articles_hidden.abstract:
Even though occupations have multiple characteristics that make them more or less likely to
be aspired to, research has yet to capture which characteristics matter most for which
adolescents. This limits our understanding of inequalities in aspirations because different
theories emphasize the role of certain occupational characteristics over others. This article
examines whether and how evaluations of multiple characteristics combine into distinct logics
of aspirations based on adolescents’ gender, class, and gender-class intersection. We combine
Swiss data from the DAB Panel Study on adolescents’ aspirations with O*NET data on
occupational characteristics. Using conditional logit models, we estimate the relationships
between occupational characteristics and the choice of aspired occupation. Results show that
girls prioritize occupations satisfying female-typed interests and those requiring higher
education levels, while boys avoid occupations with high shares of women and high
educational requirements. High-class adolescents favour artistic and investigative occupations,
whereas low-class adolescents are averse to highly educated and high-income occupations.
Intersectional analyses reveal that low-class boys are particularly disadvantaged, exhibiting the
strongest aversion to highly educated occupations. Overall, findings highlight that aspirations
are shaped by multiple occupational characteristics rather than a single dimension,
underscoring the importance of a multidimensional perspective to better understand
inequalities in adolescent aspirations.

articles_hidden.title: Staged financing beyond the venture record: Equity rounds in the accounts of Italian SMEs
articles_hidden.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro di Molfetta; Valeria Notarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles_hidden.abstract: Almost everything known about equity rounds in young firms comes from the records of professional investors, so the evidence is selected on the presence of an intermediary. We read rounds instead from the share-premium reserve, a compulsory, disclosed and restricted line of the Italian statutory balance sheet, for 3,225 certified innovative SMEs over 2016–2025: 2,991 priced capital increases on 1,330 firms. Firms about to raise grew twice as fast in the preceding year and held identical cash, yet six in ten closed it at a loss; profitability falls and intangible assets rise only after the round. Seven panel estimators place the association across firms and not within them; a taxonomy estimated blind to the event finds the mechanism in all five financial configurations, with incidence differing eightfold; six flexible learners fail to improve on the linear specification. Selection operates on growth, not on profitability, a distinction intermediated samples cannot see.

articles_hidden.title: From Working Life to Retirement: Changing Educational Inequalities in Income Trajectories in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Ordemann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Previous literature has mainly focussed on either income trajectories of higher education graduates in working life or in retirement. This paper advances this literature by investigates the inequalities of income trajectories at the transition into retirement and compare the trajectories to other educational graduates for the case of Germany. While cumulative advantage theory suggests that education-based income inequalities widen throughout working life, the institutional design of the German pension system fundamentally alters these trajectories. 
Using data from 1,741 (11,740 observations) baby boomers from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study (SOEP) I combine descriptive income trajectories with fixed effects regression and replacement rate analysis. find a stratified pattern by educational degree in pre- and post-retirement income. However, income inequality by education degree is more pronounced during work life than in retirement: At the transition into retirement income differences are compressed relative to pre-retirement disparities. This compression operates through heterogeneous replacement rates. Higher educated individuals have lower replacement rates than the rest of the educational groups. Germany’s contribution-capped statutory pension system therefore constitutes a structurally induced erosion of the income advantage that higher education generates over a working lifetime.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Multidimensional Structure of Subjective Well-Being: Evidence from Mexico
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Alberto Arellano-Esparza
articles_hidden.abstract: Most research on subjective well-being (SWB) relies on the classic tripartite model of life satisfaction, positive affect, and negative affect, which may obscure its multidimensional character. Using nationally representative data from Mexico, this study compares alternative structural models of SWB through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, evaluating configurations that integrate eudaimonic, affective, and cognitive components to test whether a multidimensional structure provides a better statistical account of the data than a unidimensional alternative. Several competing models (correlated three-factor, hierarchical, and bifactor) display robust and largely equivalent fit. This multidimensional representation consistently outperforms a unidimensional one and remains largely stable across sex and region, indicating that no single structural model uniquely captures SWB, calling for more flexible approaches to its study.

articles_hidden.title: Selection, Allocation, and Timing: Three Obstacles to Measuring the Effect of Large-Load Growth on Household Electricity Prices
articles_hidden.authors: Babu George
articles_hidden.abstract: Published estimates of how hyperscale computing load affects household electricity prices disagree about sign as well as magnitude. This article argues that much of the disagreement reflects three identification problems that existing designs often absorb rather than model directly. Large loads choose low-cost locations, making exposure endogenous. Average revenue per kilowatt-hour cannot distinguish a change in rates from a change in the composition of customers within a class. In jurisdictions that allow construction costs into rates before a plant enters service, bills may change years before the associated load appears in sales data. I examine each problem using public data. With state-level price and sales data for 2023 and 2024 for the 50 states and the District of Columbia, I find direct evidence of siting selection: the 2023 residential price level explains 22 percent of the cross-state variance in subsequent non-residential sales growth. That sorting appears to follow a state’s general cost level rather than the depth of the discount already received by large customers, a more tractable pattern for identification. Non-residential sales growth has no detectable relation to residential price growth, although the design lacks power to detect elasticities below roughly 0.9, so the null is not substantively informative. The residential-to-industrial price ratio rises with load growth, but decomposition shows that seven-tenths of the movement comes from falling non-residential prices rather than rising residential prices; the same pattern appears relative to the commercial class, and half of the association disappears after adding a four-category regional control. Translating the reduced-form slope into an implied price for incremental load shows that a pure composition account would require these kilowatt-hours to be served at about one-third of the class average, a demanding but possible figure whose confidence interval cannot adjudicate the issue. The evidence favors a regime-dependent interpretation of the literature and indicates that future work should treat capital deployment, rather than realized energy sales, as the central treatment variable.

articles_hidden.title: Bucks for Bumps: How Paid Parental Leave Pays Off for Firms
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Cookler
articles_hidden.abstract: Firms use benefits such as paid parental leave (PPL) to attract and retain employees. In the U.S., which lacks broad public PPL benefits, firms increasingly provide this benefit. Systematic evidence of its benefits remains limited, due in part to the absence of comprehensive data on firm policies. Using a novel, hand-collected database of firm policy changes, this paper estimates the causal effect of PPL expansion on employee retention using a differences-in-differences approach. PPL expansions reduce departure rates by 3.1%, an effect equivalent to a permanent wage increase of 1.8%. Retention gains for women are concentrated among the lowest paid and those in the most junior roles, while retention gains for men are broad-based. At the firm level, retention gains concentrate in the interior of the internal labor market flexibility distribution and among firms with moderate firm-specific human capital, and they are robust to concurrent benefit changes and to firm revenue trajectories. Public PPL programs, by contrast, show no comparable retention effect, consistent with the non-portability of firm-provided benefits. Combining fertility estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) with worker and firm data, the paper calculates the expected costs of PPL provision and compares them to retention gains: at realistic utilization rates, PPL expansions generate positive net returns to firms.

articles_hidden.title: Lexical Integration: Introducing Aymara Corpus Evidence into Global English
articles_hidden.authors: Robert D. Smith
articles_hidden.abstract: Indigenous Andean languages have traditionally been preserved through oral traditions, especially following the historical destruction of non-alphabetic record-keeping systems like khipus (Coletta, 2023). In the face of imperial linguistic hegemony, traditional documentation efforts often prove insufficient for long-term epistemic preservation (van den Berg, 2024). As Global English expands, the decline of Indigenous languages threatens profound Andean ways of knowing with systematic erosion (van den Berg, 2024). This paper proposes a conceptual framework to preserve Highland Andean epistemology by integrating targeted, untranslatable Aymara words—such as ch’ixi, taypi, and suma qamaña—into Global English lexicons using international corpus evidence (Bosch & Griesel, 2020). Anchored in translanguaging theory and decolonial macro- and microethics, this approach maps translational deficiencies where English lacks single-word equivalents for complex Andean concepts. The study demonstrates that bridging these lexical gaps transforms Global English into an additive vehicle for cultural preservation, counteracting academic extractivism and projecting Indigenous philosophies onto the global stage.

articles_hidden.title: FASTrack: A co-designed cloud-based planning support system for interactive cycling infrastructure scenario assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan Turner; Afshin Jafari; Sapan Tiwari; Alan Both; Dhirendra Singh; Steve Pemberton; Chris De Gruyter
articles_hidden.abstract: Testing transport interventions using city-scale transport models is typically resource intensive, requiring specialist expertise, substantial data and computational capacity. As a result, such modelling is often concentrated on major projects and larger metropolitan areas, while smaller interventions and mid-sized regional cities have limited access to comparable modelling capabilities. This is particularly relevant to active travel, where cycling infrastructure decisions frequently need to be made with relatively limited modelling and decision-support capacity. This study presents FASTrack, a cloud-based planning support software system that integrates agent-based modelling, behavioural simulation, and interactive scenario visualisation to enable proposed cycling infrastructure assessment. A case study is applied to the City of Greater Bendigo, a mid-sized regional Australian city representative of the planning contexts that existing platforms often overlook. FASTrack was developed through a co-design process over three years with local government planning partners, to address the need to rapidly assess infrastructure scenarios, quantify changes in cycling demand and behaviour, and inform infrastructure planning and investment appraisal. These requirements underpin its design, including the use of probabilistic modelling and a cloud-based workflow designed to support rapid, on-demand scenario testing with minimal specialist modelling expertise. Scenario outcomes are presented through interactive dashboard-style interfaces that detail estimated changes in network use, level of traffic stress, mode shift, cycling usage, emissions, and cost-benefit analysis aligned with national appraisal guidelines. This study demonstrates how co-design can directly shape the development of planning support systems by translating practitioner requirements into accessible modelling platforms for cycling infrastructure planning

articles_hidden.title: Violence and International Migration in Illiberal Times: The Case of El Salvador’s Authoritarian Transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey Swindle; Matthew Blanton
articles_hidden.abstract: Across a new transnational wave of illiberal governance, tough-on-crime approaches to public safety and migration are growing. The case of El Salvador, in which President Nayib Bukele suspended due process protections and imprisoned suspected gang members in mass beginning in late March 2022 under a State of Exception policy, offers a window into this process. Turning to a combination of administrative datasets and cross-national surveys, we show that despite tremendous public approval for President Bukele’s strategies as the solution to a long history of persistent gang violence and international migration, violence largely reduced before he implemented the State of Exception, and Salvadorans’ migration intentions have not declined. Moreover, we find no evidence that the policy or Bukele taking office produced a particular reduction in Salvadoran migration to either the U.S. or Mexico compared to Guatemalan and Honduran migration. Nor do we uncover clear evidence that return migration to El Salvador uniquely increased, undercutting conclusions that illiberal tough-on-crime policies like El Salvador’s are likely to address “root causes” of international migration.

articles_hidden.title: Do AI Occupational-Exposure Scores Measure AI? AIOE and Eloundou (2024) Largely Capture Cognitive Content; Webb (2020) Does Not
articles_hidden.authors: Sudhanshu Rai
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing empirical literature uses pre-built "AI occupational exposure" scores (most prominently the AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) index of Felten, Raj, and Seamans (2021) and the GPT-4 task-exposure measure of Eloundou et al. (2024)) as occupation-level treatments or predictors for AI's labor-market effects. We show that two of the most-cited scores, AIOE and Eloundou's GPT-4 measure, substantially re-label cognitive task content rather than capturing AI-specific exposure, a construct-validity problem that does not extend to a third, differently-built score (Webb 2020, patent-based). This note horse-races these three measures against transparent cognitive/manual task-content indices and the established Autor–Dorn Routine Task Intensity (RTI) measure. Across 773 occupations: (i) the ten-plus AI "applications" underlying AIOE collapse to a single factor (first principal component ≈ 88%); (ii) AIOE and Eloundou each correlate strongly with a cognitive-ability index (+0.85 / +0.70) and negatively with a manual-ability index (−0.91 / −0.83), correlate 0.86 with each other, but only moderately with RTI (−0.33 / −0.30): the confound is specifically cognitive ability level, not the classic routine-task polarization axis; (iii) each score's positive wage association reverses sign controlling for cognitive content but is barely affected by controlling for RTI; and (iv) the much-cited pre-ChatGPT "AI foresight" wage-divergence pattern collapses to near-zero under the cognitive control (not under the RTI control). Critically, this collapse is not universal: Webb's patent-text-overlap score is essentially uncorrelated with AIOE (r=0.03) and Eloundou (r=−0.03), only weakly related to cognitive content (r=0.13), and its modest wage associations do not reverse under cognitive control. The cognitive-content collapse is a signature of how a score is built: subjective crowd-relatedness ratings (AIOE) or LLM/human task judgments (Eloundou), not an inherent property of occupational AI-exposure measurement. Studies using relatedness- or judgment-based exposure scores should control for cognitive content and re-interpret accordingly; a patent-based measure is not shown here to have the same problem, though its own construct validity is untested.

articles_hidden.title: VenturePhD: A Bilateral Venture Capital Model for Doctoral Education: Reciprocal Commitments and Exit Rights
articles_hidden.authors: Koutian Wu
articles_hidden.abstract: Doctoral students may spend years building a project and a supervisory relationship before they know whether that relationship will support their training. Changing direction can be costly when one supervisor influences a student's income, research access, assessment, and references. This paper proposes VenturePhD, a policy design for doctoral education that pairs reciprocal commitments with supported transfer and exit rights. Drawing on venture-contracting research, it separates decisions about a project's continuation from decisions about student support and recognition of completed work. Students and supervisors would agree on revisable research and training plans. Universities would guarantee specified funding, appoint reviewers outside the supervisory relationship, and finance time-limited transitions. The paper specifies responsibilities and remedies, gives a worked example, and sets out hypotheses for a prospective pilot. It reports no intervention results. The empirical question is whether universities can reduce a student's dependence on a particular supervisor without weakening research quality, mentoring, or access to doctoral education.

articles_hidden.title: The Kia-Hyundai vehicle theft surge: the roles of anti-theft devices and co-occurring offenses
articles_hidden.authors: Graham Farrell; John Roman
articles_hidden.abstract: Between 2020 and 2024, vehicle theft in the United States increased 40 percent. This study addresses this as a natural experiment, using a quasi-experimental design for causal inference to attribute the increase to theft of Kia and Hyundai vehicles manufactured without engine immobilizers. It is conservatively estimated that by the end of 2024 there were over 1.1 million excess vehicle thefts and over three hundred thousand excess co-occurring offenses including homicides, violence and other serious offenses. The evidence indicates that the withdrawal of situational crime prevention measures can increase crime and criminality and that the long-term national crime declines cannot be taken for granted. Additional implications are identified.

articles_hidden.title: A Stacked Deck: Ambition, Supply, Demand, and Women’s Access to Political Power
articles_hidden.authors: Mirya Holman; Lakshmi Iyer; Christina Wolbrecht
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do women remain underrepresented in positions of political power? A central challenge to answering this question is the difficulty in disentangling possible explanations, including women’s lack of interest or ambition, differences in women’s preparedness for political office, and discrimination against women by selectors. In this paper, we are uniquely able to investigate all three kinds of explanations simultaneously. Our unique dataset of applicants to appointed boards at the local level in the United States contains detailed professional, civic, and political information about the applicants, as well as about the boards to which they apply and the decisions of the appointers. We find that women are indeed less likely to apply for political positions, particularly powerful positions. The men and women who do apply are equally qualified. Despite these qualifications, women are less likely to be appointed to boards with more authority and power.

articles_hidden.title: Turning Votes into Power: New Women Voters and Access to Local Governance
articles_hidden.authors: Mirya Holman; Christina Wolbrecht; Lakshmi Iyer
articles_hidden.abstract: Do voting rights secure access to political power for previously excluded groups? We theorize that organizational capacity and ideological congruence with political regimes determine whether voting rights produce access to governance. We test this theory with the case of American women’s suffrage and a new measure of access to power: representation on local appointed boards. Using a new dataset of more than 30,000 appointees, hundreds of women’s organizations, and local political regimes in four major cities, we find that suffrage facilitates descriptive representation, but this connection is limited to when women are ideologically aligned with the political regime. Strength of women’s organizations is associated with women’s representation, but only before suffrage. Women’s representation remained concentrated on boards concerning children, arts, and welfare. Even with the vote, women’s access to governance depended on the preferences of the established male elite.

articles_hidden.title: Questionnaire Design and Rater Cognition in 360-Degree Performance Appraisal
articles_hidden.authors: Saber Mirzaei Ahandani; Simin Ebrahimi Lialekol
articles_hidden.abstract:
Questionnaire design may play an important yet underexamined role in shaping the quality of performance appraisal data. This study examines whether redesigning response formats in a 360-degree feedback system is associated with improvements in rating behavior, response quality, and psychometric consistency. Drawing on cognitive processing and response-process perspectives, we compare a traditional numeric Likert-format questionnaire with a redesigned format incorporating behaviorally descriptive response options, modified visual presentation, and variable response ordering.
Data were collected across two appraisal periods within a large production organization employing more than 25,000 individuals. A total of 26,672 questionnaires were distributed, and 18,621 responses were obtained for the evaluation of approximately 900 managers in different levels. Following the redesign, participation rates increased from 47% to 79%, and internal consistency reliability improved from Cronbach’s α = 0.902 to α = 0.939. Response distributions also became less concentrated in extreme categories and more evenly distributed across intermediate categories, indicating greater rating differentiation and reduced response bias.
These findings are consistent with the argument that behaviorally descriptive response formats encourage greater cognitive engagement and reduce reliance on heuristic responding during performance evaluation. The study contributes to performance appraisal and multisource feedback research by highlighting the role of questionnaire design in shaping response processes, rating behavior, and measurement quality. Together, the findings provide evidence compatible with the view that relatively small and scalable questionnaire design modifications may enhance cognitive engagement, improve measurement quality, and increase the validity and practical usefulness of organizational appraisal data.

articles_hidden.title: Seizing the Agenda: Polarization and Legislative Autonomy in Brazilian Presidentialism
articles_hidden.authors: Jamil Civitarese; Fabiano Guilherme Mendes Santos
articles_hidden.abstract: Brazilian coalitional presidentialism has long been read as a system in which the executive sets the agenda and the legislature holds a veto. We argue that, since the mid-2010s, the Congress has been building agenda-setting power. We account for the shift with a formal spatial framework in which a legislature weighs the cost of acquiring agenda power against the costs caused by the executive it expects to face. Two forces drive the investment: the rightward movement of a median legislator dissatisfied with the status quo and the recent polarization of the Executive, a partner that became too radical and costly to legislate with. Reading the record from Lula's first governments through Lula III, we show how the realignment of agenda power came to constrain the president who now has to both manage the coalition and to accommodate increasing policy demands from the legislature.

articles_hidden.title: Are geographical and socioeconomic contexts exchangeable? On simple means versus random effects in the study of health inequalities
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Merlo; Kani Khalaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Multilevel random-effects (RE) models are standard in social and geographical epidemiology. They rest on the assumption of exchangeability, which means that, before seeing the data, we have no reason to distinguish one group from another: group means become draws from one common distribution. RE models were developed for repeated measurements within individuals where a shared physiology underwrites the assumption, and partial pooling improves prediction. A silent transfer later applied the same machinery to schools, hospitals, neighbourhoods and, recently, to intersectional strata. There exchangeability fails twice: individuals are not repeated measurements of their group, and groups are social positions produced by directional forces such as racism, not draws from a common distribution. We review strict, conditional and tolerant readings of exchangeability and show that they agree: social and intersectional categories are not exchangeable, as this would paradoxically require the absence of the unjustified inequalities which are the very object of study. In many intersectional analyses, shrinkage erases the small and deviating strata, where inequality lives. Modelling injustice as dispersion around a mean domesticates rather than denounces it. For describing realised health inequalities we recommend Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA). Here, each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and uncertainty is reported openly rather than smoothed. RE models keep their legitimate uses, such as prediction, cluster-randomised trials and the propensity models of causal S-MAIHDA. Exchangeability is not a property of the software. It is a claim about the world, to be justified in every application.

articles_hidden.title: Six-Year Trends in LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Keith Robert Head
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of trends in LGBTQ+ youth mental health from 2019 through 2024, drawing on data from The Trevor Project’s annual national surveys. We examine five consistently measured indicators across six years of survey data including: suicidal ideation and attempts, discrimination due to SOGI (sexual orientation and gender identity), physical threats and harm exposure, and conversion therapy exposure and threats. Suicidal thoughts among LGBTQ+ youth rose to a significant peak before easing, while actual attempts showed a steady decline, especially among adolescents, yet younger teens remained disproportionately vulnerable throughout. Over the same period, discrimination remained persistently widespread, while reports of physical violence swung sharply but ended higher than at the outset, and exposure to conversion therapy spiked briefly during the pandemic era before settling back to its earlier yet still troubling level, highlighting the significant risks young LGBTQ+ youth and young adults face. The findings highlight continuing disparities, alongside small improvements in some areas. In conclusion, we summarize key insights and recommend actions to bolster mental health support, reduce stigma and victimization, and expand affirming resources for LGBTQ+ youth.

articles_hidden.title: The Latent Interview Protocol: Recovering Enacted Question Structure for Large-Scale Interview Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Zachary Lim
articles_hidden.abstract: Interview researchers increasingly work with large corpora for which traditional line-by-line coding is costly. Current proposed indexing strategies to make the corpus more manageable still require line-by-line indexing while assuming that the planned interview protocol accurately represents what was asked in practice. This article introduces the latent interview protocol—the recurring substantive questions that organize interviews as enacted, along with the pathways linking them—and LIPE, an open-source workflow that recovers this structure by combining sentence embeddings, density-based clustering, and researcher-guided refinement. Validated protocol questions are assembled into a corpus-level structure and used to retrieve local response blocks for downstream qualitative analysis. An application to 63 semi-structured interviews on mothering during COVID-19 shows that LIPE recovers most planned protocol questions, surfaces emergent lines of inquiry, and retrieves question-anchored responses with high precision and recall. The approach makes large-scale interview indexing more tractable while preserving interpretive control over analytic boundaries.

articles_hidden.title: Accessibility as Infrastructure: A Neurodivergent Led Model for Structural Communication Safety in Disability Support Systems
articles_hidden.authors: Neil McCarthy
articles_hidden.abstract:
Disabled people frequently experience communication collapse during distress, overwhelm or coercive control, producing indirect, fragmented, masked or delayed expression rather than clear verbal articulation. National Inquiries – including the Disability Royal Commission (2023) and the NDIS Review (2023) – demonstrate that current disability and safeguarding systems are misaligned with these communication realities, relying on speech, privacy, cognitive stability and narrative coherence at precisely the moments that these capacities fail. Communication Collapse is there a predictable, embodied response shaped by trauma, cognitive load and social misunderstanding, rather than and individual deficit.
This article introduces accessibility as infrastructure, a conceptual reframing that positions communication safety as a structural requirement of safeguarding systems. Drawing on disability studies and critical social theory, it argues that safeguarding infrastructures must be redesigned to recognise neurodivergent communication as valid and actionable, particularly during shutdown, overwhelm, masking, executive- function collapse and coercive control.
Within this framework, the article presents Althing, a neurodivergent-led, trauma informed safeguarding model engineered to remain usable during distress-state communication collapse. By supporting early, low-detail, indirect or delayed signals of harm, Althing addresses structural communication failures and aligns with national reform expectations for trauma-informed, low-demand safeguarding pathways. Although conceptual, the model offers a mature foundation, for future co-design, empirical evaluation, and state-level safeguarding innovation, demonstrating how accessibility as infrastructure can strengthen communication safety at the exact moments disabled people are least able to seek help.

articles_hidden.title: Start-up certification and prices: Evidence from markups and a statutory expiry in Italy
articles_hidden.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro Di Molfetta; Valeria Nortarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles_hidden.abstract: Italy grants registered innovative start-ups fee exemptions, investor tax relief and guaranteed credit, and removes that status sixty months after incorporation. This paper asks whether certification changes firms’ markups. Markups are estimated from a translog production function on 76,466 firm-years of certified start-ups, certified innovative SMEs and ordinary SMEs over 2015–2024. Certified firms price about 12 per cent below ordinary SMEs, but within firms the gap shrinks to 2 per cent and vanishes once persistence is modelled: registration selects firms rather than changing their pricing. Exploiting the statutory expiry, and a 2020 extension that shifted it by one year for adjacent cohorts, the loss of status leaves markups unchanged on average (2SLS −0.005, first-stage F = 750). An unsupervised partition shows this null combines falls of five to six per cent in capital- and materials-intensive firms with none elsewhere; regression learners and double machine learning confirm the central estimates.

articles_hidden.title: The Human Cost of Port-Centric Development in Dar es Salaam: Displacement, Congestion and Development Without Distribution
articles_hidden.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles_hidden.abstract: Dar es Salaam's transformation into a major regional logistics hub illustrates both the developmental promise and distributive risks of infrastructure-led growth. Modernisation of the port, expansion of inland container depots (ICDs), and investment in rail and road connectivity are essential to Tanzania's trade ambitions. Yet infrastructure expansion can generate a second problem when the costs of urban transformation are concentrated on communities living in strategically valuable locations. This article examines the relationship between port-centric development, displacement, compensation and urban congestion in Dar es Salaam, drawing particularly on the experience of Kurasini, the Chamazi community-led resettlement response, recent concerns surrounding ICD expansion, and evidence from the Msimbazi flood-risk project. The analysis argues that the central problem is not simply displacement without compensation but development without distribution. Compensation systems centred principally on recognised property interests can leave tenants and economically dependent residents without adequate assistance to reconstruct their livelihoods. At the same time, the conversion of residential land into logistics infrastructure can create substantial future economic value from which displaced communities have no continuing claim. The article further argues that the proliferation of ICDs within the metropolitan area risks transferring the congestion problem from the port to surrounding communities unless logistics planning is integrated with land-use and rail infrastructure. The appropriate policy response is therefore not to reject port expansion, but to redesign its distributional architecture so that affected populations participate in compensation, resettlement, employment, value creation and the longer-term development dividend.

articles_hidden.title: Jumping to Solutions? Bureaucratic Attention Allocation in Response to Negative Performance Feedback
articles_hidden.authors: Amandine Lerusse; Joris van der Voet; Wouter Lammers
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention allocation is fundamental for governance, policy-making and management in the public administration. The attention-based view highlights how informationally and cognitively constrained bureaucrats allocate their finite attention to diagnose performance shortfalls and identify potential solutions. This study informs bureaucratic attention allocation toward solution-generation and problem-definition using a multi-method approach that combines a laboratory eye-tracking experiment with vignette-based interviews among 41 bureaucrats. We find that bureaucrats process problem-related and solution-related information in sequence and allocate more attention to solution-generation than problem-definition. The interviews demonstrate how the bureaucratic decision context gives rise to role-based, substantive, strategic and aspirational justifications for these patterns in attention allocation. We offer important implications for public administration research, theory and practice, highlighting the ever-increasing demands on bureaucratic decision-makers’ scarce attentional resources.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional Intelligence and Money Anxiety:  “An Empirical Study on Financial Stress Coping Mechanisms Among  Generation Z
articles_hidden.authors: Deepika Rathi; Jainish Bhagat; RONAK AJAYKUMAR MEHTA; Komal Sharma
articles_hidden.abstract:
Generation Z has entered adulthood under a distinctive combination of economic precarity, 
digital financial exposure, and social-media-amplified comparison, making financial stress a 
defining feature of their early financial socialisation. While emotional intelligence (EI) is well 
established in organisational and educational psychology as a predictor of stress regulation, 
its role in shaping how young adults respond to money-related anxiety remains 
underexamined in the financial-behaviour literature. This paper develops and specifies a 
structural model linking Emotional Intelligence, Money (Financial) Anxiety, and Coping 
Mechanisms among Generation Z, incorporating Financial Self-Efficacy as a boundary 
condition and Financial Literacy as a control variable. Drawing on the ability model of 
emotional intelligence (Salovey & Mayer, 1990), the transactional model of stress and coping 
(Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), and the financial-anxiety literature (Archuleta et al., 2013), 
seven hypotheses are proposed and a measurement model is specified using established, 
validated scales — the Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test (Schutte et al., 1998), 
the Financial Anxiety Scale (Archuleta et al., 2011), and the Brief COPE (Carver, 1997). A 
Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) approach is proposed as the 
Page 1 of 23 
analytical strategy, given its suitability for exploratory, prediction-oriented models with 
formative and reflective constructs. The paper details the full measurement instrument, 
sampling strategy, and a step-by-step PLS-SEM assessment protocol (measurement model 
validity, structural model evaluation, mediation and moderation testing, and PLS predict) so 
that the study can proceed directly to data collection and empirical estimation. [Once data 
collection is complete, this abstract should be revised to state the actual sample size, key 
path coefficients, and principal findings.]

articles_hidden.title: Grensoverschrijdend bevoegdheidsvacuüm in de sociale zekerheid.
articles_hidden.authors: Eric Messa
articles_hidden.abstract: Empirische en kwantificeerbare systeem-audit van het grensoverschrijdend bevoegdheidsvacuüm in de sociale zekerheid tussen België en Nederland (Verordening EG 883/2004). Bevat forensische verslaglegging van meer dan 200 overheidsinteracties, deconstructie van de En/En-paradox en een concrete beleidssynthese met drie infrastructurele bouwstenen.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Developing Indicators of Environmental Sustainability for Kathmandu, Nepal
articles_hidden.authors: Ambika P. Adhikari
